Darien’s Proposition Analyses, Descriptions, and Recommendations
• Prop. 1 – Bond Bucks for Diverse Housing – Yes
This year the propositions ballot starts us off easy with this one that provides $11.25 billion to
support much needed affordable housing of various kinds – including rental, condo, and manufactured
housing – for an impressively (and thoughtful) diverse range of low-income people, including veterans,
low-income folks, and the unhoused. Like a number of this year’s props., it has no “official” oppo-
nents. In our state with among the highest housing costs in the country, Prop. 1 isn’t a difficult choice.
A few opponents object, in general, to bond measures – esp. to general obligation bonds, like
this one, which the general taxpayers pay for. However, while the long-lasting burden and interest
costs of a bond, just as any loan, has interest costs – this bond is for housing. A durable, long-term
investment like housing is an expenditure suitable for a bond – just as you might seek a 30-year loan
for a home purchase. Additionally, of course, there’s a huge need for more affordable housing; this
bond money will help address the lack of funding for it.
A spurious further objection some make to Prop. 1 is that they don’t want to provide money for
affordable housing without “addressing” high construction costs. What? With $11 billion we’re
somehow supposed to address construction costs – things like tariffs, diesel prices, and trade
breakdowns (to say nothing of the lack of immigrant labor)?
I’ll add an important point concerning California construction costs. These costs are partly
related to much needed environmental requirements (that also save residents money!), such as ample
insulation, special windows / glass able to filter out (excessive) sunlight, white (heat-reflecting) roofs,
wildfire-safe materials, etc.
Darien's Guide to the California Ballot Propositions: November 2026 Elections 3 of 15
Supporters, in addition to the below, include construction organizations, Habitat For Humanity
California community organizations; housing and apartment building / company advocates; and
veterans’ groups.
Yes – CTA, CFT, Lgue, FCL, LCC, ACLU
No – Ref
• Prop. 2 – Reserving More State Funds for Bad Years – Yes
I hope we’ve all learned from California experience that state revenues are subject to large
swings, from booming one year to plummeting tax revenues the next. So, more than I had realized in
the past, a reserve fund is needed.
Prop. 2 would increase the amount to go into the Rainy Day Fund from the current maximum of
10% of general tax revenues to up to 20%. Importantly, like other recent revenue propositions, Prop.
2 language also exempts these set-aside funds from the “Gann Limit” constraints. So let’s better
understand the Gann Limit!
Voters are called upon to follow the way the Gann Limit works, because that limit not only
greatly affects the ability of the Legislature to budget appropriately, but this year, the Gann Limit
also comes up in multiple props. on this ballot, including Props. 40 and 41.
This limit on state spending came as a followup on the (property tax-limiting) Prop. 13
enthusiasm, through an overwhelmingly approved 1979 proposition. Under the Gann Limit, the state is
stiffly limited in how much it can allocate each year in most areas (regardless of need – and even
including how much can be put in the Rainy Day reserve). What if the state has “excess funds”,
beyond what the Gann Limit allows it to spend? Then the excess has to be returned to the taxpayers
within two years (even if, within that time, those funds are desperately needed). If you’re too low-
income to pay taxes, you won’t get any of that refund.
I’ll note that the original Gann Limit initiative (and, generally, subsequent initiative
propositions) did not benefit from the (potentially!) informed discussion of the Legislature, which could
have identified and addressed serious built-in budget conflicts or other short-sightedness. In response
to the Gann Limit, multiple props. for new state revenue sources (usually, specific taxes) in the years
since 1979 have instead dictated their own limits and specific percentages of state revenues that must
go to their program or area, as favored within the given prop. (Usually, those propositions also exempt
themselves from the Gann Limit, because that limit would not allow their favored program(s) to spend
more than a restricted amount of the new revenues.)
So, due to the Gann Limit, our state budget has often been unable to allocate desirable levels of
funds to various human-needs programs, even high priority ones. The extremity of the current situation
is outlined in a very readable May 2022 “Monthly Report from State Controller Betty T. Yee”, which
goes into more detail about this quandary. For example, (as of ‘22) “the state is required to spend
$1.60 for each dollar in unanticipated revenues at or above the [Gann Limit]” (emphasis added).
Darien's Guide to the California Ballot Propositions: November 2026 Elections 4 of 15
In these boom-bust times, I see the Rainy Day reserve not as (per opponent accusations) a
“slush fund for politicians” but as a benefit to the people of California by setting aside more money in
good years to help maintain needed state programs through economic downturns.
Yes – Dem, P&F, FCL, Lgue
No – Ref, Rep
• Prop. 3 – Funds Ed. and Health Care by Extends Existing Tax on High Incomes – Yes
Since the initial high-incomes tax prop. was passed in 2012 and renewed and extended in 2016,
it’s the wealthiest 1% in Calif. who have had to pay 98% of this somewhat higher income tax. (It’s
only the top 2% of California tax filers who are subject to the tax, at all.) The resulting tax revenues,
by going toward the state education spending requirement, enable the state to use other revenue to pay
for health care and other programs for working families. All that is especially important at a time when
DC is cutting health care funds.
This proposition simply proposes that this supplemental income tax, in place for almost 15
years, should be allowed to continue – rather than expire in 2030 (as provided in the current law).
So I think this prop. is another easy choice: A defeat of Prop. 3 would reduce the
progressiveness of CA’s income tax structure – as well as reduce state revenues by billions of dollars.
A finance-focused report by the non-partisan California Budget & Policy Center notes that the
expiration of this tax “would likely lead to significant budget shortfalls… funding for essential state
services would be put in jeopardy.”
I’m taking this “ed. funding prop.” as an opportunity for some short education on Calif’s ed.
funding. In the past, Californians had been very low in how much it spent on K-12 ed., compared to
other states – ranking near the bottom. Even through 2022, our wealthy state – with many ed.
challenges due to our state’s wide income disparities, many English learners, and more – spent less
than the national average on K-12 education!
However, our ranking has increased fairly steadily since back in 2010-11, when our state ed.
spending was 50th in the country! In the 2022-23 school year (the most recent data available) we
jumped to 13th – after being 28th the year before. (Sadly, part of that increase has been due to other
states cutting income taxes and reducing school funding!)
How did that K-12 funding change occur? Well, in 2012 the extra income tax on high incomes
passed That extra income tax is paid by millionaires and billionaires – not by the poor nor upper-
middle-class earners nor even “small” businesses. (And, after almost 15 years, those millionaires and
billionaires remain in California.) Also, remember: Much of the generation of business wealth depends
on the availability of well educated workers.
Even as CA has spent more for ed., the money spent has increased only slightly as a percentage
of CA’s GDP, one of many funding aspects noted in a helpful EdSource article. Our percentage is well
behind other highly urbanized states like NY and Illinois. And it shows: Class sizes in California are
still among the highest in the country.
The California Budget & Policy Center’s info- and chart-filled article (mentioned above) shows
why continuing this tax is so important, mentioning that “the current top tax rates have become a
Darien's Guide to the California Ballot Propositions: November 2026 Elections 5 of 15
critical source of funding for education, health care, and other state services…”. (The article also gives
helpful reminders and background info on the provisions, workings, and state budget effects of the
voter-approved 1988 Prop. 98, the minimum state education funding guarantee, that establishes an
annual minimum state funding level for public education, including community colleges.)
Incidentally, this prop. contains a “poison pill” – as Prop. 41 does – in relation to other props.
on the same topic: If “this measure receives a greater number of affirmative votes than a measure
deemed to be in conflict with it, the provisions of this measure shall prevail in their entirety, and the
other measure or measures shall be null and void,” (quoting from Section 5 of Prop. 3). So, if passing
with more votes, such a poison pill totally invalidate the other same-topic measure, even if the other
passes (with fewer votes). In the case of Prop. 3, there isn’t another prop. on the same topic, but I
mention this “poison pill” provision here to explain it early on and to show the idea comes up often.
Voters made a good choice to create this extra income tax in 2012 and 2016. A yes on Prop. 3
supports that existing tax to continue as long as needed to fund CA public schools (and, by bringing in
ed. revenues to meet Prop. 98 minimums, other crucial state programs).
Yes – Dem, CTA, Rep, P&F, Cour, CNA, FCL, PPar, ACLU, CFT
No – Rep, Jarv, Ref
• Prop. 4 – Allows Public Financing of Election Campaign – Yes
Campaign funding has changed a lot since 1988, when voters passed Prop. 73 to (generally)
prohibit public financing of election campaigns. However, the reality of campaign dollars has changed
dramatically – specially since the Supreme Court in 2010 decided Citizens United, throwing open
corporate funding to campaigns, and, in 2014, also lifted restrictions on PAC contributions to
campaigns. Even local campaigns now see spending in the millions of dollars.
Some contend that it’s too expensive for state and local governments to publicly finance
candidates, but how much more expensive is it for us, the public, if almost the only thing campaigns
can depend on is Big Money interests? With the option of public funding (and important restrictions
on funded ones), voters in some cities may choose to pay through their taxes rather than pay through
their city’xs decisions – when those decisions benefit Big Money donors and harm most of the people!
It’s true: I really don’t like my tax payments helping pay for the campaign of some candidate I
oppose! However, I don’t see public financing as a way to fund “an opponent”; I see it as a way to
fund a system of genuine elections, opening them to candidates representing the diversity of income
ranges and public views. How many lies are coming into my mail (and texts) funded by Big Money?
Maybe you’re not persuaded yet, but – for future situations – will you let municpalities make
their own choices? Prop. 4 doesn’t require public funding, but it allows it; a jurisdiction could choose
to provide the basic funding to enable a competitive campaign. At the same time it sets up
requirements and limitations on how public funds for campaigns can be used, as well as basic criteria
for candidates to qualify. As Robert Reich says in support of 4, "It's time to restore power to California
voters, not wealthy donors.."
Yes – Dem, P&F, FCL, ACLU, Lgue, Cour, ComC
No – Jarv, Ref, Rep
Darien's Guide to the California Ballot Propositions: November 2026 Elections 6 of 15
• Prop. 5 – Seeks to Improve the Recall System – Yes
If you remember the 2021 recall attempt against Governor Newsom, you might already have
some sense of the problems with the current recall process. In ‘21, jumping at the chance to get
elected governor with far less than a majority vote, 46 candidates filed to run in the recall election!
This prop. makes sensible changes in the recall law, especially for how to fill the seat of a
recalled official. Depending on the office, in a successful recall the seat would be filled either in a
subsequent election or by an appointment by the governor, or – in the case of a gubernatorial recall –
by the lieutenant governor occupying the seat.
In theory, the target of a recall is supposed to be a corrupt, criminal, or incompetent official.
Yet, with a well funded signature campaign, the recall can be used for strictly political purposes – in
place of a regular election. Part of the motivation for such misuse is the current system: If the recall
gets a majority vote, then, the same election chooses the replacement – without a majority vote! That
replacement needs only more votes than any of the other candidates to win. For example, with over 40
competing candidates, the number of votes to win could actually be a surprisingly low minority
percentage.
Calif. voters benefitted from the work of activists in the Progressive Era to gain this ability to
recall officials, but, now that this flaw (and potential political advantages) of the current recall process
has been detected, it is likely to be abused more often – and at a high price tag for each election. The
Newsom recall effort was only the fourth gubernatorial recall election in U.S. history, but it was the
second in Calif. It was slightly short of 100 years after the 1911 enactment of the CA recall law, we
had the 2003 Gray Davis recall, and the anti-Newsom effort was fewer than 20 years after that.
Before the next recall effort, I think it’s a good thing that the Legislature has given us the chance
to make these needed changes in the recall process.
Yes – P&F, FCL, Lgue, Cour, ACLU, ComC, Dem
No – Jarv, Ref, Rep
• Prop. 37 – A Bond for Loans for Middle-Income Folks to Buy Newly Built Homes – No
Oh, my! In my view, this is a text book example of the hazards of a well intended initiative,
seeking to solve an important problem, in contrast to a measure put on the ballot by the Legislature.
This initiative seeks to help folks buy homes in costly Calif. and to encourage new home construction,
thus increasing housing supply and, possibly, lowering the cost of housing overall. But the League of
Women Voters of CA raises some concerns about Prop. 37 well worth noting. If this prop. had come
through the Legislature, hearings and testimony from many points of view could have contributed to
legislative negotiations, leading to provisions that might address at least some of these concerns.
A big issue is that Prop. 37 entirely lacks a way to focus this funding on those facing the greatest
barriers, such as first-time or first-generation home buyers. Instead, most potential benefits would
likely go to those who already are socially advantaged, reinforcing existing racial and economic gaps.
Thosse factors come together in non-white neighborhoods, where historic (and current) racist housing
discrimination has greatly inhibited increases in home values, thus limiting the asset-value gains for
Darien's Guide to the California Ballot Propositions: November 2026 Elections 7 of 15
houses in white neighborhoods. Even in middle-class black neighborhoods, home owners have seen
much lower value increases. As a result, parents have less ability to help their children pay for a home.
In addition to that, while expanding home affordability is a goal of Prop. 37, the home
purchases it supports may not actually be so affordable. Prop. 37 doesn’t lower families’ total costs.
Instead, their Prop. 37 loans, for up to 17% of the down payment, would be second mortgages. With

If you remember the 2021 recall attempt against Governor Newsom, you might already have
some sense of the problems with the current recall process. In ‘21, jumping at the chance to get
elected governor with far less than a majority vote, 46 candidates filed to run in the recall election!

recalled official. Depending on the office, in a successful recall the seat would be filled either in a
subsequent election or by an appointment by the governor, or – in the case of a gubernatorial recall –
by the lieutenant governor occupying the seat.

competing candidates, the number of votes to win could actually be a surprisingly low minority
percentage.

recall officials, but, now that this flaw (and potential political advantages) of the current recall process

had the 2003 Gray Davis recall, and the anti-Newsom effort was fewer than 20 years after that.

Darien's Guide to the California Ballot Propositions: November 2026 Elections 1 of 15
Darien's Guide to the California Ballot Propositions: November 2026 Elections (rev. 1)
I provide this guide earlier than usual, knowing that we have entered a new era of voting early.
However, while voting somewhat early is often a good idea, please, beware of “rushing to judgment”.
It is nothing unusual for more (and verified) info to come out closer to the elections. Take the time you
need to inform yourself. (See the end of my guide for helpful voter resources.)
I apologize for the long Guide this time, what with 14 propositions, mostly complicated. Read
what you need – and, then, maybe a little more! There’s a lot to understand in this year’s batch.
Please do vote, especially on the important "down ballot" – local and state – races and issues.
Since there are fewer voters for those, your vote is worth proportionately more. Also, you often have
better access to or knowledge of local issues. If you don't vote, your voice goes unheard.
What is important now is to confirm that you are registered to vote! All registered CA
voters should have received their ballots by now. You can check at https://voterstatus.sos.ca.gov/, and
register today, online, if you’re not listed. (After the October 19 deadline, you can still register, even
on the day of the elections, to cast a provisional ballot – which may or may not be counted.)
Voting early at ballot dropoff locations (find full lists of both online at your county’s elections
office) is likely the best approach, for many reasons. For one, you don’t have to rely on the (currently,
not so reliable) US Postal Service. If you do mail in your vote, allow ample time before the deadline
and be sure to read and follow the directions carefully! Many mail-in votes are discarded for basic
errors. (I don’t endorse candidates, but I’ll say that the Sup. of Instruction race is worth your care.)
The Short Version (My “Bare” Recommendations)
• Prop. 1 – Bond Bucks for Diverse Housing – Yes
• Prop. 2 – Reserving More State Funds for Bad Years – Yes
• Prop. 3 – Funds Ed. and Health Care by Extending the Existing Tax on High Incomes – Yes
• Prop. 4 – Allows Public Financing of Election Campaign – Yes
• Prop. 5 – A Chance to Improve the Recall System – Yes
• Prop. 37 – Bond for Loans to Build New Middle-Income Homes – No
• Prop. 38 – Deceptive Bond for Immunology Research – No
• Prop. 39 – Unnecessary & Obstructive ID Requirements for Voting – No
• Prop. 40 – Why There’s So Much You Need to Know About the Wealth Tax – Yes
• Prop. 41 – To Make the 1979 Gann Limit Live on and on – No
• Prop. 42 – No Wealth Taxes and No Retroactive Ones (so no Prop. 40) – No
• Prop. 43 – A Tough Two-Thirds Vote Requirement on Local Tax Measures – No
• Prop. 44 – Do Most of Us Know Enough About Health Clinics to Vote Wisely? – No
• Prop. 45 – Reduces Environmental Review Protections – No
Struggling to remember all this? I have some helps!
Darien's Guide to the California Ballot Propositions: November 2026 Elections 2 of 15
• With five, alive! Yes on 1-5.
• Vote yes on the single digit propositions (1-5) and no on all the two-digit ones except 40.
• Yes on 40; no on 41 and 42.

(When any of these groups is not listed in the yes or no under a prop., it did not take a position.)

Darien’s Proposition Analyses, Descriptions, and Recommendations
• Prop. 1 – Bond Bucks for Diverse Housing – Yes
This year the propositions ballot starts us off easy with this one that provides $11.25 billion to
support much needed affordable housing of various kinds – including rental, condo, and manufactured
housing – for an impressively (and thoughtful) diverse range of low-income people, including veterans,
low-income folks, and the unhoused. Like a number of this year’s props., it has no “official” oppo-
nents. In our state with among the highest housing costs in the country, Prop. 1 isn’t a difficult choice.
A few opponents object, in general, to bond measures – esp. to general obligation bonds, like
this one, which the general taxpayers pay for. However, while the long-lasting burden and interest
costs of a bond, just as any loan, has interest costs – this bond is for housing. A durable, long-term
investment like housing is an expenditure suitable for a bond – just as you might seek a 30-year loan
for a home purchase. Additionally, of course, there’s a huge need for more affordable housing; this
bond money will help address the lack of funding for it.
A spurious further objection some make to Prop. 1 is that they don’t want to provide money for
affordable housing without “addressing” high construction costs. What? With $11 billion we’re
somehow supposed to address construction costs – things like tariffs, diesel prices, and trade
breakdowns (to say nothing of the lack of immigrant labor)?
I’ll add an important point concerning California construction costs. These costs are partly
related to much needed environmental requirements (that also save residents money!), such as ample
insulation, special windows / glass able to filter out (excessive) sunlight, white (heat-reflecting) roofs,
wildfire-safe materials, etc.
Darien's Guide to the California Ballot Propositions: November 2026 Elections 3 of 15
Supporters, in addition to the below, include construction organizations, Habitat For Humanity
California community organizations; housing and apartment building / company advocates; and
veterans’ groups.
Yes – CTA, CFT, Lgue, FCL, LCC, ACLU
No – Ref
• Prop. 2 – Reserving More State Funds for Bad Years – Yes
I hope we’ve all learned from California experience that state revenues are subject to large
swings, from booming one year to plummeting tax revenues the next. So, more than I had realized in
the past, a reserve fund is needed.
Prop. 2 would increase the amount to go into the Rainy Day Fund from the current maximum of
10% of general tax revenues to up to 20%. Importantly, like other recent revenue propositions, Prop.
2 language also exempts these set-aside funds from the “Gann Limit” constraints. So let’s better
understand the Gann Limit!
Voters are called upon to follow the way the Gann Limit works, because that limit not only
greatly affects the ability of the Legislature to budget appropriately, but this year, the Gann Limit
also comes up in multiple props. on this ballot, including Props. 40 and 41.
This limit on state spending came as a followup on the (property tax-limiting) Prop. 13
enthusiasm, through an overwhelmingly approved 1979 proposition. Under the Gann Limit, the state is
stiffly limited in how much it can allocate each year in most areas (regardless of need – and even
including how much can be put in the Rainy Day reserve). What if the state has “excess funds”,
beyond what the Gann Limit allows it to spend? Then the excess has to be returned to the taxpayers
within two years (even if, within that time, those funds are desperately needed). If you’re too low-
income to pay taxes, you won’t get any of that refund.
I’ll note that the original Gann Limit initiative (and, generally, subsequent initiative
propositions) did not benefit from the (potentially!) informed discussion of the Legislature, which could
have identified and addressed serious built-in budget conflicts or other short-sightedness. In response
to the Gann Limit, multiple props. for new state revenue sources (usually, specific taxes) in the years
since 1979 have instead dictated their own limits and specific percentages of state revenues that must
go to their program or area, as favored within the given prop. (Usually, those propositions also exempt
themselves from the Gann Limit, because that limit would not allow their favored program(s) to spend
more than a restricted amount of the new revenues.)
So, due to the Gann Limit, our state budget has often been unable to allocate desirable levels of
funds to various human-needs programs, even high priority ones. The extremity of the current situation
is outlined in a very readable May 2022 “Monthly Report from State Controller Betty T. Yee”, which
goes into more detail about this quandary. For example, (as of ‘22) “the state is required to spend
$1.60 for each dollar in unanticipated revenues at or above the [Gann Limit]” (emphasis added).
Darien's Guide to the California Ballot Propositions: November 2026 Elections 4 of 15
In these boom-bust times, I see the Rainy Day reserve not as (per opponent accusations) a
“slush fund for politicians” but as a benefit to the people of California by setting aside more money in
good years to help maintain needed state programs through economic downturns.
Yes – Dem, P&F, FCL, Lgue
No – Ref, Rep
• Prop. 3 – Funds Ed. and Health Care by Extends Existing Tax on High Incomes – Yes
Since the initial high-incomes tax prop. was passed in 2012 and renewed and extended in 2016,
it’s the wealthiest 1% in Calif. who have had to pay 98% of this somewhat higher income tax. (It’s
only the top 2% of California tax filers who are subject to the tax, at all.) The resulting tax revenues,
by going toward the state education spending requirement, enable the state to use other revenue to pay
for health care and other programs for working families. All that is especially important at a time when
DC is cutting health care funds.
This proposition simply proposes that this supplemental income tax, in place for almost 15
years, should be allowed to continue – rather than expire in 2030 (as provided in the current law).
So I think this prop. is another easy choice: A defeat of Prop. 3 would reduce the
progressiveness of CA’s income tax structure – as well as reduce state revenues by billions of dollars.
A finance-focused report by the non-partisan California Budget & Policy Center notes that the
expiration of this tax “would likely lead to significant budget shortfalls… funding for essential state
services would be put in jeopardy.”
I’m taking this “ed. funding prop.” as an opportunity for some short education on Calif’s ed.
funding. In the past, Californians had been very low in how much it spent on K-12 ed., compared to
other states – ranking near the bottom. Even through 2022, our wealthy state – with many ed.
challenges due to our state’s wide income disparities, many English learners, and more – spent less
than the national average on K-12 education!
However, our ranking has increased fairly steadily since back in 2010-11, when our state ed.
spending was 50th in the country! In the 2022-23 school year (the most recent data available) we
jumped to 13th – after being 28th the year before. (Sadly, part of that increase has been due to other
states cutting income taxes and reducing school funding!)
How did that K-12 funding change occur? Well, in 2012 the extra income tax on high incomes
passed That extra income tax is paid by millionaires and billionaires – not by the poor nor upper-
middle-class earners nor even “small” businesses. (And, after almost 15 years, those millionaires and
billionaires remain in California.) Also, remember: Much of the generation of business wealth depends
on the availability of well educated workers.
Even as CA has spent more for ed., the money spent has increased only slightly as a percentage
of CA’s GDP, one of many funding aspects noted in a helpful EdSource article. Our percentage is well
behind other highly urbanized states like NY and Illinois. And it shows: Class sizes in California are
still among the highest in the country.
The California Budget & Policy Center’s info- and chart-filled article (mentioned above) shows
why continuing this tax is so important, mentioning that “the current top tax rates have become a
Darien's Guide to the California Ballot Propositions: November 2026 Elections 5 of 15
critical source of funding for education, health care, and other state services…”. (The article also gives
helpful reminders and background info on the provisions, workings, and state budget effects of the
voter-approved 1988 Prop. 98, the minimum state education funding guarantee, that establishes an
annual minimum state funding level for public education, including community colleges.)
Incidentally, this prop. contains a “poison pill” – as Prop. 41 does – in relation to other props.
on the same topic: If “this measure receives a greater number of affirmative votes than a measure
deemed to be in conflict with it, the provisions of this measure shall prevail in their entirety, and the
other measure or measures shall be null and void,” (quoting from Section 5 of Prop. 3). So, if passing
with more votes, such a poison pill totally invalidate the other same-topic measure, even if the other
passes (with fewer votes). In the case of Prop. 3, there isn’t another prop. on the same topic, but I
mention this “poison pill” provision here to explain it early on and to show the idea comes up often.
Voters made a good choice to create this extra income tax in 2012 and 2016. A yes on Prop. 3
supports that existing tax to continue as long as needed to fund CA public schools (and, by bringing in
ed. revenues to meet Prop. 98 minimums, other crucial state programs).
Yes – Dem, CTA, Rep, P&F, Cour, CNA, FCL, PPar, ACLU, CFT
No – Rep, Jarv, Ref
• Prop. 4 – Allows Public Financing of Election Campaign – Yes
Campaign funding has changed a lot since 1988, when voters passed Prop. 73 to (generally)
prohibit public financing of election campaigns. However, the reality of campaign dollars has changed
dramatically – specially since the Supreme Court in 2010 decided Citizens United, throwing open
corporate funding to campaigns, and, in 2014, also lifted restrictions on PAC contributions to
campaigns. Even local campaigns now see spending in the millions of dollars.
Some contend that it’s too expensive for state and local governments to publicly finance
candidates, but how much more expensive is it for us, the public, if almost the only thing campaigns
can depend on is Big Money interests? With the option of public funding (and important restrictions
on funded ones), voters in some cities may choose to pay through their taxes rather than pay through
their city’xs decisions – when those decisions benefit Big Money donors and harm most of the people!
It’s true: I really don’t like my tax payments helping pay for the campaign of some candidate I
oppose! However, I don’t see public financing as a way to fund “an opponent”; I see it as a way to
fund a system of genuine elections, opening them to candidates representing the diversity of income
ranges and public views. How many lies are coming into my mail (and texts) funded by Big Money?
Maybe you’re not persuaded yet, but – for future situations – will you let municpalities make
their own choices? Prop. 4 doesn’t require public funding, but it allows it; a jurisdiction could choose
to provide the basic funding to enable a competitive campaign. At the same time it sets up
requirements and limitations on how public funds for campaigns can be used, as well as basic criteria
for candidates to qualify. As Robert Reich says in support of 4, "It's time to restore power to California
voters, not wealthy donors.."
Yes – Dem, P&F, FCL, ACLU, Lgue, Cour, ComC
No – Jarv, Ref, Rep
Darien's Guide to the California Ballot Propositions: November 2026 Elections 6 of 15
• Prop. 5 – Seeks to Improve the Recall System – Yes
If you remember the 2021 recall attempt against Governor Newsom, you might already have
some sense of the problems with the current recall process. In ‘21, jumping at the chance to get
elected governor with far less than a majority vote, 46 candidates filed to run in the recall election!
This prop. makes sensible changes in the recall law, especially for how to fill the seat of a
recalled official. Depending on the office, in a successful recall the seat would be filled either in a
subsequent election or by an appointment by the governor, or – in the case of a gubernatorial recall –
by the lieutenant governor occupying the seat.
In theory, the target of a recall is supposed to be a corrupt, criminal, or incompetent official.
Yet, with a well funded signature campaign, the recall can be used for strictly political purposes – in
place of a regular election. Part of the motivation for such misuse is the current system: If the recall
gets a majority vote, then, the same election chooses the replacement – without a majority vote! That
replacement needs only more votes than any of the other candidates to win. For example, with over 40
competing candidates, the number of votes to win could actually be a surprisingly low minority
percentage.
Calif. voters benefitted from the work of activists in the Progressive Era to gain this ability to
recall officials, but, now that this flaw (and potential political advantages) of the current recall process
has been detected, it is likely to be abused more often – and at a high price tag for each election. The
Newsom recall effort was only the fourth gubernatorial recall election in U.S. history, but it was the
second in Calif. It was slightly short of 100 years after the 1911 enactment of the CA recall law, we
had the 2003 Gray Davis recall, and the anti-Newsom effort was fewer than 20 years after that.
Before the next recall effort, I think it’s a good thing that the Legislature has given us the chance
to make these needed changes in the recall process.

content.text:
se, even if the Leg. had approved some such prop. (the CA Democratic Party
Darien's Guide to the California Ballot Propositions: November 2026 Elections 10 of 15
supports it), with Governor Newsom opposing it (along with most other tax increases), it wouldn’t have
become law. In other words, sometimes only an initiative is able to grapple with a hot issue.
Prop. 40 taxes walth to pay for health care. So far, few politicians (nor most others) have
offered real ways to reduce health care costs (since they’re mostly ignoring Single Payer Healthcare –
which the public tends to support!). (Do you want to know more about why? Cal Matters has a good
(fairly short!) article about a 181-page report on that!) And health care costs keep on increasing.
Worse yet, due to Trump’s huge federal health care cuts, CA faces millions in costs in 2027 –
and, possibly, beyond. So a healthcare workers’ union, Service Employees International Union-United
Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW), put together this proposal to keep the workers their jobs and
our state its healthcare funding: Tax the very rich (who got Trump tax cuts)! And – since the rich
manage to avoid most income taxes – this tax is based on the value of their assets, their wealth.
In response, the threatened billionaires have a massive campaign (at nearly $200 million)
against 40 – including putting the competing Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. If either of those passes
with more votes than Prop. 40, then their provisions would block 40 – even if 40 gets a majority vote.
And also some non-billionaires oppose 40. Will it drive wealthy people and businesses out of
California, reducing our tax base and annual state budget revenues? Good question, but I suggest CA
can manage well enough. CA offers many advantages to individuals and businesses (even beyond
beautiful natural wonders and reasonable weather): many well educated people, a location that attracts
employees, good freeways, international ports, commercial centers, etc. Would the wealthy leave Calif.
over this one-time tax? That’s likely the biggest question on 40. And no one knows the answer,
We do know what 40 woulf enact, and that is only one thing: a “wealth tax”, at 5%, on
Californians whose net worth exceeded $1 billion as of 1/1/26. That net worth would be measured
based on assest like stocks, bonds, cars, privately owned businesses, intellectual property, and art and
other collections. Entirely excluded from the calculation and tax would be real estate (already covered
under property taxes) and nearly all pensions and retirement accounts. (Nearly all? Well, if you’ve
got a Roth with over $10 million, that could count.) Only some 200 Californians would be subject to
the tax (out of about 34 million Californians) – not likely you, not likely ever.
The resulting revenues – some tens of billions of dollars – would go 90% to “health care
services for the public” and 10% to other public-friendly services.
A lot of this info is in your very helpful Official Voter Information Guide. Not in there are the
reservations that some progressives have and their objections to aspects of 40. They note that other
state programs need funds, too – 90% for healthcare only? However, this measure does give the
Legislature some flexibility in the kinds of healthcare spending, and the Prop. 40 money frees us other
revenues for other kinds of programs, beyond what is under the remaining 10%. Others point to con-
cerning collateral effects: sowing division in the labor movement between different sectors, instead of
seeking a more collaborative approach. And, further – once Prop. 40 funds are used up – will there be
any money for currently existing programs, like ob-gyn services from Planned Parenthood?
Will the Legislature seek to amend the tax after passage, as 40 allows and some are concerned
about? Of course, legislative flexibility is something helpful that initiatives usually lack, so that’s
Darien's Guide to the California Ballot Propositions: November 2026 Elections 11 of 15
helpful. In any case, the Leg. membes worry about re-election; I expect they’ll be very careful not to
alienate their voters with either a weaker tax or one that extends to more people or other assets.
Then again, if 40 proves to be surprisingly popular, and even successful, this one-time tax might
open up the public imagination! The idea of wealth taxes could enter the realm of serious political
discourse, and that could be what really scares the very wealthy.
I do wish for us to be able to maintain people’s access to health care in California, which is not
only an ethical position but also a sound public health practice (and, often, a money saver – vs. ER
visits and care after something is severe). And I don’t see other promising options on the near horizon.
In my philosophy of governance, I support 40 because it funds a robust society by taxing the
wealth that society helps generate, with all our (costly) infrastructure,. And I believe Calif. has the
capacity to generate new wealth.
At the same time, how feasible is Prop. 40? On the one hand is the challenge of accurately
assessing individuals’ wealth, and on the other hand are the many legal challenges the wealthy are
likely to assay.
What if 40 does not pass (or passes but with fewer votes than Props. 41 or 42, so that it’s
invalidated by the “poison pill” in those two props)? Or, even if it does go into effect, it may get tied
up in the courts for years. If so my wish may become another challenging project. But let’s try!
Yes – P&F, Dem, Cour, CFT, CNA, UHW (of course!)
No – CTA, PPar, Jarv, Ref, CofC, Rep
• Prop. 41 – To Make the 1979 Gann Limit Live on and on – No
Overall, 41 is targetted at 40 – at the least, to foment confusion but also to stop 40 if 41 gets
more votes. Beyond that, 41 would bind future voters by restricting the possibilities to enact flexible
responses to future state financial needs.
Remember the Gann Limit? I talked about that fairly extensively above, under Prop. 2. Please
review that, because I think I presented a strong case that the Gann Limit has become harmful. In my
view (apparently supported by former Calif. Controller Betty Yee’s 2022 report). That limit makes the
CA budget almost unworkable; it would be a mistake to stiffen its effects!
Nonetheless, Prop. 41 basically seeks to give the 1979 Gann Limit a transfusion of fresh blood;
41 would require all future propositions to be bound by that limit.
The Gann constraints are from an era that sought to severely limit government expenditures,
even when the government had the revenues to support them. However, I believe more voters now
appreciate government programs. In more recent years, propositions seeking special income sources
(I.e., taxes) have been careful to include in their language an exemption from the Gann Limit. (For
example, Prop. 40 does so – as it would have to, since its revenue would go way beyond what that limit
allows.) The fact that so many other props. have also done so – and yet have often been approved by
the voters – is an indication that the severe restrictions of the Gann Limit are no longer realistic.
As you can see from the supporter and opponent list, some folks do want to return to that era of
fewer government programs. Their attitude about such programs is reflected in the actual language of
Darien's Guide to the California Ballot Propositions: November 2026 Elections 12 of 15
the prop., which at one point (in (d) of section 1 – bold added) states, “Before asking taxpayers to pay
even more of their hard-earned money to support programs that are ineffective...”. It’s likely that
those same folks would oppose Prop. 40, and Prop. 41 serves those interests with a “poison pill”. (I
explained more about poison pills near the end of the Prop. 3 discussion.) If 41 passes with more votes
than 40, then all of 40 is invalid.
Prop. 41 also includes a requirement for a state audit on any tax proposals and/or initiatives.
The audit will look for possible spending cuts. If such propositions are defeated – or don’t even qualify
for the ballot – the state would be stuck with paying millions a year for the required audits.
It’s all a bad idea!
No – P&F, FCL, Dem, UHW, Lgue, ACLU
Yes – Jarv, Ref
• Prop. 42 – No Wealth Taxes and No Retroactive Ones (so no Prop. 40) – No
I’m assuming you’re familiar with Prop. 40 (or see above!). Remember how it imposes a tax on
certain kinds of wealth (not retirement accounts!)? Prop. 42 would forbid all that: no wealth taxes.
Remember how 40 also imposes its tax on that wealth as of 1/1/26 – a retroactive date (so wealthy
folks can’t easily get around the tax)? Prop. 42 would forbid that, too: no retroactive taxes.
Prop. 40 isn’t the sole target. If this prop. passes, no wealth taxes of any kind may be
considered for California. Why, before any attempts, would voters rule out an entire class of taxation?
The financial support for 42 – nearly $100 million raised so far (per Cal Matters) – comes
mostly from the same billionaires opposing Prop. 40, although some other groups (generally
conservative), especially profession-related ones (peace officers, firefighters, building and
construction), are also supporting 42.
While we’ve learned that nothing is impossible in politics, the claim of an alleged threat to
pensions and retirement accounts is a red herring.

For almost any measure, a 2/3 requirement to pass means it hardly ever passes! We’ve already
seen that effect in a number of proposals by local governments (which already suffer from that 2/3
barrier). In a heart-breaking case this spring, the defeated measure got (as I recall) over 65% support.
Prop. 43 would extend the 2/3 bar to local citizen-driven special tax ballot initiatives.
In other words, this measure would seek to suppress citizen-driven efforts by discarding the
maority-rule basis of most democratic decision. I believe that, in a democracy, one must have
compelling reason (such as important minority rights) to consider requiring more than a simple
majority to make most decisions. So what is Prop. 43’s compelling argument?

look at who Prop. 43 would benefit.
The pro argument goes on to say it “protects homeowners”, because “Some cities now charge
real estate transfer taxes as high as 6%”. Well, it’s true that San Francisco, with the highest transfer tax
rate (or one of the highest – the helpful chart at https://taxo.com/transfer-tax-california-2026/ shows
only selected city rates) levies up to 6% in transfer taxes, but thats on homes selling at $25 million and
above! Also, that S.F. rate drops to 2.25% for home under $10 million and over $5 million. (At $5
million and below, it’s a very low .75% – and continues on down.)
The next highest (selected) city rate on the chart is in L.A., at 5.5% for homes over $10 million.
Like the handful of other cities that do tax at more than minimal rates, L.A. rates rapidly graduate
down. In other words, the pro argument doesn’t lie, but it’s certainly irrelevant to struggling families!

wealthy people! But in our democracy, we’re not supposed to be ruled by the (one-third) minority!

• Prop. 45 – Reduces Environmental Review Protections – No
This ballot proposal wants to revise the environmental review process,. In California and most
other states, we see numerous examples of adverse environmental consequences from inadequately
reviewed projects, from housing to water projects. At the same time, valuable projects, even essential
ones, can be delayed by and altered in the course of mandated California Environmental Quality Act
(CEQA) environmental reviews, driving up costs.
In the age of data centers and other potentially harmful projects, do we really want to weaken
environmental review and protections?
It isn’t easy or quick to seek to find an agreeable middle ground between concerned people and
project developers. Allowing enough time to identify problems and work out options is important,
even though it may delay work. Also, project planners can better understand local concerns by
consulting and collaborating with affected residents and communities. But when we look at the
specific and basic aspects of Prop. 45, it lacks these foundational aspects – as well as others.
What about time for public participation, careful studies, and analysis? Under 45, very large
projects will be pushed along with the same timeline as smaller ones.
As for community consultation, the prop. requires (per the Official Voter Information Guide –
emphasis added). “the agency and applicant to consult about the project only with California native
tribes that have been formally recognized by the federal government. (Current law requires
consultation with a wider range of tribes.)” That referenced wider range of tribes could include any of
the approximately 160 tribes in California – out of over whom only about 109 are formally
recognized. That leaves out about 32%, nearly one-third, who would not be consulted about what
happens on their ancestral lands!

helpful. In any case, the Leg. membes worry about re-election; I expect they’ll be very careful not to

open up the public imagination! The idea of wealth taxes could enter the realm of serious political

wealth that society helps generate, with all our (costly) infrastructure,. And I believe Calif. has the
capacity to generate new wealth.

assessing individuals’ wealth, and on the other hand are the many legal challenges the wealthy are
likely to assay.
What if 40 does not pass (or passes but with fewer votes than Props. 41 or 42, so that it’s
invalidated by the “poison pill” in those two props)? Or, even if it does go into effect, it may get tied
up in the courts for years. If so my wish may become another challenging project. But let’s try!

• Prop. 41 – To Make the 1979 Gann Limit Live on and on – No

more votes. Beyond that, 41 would bind future voters by restricting the possibilities to enact flexible
responses to future state financial needs.
Remember the Gann Limit? I talked about that fairly extensively above, under Prop. 2. Please
review that, because I think I presented a strong case that the Gann Limit has become harmful. In my
view (apparently supported by former Calif. Controller Betty Yee’s 2022 report). That limit makes the
CA budget almost unworkable; it would be a mistake to stiffen its effects!
Nonetheless, Prop. 41 basically seeks to give the 1979 Gann Limit a transfusion of fresh blood;
41 would require all future propositions to be bound by that limit.
The Gann constraints are from an era that sought to severely limit government expenditures,
even when the government had the revenues to support them. However, I believe more voters now
appreciate government programs. In more recent years, propositions seeking special income sources
(I.e., taxes) have been careful to include in their language an exemption from the Gann Limit. (For
example, Prop. 40 does so – as it would have to, since its revenue would go way beyond what that limit
allows.) The fact that so many other props. have also done so – and yet have often been approved by
the voters – is an indication that the severe restrictions of the Gann Limit are no longer realistic.
As you can see from the supporter and opponent list, some folks do want to return to that era of
fewer government programs. Their attitude about such programs is reflected in the actual language of

the prop., which at one point (in (d) of section 1 – bold added) states, “Before asking taxpayers to pay
even more of their hard-earned money to support programs that are ineffective...”. It’s likely that
those same folks would oppose Prop. 40, and Prop. 41 serves those interests with a “poison pill”. (I
explained more about poison pills near the end of the Prop. 3 discussion.) If 41 passes with more votes
than 40, then all of 40 is invalid.
Prop. 41 also includes a requirement for a state audit on any tax proposals and/or initiatives.
The audit will look for possible spending cuts. If such propositions are defeated – or don’t even qualify
for the ballot – the state would be stuck with paying millions a year for the required audits.
It’s all a bad idea!

Yes – Jarv, Ref

certain kinds of wealth (not retirement accounts!)? Prop. 42 would forbid all that: no wealth taxes.
Remember how 40 also imposes its tax on that wealth as of 1/1/26 – a retroactive date (so wealthy
folks can’t easily get around the tax)? Prop. 42 would forbid that, too: no retroactive taxes.
Prop. 40 isn’t the sole target. If this prop. passes, no wealth taxes of any kind may be
considered for California. Why, before any attempts, would voters rule out an entire class of taxation?

mostly from the same billionaires opposing Prop. 40, although some other groups (generally
conservative), especially profession-related ones (peace officers, firefighters, building and
construction), are also supporting 42.

pensions and retirement accounts is a red herring.
This prop. is on the ballot particularly to oppose Prop. 40: Like 41, Prop. 42 has a “poison pill”.
(See explanation near the end of the Prop. 3 discussion.)

Yes – Jarv, Ref

For almost any measure, a 2/3 requirement to pass means it hardly ever passes! We’ve already
seen that effect in a number of proposals by local governments (which already suffer from that 2/3
barrier). In a heart-breaking case this spring, the defeated measure got (as I recall) over 65% support.
Prop. 43 would extend the 2/3 bar to local citizen-driven special tax ballot initiatives.
In other words, this measure would seek to suppress citizen-driven efforts by discarding the
maority-rule basis of most democratic decision. I believe that, in a democracy, one must have
compelling reason (such as important minority rights) to consider requiring more than a simple
majority to make most decisions. So what is Prop. 43’s compelling argument?

In the prop’s pro argument, they speak of (my emphasis) “California families are struggling”.
But 43 certainly is not prioritizing struggling families (who often want to support the services local
governmentsts might provide – fire departments, road repair, local schools, etc.) Let’s take a closer
look at who Prop. 43 would benefit.
The pro argument goes on to say it “protects homeowners”, because “Some cities now charge
real estate transfer taxes as high as 6%”. Well, it’s true that San Francisco, with the highest transfer tax
rate (or one of the highest – the helpful chart at https://taxo.com/transfer-tax-california-2026/ shows
only selected city rates) levies up to 6% in transfer taxes, but thats on homes selling at $25 million and
above! Also, that S.F. rate drops to 2.25% for home under $10 million and over $5 million. (At $5
million and below, it’s a very low .75% – and continues on down.)
The next highest (selected) city rate on the chart is in L.A., at 5.5% for homes over $10 million.
Like the handful of other cities that do tax at more than minimal rates, L.A. rates rapidly graduate
down. In other words, the pro argument doesn’t lie, but it’s certainly irrelevant to struggling families!
I hope these examples make clear that this prop. is written primarily to protect the interests of
wealthy people! But in our democracy, we’re not supposed to be ruled by the (one-third) minority!
As the rebuttal to the pro argument says (slightly paraphrased), Prop. 43 doesn’t cut your taxes,
it cuts the power of your vote.
No – P&F, FCL, Dem, Lgue, Ref, ACLU, CFT
Yes – Jarv, Rep
• Prop. 44 – Do Most of Us Know Enough About Health Clinics to Vote Wisely? – No
What do most of us know about budgets for health clinics? Not much! And, to me, that’s a
reason to object to, or at least be highly suspicious of, props. like this one. It reminds me of the
(defeated) prop. about dialysis clinics – and for good reason! That prop. – like this one – was also put
on the ballot through the efforts of the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare
Workers West (SEIU-UHW).
SEIU-UHW chooses to use initiatives to push for its goals, and that tactic can be good, when it
serves a wider public interest, or bad. SEIU-UHW has used ballot initiatives as a strategy to pressure
its opponents to negotiate on union issues or to otherwise address healthcare worker issues. They’re
the ones who put Prop. 40 on the ballot – challenging the legislative silence on wealth taxes.
Since 2012 they’ve sponsored 48 ballot initiatives, and – although most have failed – the union
has also won some gains for its workers. So I think it’s important to look more at that history when
considering the value of any particular one of their initiatives.
Going back to the 2022 dialysis proposition, I objected then that most of us don’t know much
about the proper operations of a dialysis clinic, so those details aren’t appropriate to be made law
through ballot measure. Why should medical decisions be made by unknowledgeable voters?
I have the same basic objection to Prop. 44.
In both cases, the changes proposed by the prop. sound sort of reasonable on their face; that’s
how SEIU-UHW is able to get people to sign their initiative petitions! In the case of Prop. 44, it calls
for Federally Qualified Health Care Centers (FQHCC), providing care as “safety-net clinics”, to spend

90% of their annual revenue on health care services. That sounds like a good thing to push for.

the percentage varies. The FQHCC say many of them could go out of business under Prop. 44, leading
to underserved communities with even fewer options.
We elect legislators to work full time (well, sort of!) to hear and consider expert input on the
details of the subjects of laws. I don’t think it’s a good way to run our state, to have voters trying to
decide on laws for areas in which we are unavoidably ignorant. Are clinic executives paid too much?
How should we know the “market rates” for such executive pay, let alone whatever special
circumstances might influence that pay or any other non-health care services costs?
Ideally, the Leg. does its job and makes needed laws. Initiatives are supposed to come in when
the Leg. falls short in an area. But there are many highly technical areas where it makes no sense to
ask the public to hammer out details!
The dialysis prop. was defeated, and I think this one should be. We can’t stop SEIU-UHW from
trying to put initiatives on the ballot, but we don’t have to vote for every one. Better yet, we can have
fewer bad props. by not signing initiative petitions on subjects we don’t know well!

Yes – P&F, UHW, Ref

other states, we see numerous examples of adverse environmental consequences from inadequately
reviewed projects, from housing to water projects. At the same time, valuable projects, even essential
ones, can be delayed by and altered in the course of mandated California Environmental Quality Act

In the age of data centers and other potentially harmful projects, do we really want to weaken
environmental review and protections?

project developers. Allowing enough time to identify problems and work out options is important,

consulting and collaborating with affected residents and communities. But when we look at the
specific and basic aspects of Prop. 45, it lacks these foundational aspects – as well as others.

projects will be pushed along with the same timeline as smaller ones.

emphasis added). “the agency and applicant to consult about the project only with California native
tribes that have been formally recognized by the federal government. (Current law requires
consultation with a wider range of tribes.)” That referenced wider range of tribes could include any of
the approximately 160 tribes in California – out of over whom only about 109 are formally
recognized. That leaves out about 32%, nearly one-third, who would not be consulted about what
happens on their ancestral lands!

Additionally, to identify an approach with reduced harms, it can be very helpful to consider
various options to reach a project’s goal. Yet 45 “Allows the applicant to develop only one project
alternative for the agency to consider. (Current law requires the agency—not the applicant—to
develop and consider multiple project alternatives that could reduce environmental impacts.)”
(Again, per the Official Voter Information Guide, with bold added.)
Remember in Prop. 44, when I decried measures in areas that most of us don’t know so much
about? I have serious doubts that specifying the details of environmental review is an area that is
appropriate for a ballot measure. Somehow, people sign these initiative petitions, but that doesn’t mean
we have to go along with passing a long, detailed initiative that’s not appropriate for a voter decsion!
Also, as the Friends Committee on Legislation of California brings up, it may be possible that
this prop. would “dramatically weaken environmental reviews of proposed data centers.”
No – P&F, FCL, Lgue, CFT
Yes – Jarv, Ref, CoC, Rep

90% of their annual revenue on health care services. That sounds like a good thing to push for.
However, currently, FQHCC report spending an average of about 80% on health care services, although
the percentage varies. The FQHCC say many of them could go out of business under Prop. 44, leading
to underserved communities with even fewer options.
We elect legislators to work full time (well, sort of!) to hear and consider expert input on the
details of the subjects of laws. I don’t think it’s a good way to run our state, to have voters trying to
decide on laws for areas in which we are unavoidably ignorant. Are clinic executives paid too much?
How should we know the “market rates” for such executive pay, let alone whatever special
circumstances might influence that pay or any other non-health care services costs?
Ideally, the Leg. does its job and makes needed laws. Initiatives are supposed to come in when
the Leg. falls short in an area. But there are many highly technical areas where it makes no sense to
ask the public to hammer out details!
The dialysis prop. was defeated, and I think this one should be. We can’t stop SEIU-UHW from
trying to put initiatives on the ballot, but we don’t have to vote for every one. Better yet, we can have
fewer bad props. by not signing initiative petitions on subjects we don’t know well!
No – FCL, Jarv, PPar, Dem, Lgue
Yes – P&F, UHW, Ref
• Prop. 45 – Reduces Environmental Review Protections – No
This ballot proposal wants to revise the environmental review process,. In California and most
other states, we see numerous examples of adverse environmental consequences from inadequately
reviewed projects, from housing to water projects. At the same time, valuable projects, even essential
ones, can be delayed by and altered in the course of mandated California Environmental Quality Act
(CEQA) environmental reviews, driving up costs.
In the age of data centers and other potentially harmful projects, do we really want to weaken
environmental review and protections?
It isn’t easy or quick to seek to find an agreeable middle ground between concerned people and
project developers. Allowing enough time to identify problems and work out options is important,
even though it may delay work. Also, project planners can better understand local concerns by
consulting and collaborating with affected residents and communities. But when we look at the
specific and basic aspects of Prop. 45, it lacks these foundational aspects – as well as others.
What about time for public participation, careful studies, and analysis? Under 45, very large
projects will be pushed along with the same timeline as smaller ones.
As for community consultation, the prop. requires (per the Official Voter Information Guide –
emphasis added). “the agency and applicant to consult about the project only with California native
tribes that have been formally recognized by the federal government. (Current law requires
consultation with a wider range of tribes.)” That referenced wider range of tribes could include any of
the approximately 160 tribes in California – out of over whom only about 109 are formally
recognized. That leaves out about 32%, nearly one-third, who would not be consulted about what
happens on their ancestral lands!
Darien's Guide to the California Ballot Propositions: November 2026 Elections 15 of 15
Additionally, to identify an approach with reduced harms, it can be very helpful to consider
various options to reach a project’s goal. Yet 45 “Allows the applicant to develop only one project
alternative for the agency to consider. (Current law requires the agency—not the applicant—to
develop and consider multiple project alternatives that could reduce environmental impacts.)”
(Again, per the Official Voter Information Guide, with bold added.)
Remember in Prop. 44, when I decried measures in areas that most of us don’t know so much
about? I have serious doubts that specifying the details of environmental review is an area that is
appropriate for a ballot measure. Somehow, people sign these initiative petitions, but that doesn’t mean
we have to go along with passing a long, detailed initiative that’s not appropriate for a voter decsion!
Also, as the Friends Committee on Legislation of California brings up, it may be possible that
this prop. would “dramatically weaken environmental reviews of proposed data centers.”
No – P&F, FCL, Lgue, CFT
Yes – Jarv, Ref, CoC, Rep

Background
California has a housing afordability
crisis. Despite recent stabilization,
California housing costs have risen
sharply since the COVID pandemic
in 2020. According to the California
Legislative Analyst’s Ofce (LAO),
California’s mid-tier home prices are
now more than double the national
average, while entry-level home prices
are 30% above the national average.2
In response, the state has increased
its focus on afordable housing,
almost tripling the number of homes
it subsidizes over the past six years.3
The state ofers nonprofts and
housing developers inexpensive loans
and grants for new housing units,
which then must be rented or sold to
low-income Californians.
To fund construction and housing
costs, California has historically used
general obligation (GO) bonds. The
state repays GO bonds over time
through its General Fund. Since 1990,
California has repeatedly used GO
bonds to pay for housing assistance,4
often coupling housing subsidies
with support for military veterans.
Most recently, in 2024, Californians
approved a $6.38 billion housing bond
measure, with $2 billion specifcally
dedicated to afordable housing.5
Authorizes Bonds for Afordable Housing Programs
Purpose
This measure, proposed by the legislature, would authorize $11.25 billion in general obligation
bonds to fund afordable housing and homeownership programs, with repayment coming from
the state’s General Fund over time.1
Figure 1. Spending Breakdown of Proposition 122
Afordable Multifamily Housing Programs $7.2 billion

Infrastructure Programs $500 million

Local Pilot Programs $200 million
Proposal
Proposition 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in GO bonds, with the funding
divided into diferent housing programs.
As Figure 1 shows, the majority of Proposition 1 bond funding ($7.2 billion) would go to
acquiring, building, or renovating rental housing, such as apartment buildings. Other
funds would assist low- and moderate-income households, veterans, and farm workers
in purchasing housing. The measure would also fund infrastructure projects such as
water, sewage, and parks necessary for new housing, and it would provide funds to
California public universities to assist with student housing.
The LAO estimates that the bonds could be used toward 40,000 multifamily rental units,
2,500 units for farmworkers, and about 1,200 beds for university students. The funds
would also help as many as 40,000 households, including about 2,100 veterans, with
homeownership.6
Fiscal Impact
Veterans who participate in the housing program would make a monthly payment to
the state; as a result, the state would need to repay only $10 billion instead of the full
$11.25 billion.7 The LAO predicts the cost to the General Fund would be $500-600 million
annually for the next 25 years.8 Including interest and adjusting for infation, the state
would ultimately pay 15% more than if it paid upfront. Additionally, the state estimates
an increase in administrative costs to accommodate the expansion of housing programs.
However, these costs are covered in the pre-planned bond spending.9

02
CALIFORNIA Strengthens State Rainy Day Fund
Purpose
Proposition 2 is a constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by the legislature, that would
strengthen California’s rainy day fund by increasing the cap on how much money the state can set
aside each year. The measure also would make it easier for the state to use tax revenues to pay
down debt.1
Research Assistant: Arushi Goyal ’28
Background
The Budget Stabilization Account (BSA), also known as the rainy day fund,
is California’s largest state budget reserve. The state uses this fund to save
money when revenues are strong and to reduce cuts to public services when
revenues are weak. This fund is especially important in California because
the state’s revenues depend heavily on taxes on the incomes of high-income
residents, which can vary greatly from year to year, thus creating “boom and
bust” budget cycles.2
The state automatically sets aside 1.5% of General Fund revenues each year.
It also sets aside “excess” capital gains revenues in years when they exceed
8% of General Fund tax revenues. Generally, the state deposits 50% of these
set-aside revenues into the rainy day fund and uses the other 50% to pay
down certain types of state debt. Currently, the state can use these excess
revenues to pay down only pension and retiree health debt, and cannot make
extra payments on other forms of debt such as unemployment insurance
debt and certain education and Medi-Cal obligations. This requirement is
set to end in 2030, after which some or all of that money may be put into the
rainy day fund.3
Under current law, the rainy day fund is capped at 10% of estimated General
Fund tax revenues. When this limit is reached, any dollars that would other-
wise go into the rainy day fund must be spent on infrastructure.4 California
also has a constitutional spending cap, commonly known as the Gann Limit,
which was passed by the voters as Proposition 4 in 1979 and which capped
spending at 1978-79 levels, adjusted each year for infation and population
growth.5 Most spending counts toward this limit, including money deposited
into reserves. Withdrawals from state reserves during budget emergencies
do not count against the Gann Limit, but when state revenues are high, the
spending cap can limit California’s ability to build its reserves.
The rainy day fund can be tapped only during a budget emergency. The gover-
nor must formally declare an emergency before deposits can be reduced or
suspended or money can be withdrawn. The declaration can come late in the
fscal year, sometimes after the legislature’s deadline to pass a budget. This
can leave lawmakers passing a budget that assumes an emergency before
one is ofcially declared.6
In the state legislature the vote to place this measure on the ballot was 59-8
in the Assembly and 29-2 in the Senate.7
Proposal
If approved, Proposition 2 would:8
• Double the BSA cap from 10% to 20% of
estimated General Fund tax revenues.
• Set aside more General Fund revenues during
“boom” years.
• Expand the types of state debt that may be paid
down with set-aside revenues.
• Extend the debt-paydown requirement by 10
years, to 2039-40.
• Change how rainy day fund and other deposits
count toward the Gann Limit.
• Create a simpler process for declaring a budget
emergency.
Fiscal Impact
The LAO estimates that Proposition 2 would
increase the state’s budget reserves. Having more
money in the BSA would make it easier for the
state to balance its budget during downturns. The
measure could also cause the state to pay down
debt more aggressively.9

CALIFORNIA Makes permanent existing voter-approved income tax rates for high-income
Californians
Purpose
Proposition 3, a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature, would make permanent
the existing voter-approved income tax rates on high-income Californians, which are currently set
to expire in 2031, and to allocate the resulting revenues to K-12 schools and community colleges.1
Research Assistant: Shayan Abbasi ’29
Background
The personal income tax is California’s largest revenue source.
It provides more than half of the state’s General Fund, the state’s
main operating account, which funds public services including
education, health care, and corrections. The tax applies to most
types of income, such as wages, salaries, interest, and capital gains,
which the state treats as ordinary income. California’s income tax
rates are progressive, starting low and gradually rising for taxpayers
with higher incomes.2
Over the past two decades, voters have approved or extended tax
increases on high-income earners several times.
• In 2004, voters approved Proposition 63, a 1% surcharge on
income taxes of residents with taxable income of more than
$1 million.
• In 2012, amid the fscal challenges brought on by the Great
Recession, California voters approved Proposition 30, which
temporarily increased income tax rates on high-income
taxpayers to fund state services and stave of cuts to public
education. This measure raised the top marginal rate from
9.3% to 12.3%. Combined with the 1% surcharge, the state’s
income tax on the highest earners became 13.3% — the highest
in the nation.
• In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55, which extended these
higher income tax rates through 2030, with 63% voting yes.3
The top 2% of California taxpayers pay these higher rates (10.3% or
higher), and these taxpayers now pay about half of all state income
taxes. Since Proposition 30’s initial passage in 2012, the measure
has raised more than $104 billion for schools and other state
services and has become a foundational part of the state’s budget
and its Rainy Day Fund.4
Figure 1 shows the income tax rates for Californians under current
law, which will continue if Prop. 3 passes, and how the rates for
high-earners will decrease after 2030 if Prop. 3 is rejected. 5

Proposal
Proposition 3, ofcially titled “The California Children’s Education
and Health Care Protection Act of 2026,” would amend Section 36 of
Article XIII of the California Constitution to make the higher income
tax rates established by Proposition 30 of 2012 permanent instead of
letting them expire in 2030.6 The measure does not change the exist-
ing rates or brackets, which adjust for infation each year, and it does
not increase taxes on individuals earning less than about $371,000 or
couples earning less than about $743,000 in today’s dollars.7
Revenues would continue to be deposited into the Education
Protection Account, with 89% of the education funds allocated to
K-12 school districts, county ofces of education, and charter schools,
and 11% allocated to community college districts.8 Local school
boards would retain the authority to decide how the revenues are
spent, provided that spending determinations are made in open
session of a public meeting, and none of the funds may be used for
administrator salaries or other administrative costs. Each district
must annually publish online an accounting of how much money it
received and how it was spent, and the funds are subject to an annual
independent audit, with elected ofcials facing prosecution and
criminal penalties if they misuse them.9 The measure also increases
the General Fund revenues available for health care, budget reserves,
and other programs, and it directs that in certain years a portion of
surplus revenues, up to a maximum of $2 billion in a single fscal
year, be allocated to health care services for children and their families
through Medi-Cal.10
Fiscal Impact
If the current income tax rates are allowed
to expire as scheduled, the California
Legislative Analyst’s Ofce (LAO) estimates
that the state would lose between $5 billion
and $15 billion in annual revenue beginning
in 2031.11 For context, this year the state
plans to spend about $250 billion from
the General Fund, with about half of that
spending going to schools, community
colleges, and the state’s public universities,
and about another one-third going to health
and human services programs, mainly
Medi-Cal, the state’s low-income health
insurance program.12

CALIFORNIA Strengthens State Rainy Day Fund
Purpose
Proposition 2 is a constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by the legislature, that would
strengthen California’s rainy day fund by increasing the cap on how much money the state can set
aside each year. The measure also would make it easier for the state to use tax revenues to pay
down debt.1
Research Assistant: Arushi Goyal ’28
Background
The Budget Stabilization Account (BSA), also known as the rainy day fund,
is California’s largest state budget reserve. The state uses this fund to save
money when revenues are strong and to reduce cuts to public services when
revenues are weak. This fund is especially important in California because
the state’s revenues depend heavily on taxes on the incomes of high-income
residents, which can vary greatly from year to year, thus creating “boom and
bust” budget cycles.2
The state automatically sets aside 1.5% of General Fund revenues each year.
It also sets aside “excess” capital gains revenues in years when they exceed
8% of General Fund tax revenues. Generally, the state deposits 50% of these
set-aside revenues into the rainy day fund and uses the other 50% to pay
down certain types of state debt. Currently, the state can use these excess
revenues to pay down only pension and retiree health debt, and cannot make
extra payments on other forms of debt such as unemployment insurance
debt and certain education and Medi-Cal obligations. This requirement is
set to end in 2030, after which some or all of that money may be put into the
rainy day fund.3
Under current law, the rainy day fund is capped at 10% of estimated General
Fund tax revenues. When this limit is reached, any dollars that would other-
wise go into the rainy day fund must be spent on infrastructure.4 California
also has a constitutional spending cap, commonly known as the Gann Limit,
which was passed by the voters as Proposition 4 in 1979 and which capped
spending at 1978-79 levels, adjusted each year for infation and population
growth.5 Most spending counts toward this limit, including money deposited
into reserves. Withdrawals from state reserves during budget emergencies
do not count against the Gann Limit, but when state revenues are high, the
spending cap can limit California’s ability to build its reserves.
The rainy day fund can be tapped only during a budget emergency. The gover-
nor must formally declare an emergency before deposits can be reduced or
suspended or money can be withdrawn. The declaration can come late in the
fscal year, sometimes after the legislature’s deadline to pass a budget. This
can leave lawmakers passing a budget that assumes an emergency before
one is ofcially declared.6
In the state legislature the vote to place this measure on the ballot was 59-8
in the Assembly and 29-2 in the Senate.7
Proposal
If approved, Proposition 2 would:8
• Double the BSA cap from 10% to 20% of
estimated General Fund tax revenues.
• Set aside more General Fund revenues during
“boom” years.
• Expand the types of state debt that may be paid
down with set-aside revenues.
• Extend the debt-paydown requirement by 10
years, to 2039-40.
• Change how rainy day fund and other deposits
count toward the Gann Limit.
• Create a simpler process for declaring a budget
emergency.
Fiscal Impact
The LAO estimates that Proposition 2 would
increase the state’s budget reserves. Having more
money in the BSA would make it easier for the
state to balance its budget during downturns. The
measure could also cause the state to pay down
debt more aggressively.9
