CALIFORNIA Makes permanent existing voter-approved income tax rates for high-income
Californians
Purpose
Proposition 3, a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature, would make permanent
the existing voter-approved income tax rates on high-income Californians, which are currently set
to expire in 2031, and to allocate the resulting revenues to K-12 schools and community colleges.1
Research Assistant: Shayan Abbasi ’29
Background
The personal income tax is California’s largest revenue source.
It provides more than half of the state’s General Fund, the state’s
main operating account, which funds public services including
education, health care, and corrections. The tax applies to most
types of income, such as wages, salaries, interest, and capital gains,
which the state treats as ordinary income. California’s income tax
rates are progressive, starting low and gradually rising for taxpayers
with higher incomes.2
Over the past two decades, voters have approved or extended tax
increases on high-income earners several times.
• In 2004, voters approved Proposition 63, a 1% surcharge on
income taxes of residents with taxable income of more than
$1 million.
• In 2012, amid the fscal challenges brought on by the Great
Recession, California voters approved Proposition 30, which
temporarily increased income tax rates on high-income
taxpayers to fund state services and stave of cuts to public
education. This measure raised the top marginal rate from
9.3% to 12.3%. Combined with the 1% surcharge, the state’s
income tax on the highest earners became 13.3% — the highest
in the nation.
• In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55, which extended these
higher income tax rates through 2030, with 63% voting yes.3
The top 2% of California taxpayers pay these higher rates (10.3% or
higher), and these taxpayers now pay about half of all state income
taxes. Since Proposition 30’s initial passage in 2012, the measure
has raised more than $104 billion for schools and other state
services and has become a foundational part of the state’s budget
and its Rainy Day Fund.4
Figure 1 shows the income tax rates for Californians under current
law, which will continue if Prop. 3 passes, and how the rates for
high-earners will decrease after 2030 if Prop. 3 is rejected. 5

Proposal
Proposition 3, ofcially titled “The California Children’s Education
and Health Care Protection Act of 2026,” would amend Section 36 of
Article XIII of the California Constitution to make the higher income
tax rates established by Proposition 30 of 2012 permanent instead of
letting them expire in 2030.6 The measure does not change the exist-
ing rates or brackets, which adjust for infation each year, and it does
not increase taxes on individuals earning less than about $371,000 or
couples earning less than about $743,000 in today’s dollars.7
Revenues would continue to be deposited into the Education
Protection Account, with 89% of the education funds allocated to
K-12 school districts, county ofces of education, and charter schools,
and 11% allocated to community college districts.8 Local school
boards would retain the authority to decide how the revenues are
spent, provided that spending determinations are made in open
session of a public meeting, and none of the funds may be used for
administrator salaries or other administrative costs. Each district
must annually publish online an accounting of how much money it
received and how it was spent, and the funds are subject to an annual
independent audit, with elected ofcials facing prosecution and
criminal penalties if they misuse them.9 The measure also increases
the General Fund revenues available for health care, budget reserves,
and other programs, and it directs that in certain years a portion of
surplus revenues, up to a maximum of $2 billion in a single fscal
year, be allocated to health care services for children and their families
through Medi-Cal.10
Fiscal Impact
If the current income tax rates are allowed
to expire as scheduled, the California
Legislative Analyst’s Ofce (LAO) estimates
that the state would lose between $5 billion
and $15 billion in annual revenue beginning
in 2031.11 For context, this year the state
plans to spend about $250 billion from
the General Fund, with about half of that
spending going to schools, community
colleges, and the state’s public universities,
and about another one-third going to health
and human services programs, mainly
Medi-Cal, the state’s low-income health
insurance program.12

Purpose
Proposition 3, a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature, would make permanent
the existing voter-approved income tax rates on high-income Californians, which are currently set
to expire in 2031, and to allocate the resulting revenues to K-12 schools and community colleges.1
Research Assistant: Shayan Abbasi ’29
Background
The personal income tax is California’s largest revenue source.
It provides more than half of the state’s General Fund, the state’s
main operating account, which funds public services including
education, health care, and corrections. The tax applies to most
types of income, such as wages, salaries, interest, and capital gains,
which the state treats as ordinary income. California’s income tax
rates are progressive, starting low and gradually rising for taxpayers
with higher incomes.2
Over the past two decades, voters have approved or extended tax
increases on high-income earners several times.
• In 2004, voters approved Proposition 63, a 1% surcharge on
income taxes of residents with taxable income of more than
$1 million.
• In 2012, amid the fscal challenges brought on by the Great
Recession, California voters approved Proposition 30, which
temporarily increased income tax rates on high-income
taxpayers to fund state services and stave of cuts to public
education. This measure raised the top marginal rate from
9.3% to 12.3%. Combined with the 1% surcharge, the state’s
income tax on the highest earners became 13.3% — the highest
in the nation.
• In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55, which extended these
higher income tax rates through 2030, with 63% voting yes.3
The top 2% of California taxpayers pay these higher rates (10.3% or
higher), and these taxpayers now pay about half of all state income
taxes. Since Proposition 30’s initial passage in 2012, the measure
has raised more than $104 billion for schools and other state
services and has become a foundational part of the state’s budget
and its Rainy Day Fund.4
Figure 1 shows the income tax rates for Californians under current
law, which will continue if Prop. 3 passes, and how the rates for
high-earners will decrease after 2030 if Prop. 3 is rejected. 5

Proposition 3, ofcially titled “The California Children’s Education
and Health Care Protection Act of 2026,” would amend Section 36 of
Article XIII of the California Constitution to make the higher income
tax rates established by Proposition 30 of 2012 permanent instead of
letting them expire in 2030.6 The measure does not change the exist-
ing rates or brackets, which adjust for infation each year, and it does
not increase taxes on individuals earning less than about $371,000 or
couples earning less than about $743,000 in today’s dollars.7
Revenues would continue to be deposited into the Education
Protection Account, with 89% of the education funds allocated to
K-12 school districts, county ofces of education, and charter schools,
and 11% allocated to community college districts.8 Local school
boards would retain the authority to decide how the revenues are
spent, provided that spending determinations are made in open
session of a public meeting, and none of the funds may be used for
administrator salaries or other administrative costs. Each district
must annually publish online an accounting of how much money it
received and how it was spent, and the funds are subject to an annual
independent audit, with elected ofcials facing prosecution and
criminal penalties if they misuse them.9 The measure also increases
the General Fund revenues available for health care, budget reserves,
and other programs, and it directs that in certain years a portion of
surplus revenues, up to a maximum of $2 billion in a single fscal
year, be allocated to health care services for children and their families
through Medi-Cal.10

If the current income tax rates are allowed

plans to spend about $250 billion from

spending going to schools, community
colleges, and the state’s public universities,
and about another one-third going to health
and human services programs, mainly
Medi-Cal, the state’s low-income health
insurance program.12

PROP
02
CALIFORNIA Strengthens State Rainy Day Fund
Purpose
Proposition 2 is a constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by the legislature, that would
strengthen California’s rainy day fund by increasing the cap on how much money the state can set
aside each year. The measure also would make it easier for the state to use tax revenues to pay
down debt.1
Research Assistant: Arushi Goyal ’28
Background
The Budget Stabilization Account (BSA), also known as the rainy day fund,
is California’s largest state budget reserve. The state uses this fund to save
money when revenues are strong and to reduce cuts to public services when
revenues are weak. This fund is especially important in California because
the state’s revenues depend heavily on taxes on the incomes of high-income
residents, which can vary greatly from year to year, thus creating “boom and
bust” budget cycles.2
The state automatically sets aside 1.5% of General Fund revenues each year.
It also sets aside “excess” capital gains revenues in years when they exceed
8% of General Fund tax revenues. Generally, the state deposits 50% of these
set-aside revenues into the rainy day fund and uses the other 50% to pay
down certain types of state debt. Currently, the state can use these excess
revenues to pay down only pension and retiree health debt, and cannot make
extra payments on other forms of debt such as unemployment insurance
debt and certain education and Medi-Cal obligations. This requirement is
set to end in 2030, after which some or all of that money may be put into the
rainy day fund.3
Under current law, the rainy day fund is capped at 10% of estimated General
Fund tax revenues. When this limit is reached, any dollars that would other-
wise go into the rainy day fund must be spent on infrastructure.4 California
also has a constitutional spending cap, commonly known as the Gann Limit,
which was passed by the voters as Proposition 4 in 1979 and which capped
spending at 1978-79 levels, adjusted each year for infation and population
growth.5 Most spending counts toward this limit, including money deposited
into reserves. Withdrawals from state reserves during budget emergencies
do not count against the Gann Limit, but when state revenues are high, the
spending cap can limit California’s ability to build its reserves.
The rainy day fund can be tapped only during a budget emergency. The gover-
nor must formally declare an emergency before deposits can be reduced or
suspended or money can be withdrawn. The declaration can come late in the
fscal year, sometimes after the legislature’s deadline to pass a budget. This
can leave lawmakers passing a budget that assumes an emergency before
one is ofcially declared.6
In the state legislature the vote to place this measure on the ballot was 59-8
in the Assembly and 29-2 in the Senate.7
Proposal
If approved, Proposition 2 would:8
• Double the BSA cap from 10% to 20% of
estimated General Fund tax revenues.
• Set aside more General Fund revenues during
“boom” years.
• Expand the types of state debt that may be paid
down with set-aside revenues.
• Extend the debt-paydown requirement by 10
years, to 2039-40.
• Change how rainy day fund and other deposits
count toward the Gann Limit.
• Create a simpler process for declaring a budget
emergency.
Fiscal Impact
The LAO estimates that Proposition 2 would
increase the state’s budget reserves. Having more
money in the BSA would make it easier for the
state to balance its budget during downturns. The
measure could also cause the state to pay down
debt more aggressively.9

fscal instability.11
• Help the state protect vital services and avoid deeper
cuts during downturns.12
• Prevent politicians from overspending during “boom”

• Pay down debt faster.14

to the state without fxing the underlying UI system.19
A NO vote would preserve current rules for state budget
reserves and debt payments.

PROP
03
CALIFORNIA Makes permanent existing voter-approved income tax rates for high-income
Californians
Purpose
Proposition 3, a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature, would make permanent
the existing voter-approved income tax rates on high-income Californians, which are currently set
to expire in 2031, and to allocate the resulting revenues to K-12 schools and community colleges.1
Research Assistant: Shayan Abbasi ’29
Background
The personal income tax is California’s largest revenue source.
It provides more than half of the state’s General Fund, the state’s
main operating account, which funds public services including
education, health care, and corrections. The tax applies to most
types of income, such as wages, salaries, interest, and capital gains,
which the state treats as ordinary income. California’s income tax
rates are progressive, starting low and gradually rising for taxpayers
with higher incomes.2
Over the past two decades, voters have approved or extended tax
increases on high-income earners several times.
• In 2004, voters approved Proposition 63, a 1% surcharge on
income taxes of residents with taxable income of more than
$1 million.
• In 2012, amid the fscal challenges brought on by the Great
Recession, California voters approved Proposition 30, which
temporarily increased income tax rates on high-income
taxpayers to fund state services and stave of cuts to public
education. This measure raised the top marginal rate from
9.3% to 12.3%. Combined with the 1% surcharge, the state’s
income tax on the highest earners became 13.3% — the highest
in the nation.
• In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55, which extended these
higher income tax rates through 2030, with 63% voting yes.3
The top 2% of California taxpayers pay these higher rates (10.3% or
higher), and these taxpayers now pay about half of all state income
taxes. Since Proposition 30’s initial passage in 2012, the measure
has raised more than $104 billion for schools and other state
services and has become a foundational part of the state’s budget
and its Rainy Day Fund.4
Figure 1 shows the income tax rates for Californians under current
law, which will continue if Prop. 3 passes, and how the rates for
high-earners will decrease after 2030 if Prop. 3 is rejected. 5
ROSEINSTITUTE.CMC.EDU
ROSEINSTITUTE.CMC.EDU
Proposal
Proposition 3, ofcially titled “The California Children’s Education
and Health Care Protection Act of 2026,” would amend Section 36 of
Article XIII of the California Constitution to make the higher income
tax rates established by Proposition 30 of 2012 permanent instead of
letting them expire in 2030.6 The measure does not change the exist-
ing rates or brackets, which adjust for infation each year, and it does
not increase taxes on individuals earning less than about $371,000 or
couples earning less than about $743,000 in today’s dollars.7
Revenues would continue to be deposited into the Education
Protection Account, with 89% of the education funds allocated to
K-12 school districts, county ofces of education, and charter schools,
and 11% allocated to community college districts.8 Local school
boards would retain the authority to decide how the revenues are
spent, provided that spending determinations are made in open
session of a public meeting, and none of the funds may be used for
administrator salaries or other administrative costs. Each district
must annually publish online an accounting of how much money it
received and how it was spent, and the funds are subject to an annual
independent audit, with elected ofcials facing prosecution and
criminal penalties if they misuse them.9 The measure also increases
the General Fund revenues available for health care, budget reserves,
and other programs, and it directs that in certain years a portion of
surplus revenues, up to a maximum of $2 billion in a single fscal
year, be allocated to health care services for children and their families
through Medi-Cal.10
Fiscal Impact
If the current income tax rates are allowed
to expire as scheduled, the California
Legislative Analyst’s Ofce (LAO) estimates
that the state would lose between $5 billion
and $15 billion in annual revenue beginning
in 2031.11 For context, this year the state
plans to spend about $250 billion from
the General Fund, with about half of that
spending going to schools, community
colleges, and the state’s public universities,
and about another one-third going to health
and human services programs, mainly
Medi-Cal, the state’s low-income health
insurance program.12

CALIFORNIA Prohibits Enactment of New Taxes on Asset Ownership and Retroactive Taxes
Purpose
Proposition 42 is a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment that would make it more difcult
to adopt a wealth tax in California by prohibiting enactment of new taxes on ownership of
fnancial assets or other personal property, or taxes that would apply retroactively based on a
taxpayer’s past activities.1
Research Assistant: Kaylin Nydam ’29
Background
Currently, individuals who reside or work in
the State of California must pay income and
capital gains taxes on income from investments.
However, the state does not tax ownership of
fnancial assets such as stocks, bonds, and
retirement accounts, or most other forms of
personal property.2
Proposal
Proposition 42 would prevent the state from imposing new taxes on
ownership of “retirement holdings, individually-owned assets, and other
forms of personal savings,” which are defned to include pensions,
retirement accounts, mutual funds, and all tangible and intangible
personal property, including business interests, digital assets, intellectu-
al property, and personal belongings.3
Furthermore, the measure would prevent the state from taxing individu-
als retroactively based on their past activities or residency status—such
as billionaires who have left the state to avoid taxes on their wealth.4
Proposition 42, like Proposition 41, aims to make it more difcult to
impose a wealth tax on billionaires, as proposed by Proposition 40.
Specifcally, Proposition 40 would levy a one-time tax of fve percent
on the personal property assets of taxpayers and trusts with net worth
exceeding one billion dollars; most of the resulting revenue would be
used to fund health care programs.5 Proposition 42 contains language
stipulating that if it and a conficting measure both pass, the conficting
measure would be nullifed if Proposition 42 receives more votes.6
Fiscal Impact
By limiting the types of assets that can be taxed, this measure potentially
decreases future state tax revenue. According to the Legislative Analyst’s
Ofce (LAO), the extent to which future revenues would be reduced is
unclear.7 Moreover, blocking the billionaire tax could help the state keep
some of its wealthiest residents, averting the loss of income tax revenue
from those residents.

Requires a Two-Thirds Vote to Approve Local Special Tax Initiatives
PROP
43 Purpose
Proposition 43 is a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature that would raise the
vote share required to enact special tax initiatives proposed by citizens from a simple majority
to a two-thirds majority.1
CALIFORNIA
Research Assistant: Kahani Malhotra ’27
Background
In 1978, California voters passed Proposition 13, requiring that any special tax proposed by a
local government must receive a two-thirds vote from the electorate before being enacted,2
with a special tax being defned as any tax imposed for a specifc purpose rather than general
governmental need.3 In 1996, Proposition 218 further increased the power of voters to approve
taxes by requiring that any general tax imposed by a local government must receive majority
voter approval, and reafrmed that special taxes require two-thirds voter approval.4
Two decades later, a court decision narrowed the scope of Proposition 218. In 2017, the
California Supreme Court ruled in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland that a signifcant
requirement for general taxes — that they be placed on the ballot during general elections —
did not apply to citizen initiatives.5 Ultimately, the court categorized taxes imposed by local
governments as diferent from taxes imposed by citizen initiatives.
The ruling raised an important question: Are special taxes imposed by citizen initiatives exempt
from the two-thirds vote requirement that applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local
governments? A memo from the San Francisco attorney’s ofce interpreting the ruling seemed
to indicate that the answer was yes.6 But the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association disagreed.
In 2018, the Association sued San Francisco for allowing two separate citizen-driven measures
to pass with a simple-majority vote rather than a supermajority vote. A judge ruled against the
Association, afrming that the special tax measures were rightfully passed by majority vote
since they were proposed by citizens.7 A state appeals court shot down the Association’s further
attempts to overturn citizen-initiated local taxes passed in 20208 and 2021.9
In 2023, the Association and the California Business Roundtable qualifed an initiative10 for the
2024 ballot cycle that would have mandated any special tax initiative to require a two-thirds
majority vote regardless of whether a local government or citizens proposed it.11 But in June
2024, the California Supreme Court ruled unanimously that passage of the initiative would lead
to a “revision,” rather than an amendment, of the state constitution, “based on its far-reaching
changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained at the
state and local levels.” While amendments may be made by citizen initiatives, revisions require
“a constitutional convention and popular ratifcation.”12 Thus, enacting the proposal by initiative
would be unconstitutional.
In 2026, the same two organizations qualifed an initiative for the 2026 general election
ballot that would have amended the state constitution to require a two-thirds majority to pass
citizen-led local special tax initiatives, alongside other tax limiting provisions.13 Following a
legislative compromise, which included the passage of ACA 22,14 the organizations withdrew the
initiative in favor of Proposition 43 being placed on this year’s ballot as a legislatively referred
constitutional amendment.15 Though ACA 22 passed nearly unanimously in the Assembly (68-2)
and Senate (35-1), its author, Assemblymember Bufy Wicks (D-14), announced on June 29 that
she was “adamantly opposed to it.16
Proposal
Proposition 43 would amend the
California Constitution to require that
citizen-driven special tax initiatives
require a two-thirds majority vote
for passage. It would add Section
4.5 to Article XIII A of the California
Constitution, detailing that any local
government — including voters
within a local government exercising
the initiative power — must obtain
a two-thirds vote to enact, extend,
or increase a special tax starting on
January 1, 2027.
The amendment also prohibits local
government and members of the
electorate from levying ad valorem
property taxes — taxes based on the
value of real estate or tangible per-
sonal property — except for certain
preapproved, dedicated property
taxes, whose terms are delineated in
the Constitution.17
Fiscal Impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s
Ofce (LAO) estimates that Propo-
sition 43 would reduce local govern-
ment tax revenues. The total fscal
impact is largely unknown, however,
as it depends on future decisions by
voters and local governments.18

Purpose
Proposition 42 is a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment that would make it more difcult
to adopt a wealth tax in California by prohibiting enactment of new taxes on ownership of
fnancial assets or other personal property, or taxes that would apply retroactively based on a
taxpayer’s past activities.1
Research Assistant: Kaylin Nydam ’29
Background
Currently, individuals who reside or work in
the State of California must pay income and
capital gains taxes on income from investments.
However, the state does not tax ownership of
fnancial assets such as stocks, bonds, and
retirement accounts, or most other forms of
personal property.2
Proposal
Proposition 42 would prevent the state from imposing new taxes on
ownership of “retirement holdings, individually-owned assets, and other
forms of personal savings,” which are defned to include pensions,
retirement accounts, mutual funds, and all tangible and intangible
personal property, including business interests, digital assets, intellectu-
al property, and personal belongings.3
Furthermore, the measure would prevent the state from taxing individu-
als retroactively based on their past activities or residency status—such
as billionaires who have left the state to avoid taxes on their wealth.4
Proposition 42, like Proposition 41, aims to make it more difcult to
impose a wealth tax on billionaires, as proposed by Proposition 40.
Specifcally, Proposition 40 would levy a one-time tax of fve percent
on the personal property assets of taxpayers and trusts with net worth
exceeding one billion dollars; most of the resulting revenue would be
used to fund health care programs.5 Proposition 42 contains language
stipulating that if it and a conficting measure both pass, the conficting
measure would be nullifed if Proposition 42 receives more votes.6
Fiscal Impact
By limiting the types of assets that can be taxed, this measure potentially
decreases future state tax revenue. According to the Legislative Analyst’s
Ofce (LAO), the extent to which future revenues would be reduced is
unclear.7 Moreover, blocking the billionaire tax could help the state keep
some of its wealthiest residents, averting the loss of income tax revenue
from those residents.

PROP
43 Purpose
Proposition 43 is a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature that would raise the
vote share required to enact special tax initiatives proposed by citizens from a simple majority
to a two-thirds majority.1
CALIFORNIA
Research Assistant: Kahani Malhotra ’27
Background
In 1978, California voters passed Proposition 13, requiring that any special tax proposed by a
local government must receive a two-thirds vote from the electorate before being enacted,2
with a special tax being defned as any tax imposed for a specifc purpose rather than general
governmental need.3 In 1996, Proposition 218 further increased the power of voters to approve
taxes by requiring that any general tax imposed by a local government must receive majority
voter approval, and reafrmed that special taxes require two-thirds voter approval.4
Two decades later, a court decision narrowed the scope of Proposition 218. In 2017, the
California Supreme Court ruled in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland that a signifcant
requirement for general taxes — that they be placed on the ballot during general elections —
did not apply to citizen initiatives.5 Ultimately, the court categorized taxes imposed by local
governments as diferent from taxes imposed by citizen initiatives.
The ruling raised an important question: Are special taxes imposed by citizen initiatives exempt
from the two-thirds vote requirement that applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local
governments? A memo from the San Francisco attorney’s ofce interpreting the ruling seemed
to indicate that the answer was yes.6 But the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association disagreed.
In 2018, the Association sued San Francisco for allowing two separate citizen-driven measures
to pass with a simple-majority vote rather than a supermajority vote. A judge ruled against the
Association, afrming that the special tax measures were rightfully passed by majority vote
since they were proposed by citizens.7 A state appeals court shot down the Association’s further
attempts to overturn citizen-initiated local taxes passed in 20208 and 2021.9
In 2023, the Association and the California Business Roundtable qualifed an initiative10 for the
2024 ballot cycle that would have mandated any special tax initiative to require a two-thirds
majority vote regardless of whether a local government or citizens proposed it.11 But in June
2024, the California Supreme Court ruled unanimously that passage of the initiative would lead
to a “revision,” rather than an amendment, of the state constitution, “based on its far-reaching
changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained at the
state and local levels.” While amendments may be made by citizen initiatives, revisions require
“a constitutional convention and popular ratifcation.”12 Thus, enacting the proposal by initiative
would be unconstitutional.
In 2026, the same two organizations qualifed an initiative for the 2026 general election
ballot that would have amended the state constitution to require a two-thirds majority to pass
citizen-led local special tax initiatives, alongside other tax limiting provisions.13 Following a
legislative compromise, which included the passage of ACA 22,14 the organizations withdrew the
initiative in favor of Proposition 43 being placed on this year’s ballot as a legislatively referred
constitutional amendment.15 Though ACA 22 passed nearly unanimously in the Assembly (68-2)
and Senate (35-1), its author, Assemblymember Bufy Wicks (D-14), announced on June 29 that
she was “adamantly opposed to it.16
Proposal
Proposition 43 would amend the
California Constitution to require that
citizen-driven special tax initiatives
require a two-thirds majority vote
for passage. It would add Section
4.5 to Article XIII A of the California
Constitution, detailing that any local
government — including voters
within a local government exercising
the initiative power — must obtain
a two-thirds vote to enact, extend,
or increase a special tax starting on
January 1, 2027.
The amendment also prohibits local
government and members of the
electorate from levying ad valorem
property taxes — taxes based on the
value of real estate or tangible per-
sonal property — except for certain
preapproved, dedicated property
taxes, whose terms are delineated in
the Constitution.17
Fiscal Impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s
Ofce (LAO) estimates that Propo-
sition 43 would reduce local govern-
ment tax revenues. The total fscal
impact is largely unknown, however,
as it depends on future decisions by
voters and local governments.18

vote share required to enact special tax initiatives proposed by citizens from a simple majority

Research Assistant: Kahani Malhotra ’27
Background
In 1978, California voters passed Proposition 13, requiring that any special tax proposed by a
local government must receive a two-thirds vote from the electorate before being enacted,2
with a special tax being defned as any tax imposed for a specifc purpose rather than general
governmental need.3 In 1996, Proposition 218 further increased the power of voters to approve
taxes by requiring that any general tax imposed by a local government must receive majority
voter approval, and reafrmed that special taxes require two-thirds voter approval.4
Two decades later, a court decision narrowed the scope of Proposition 218. In 2017, the
California Supreme Court ruled in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland that a signifcant
requirement for general taxes — that they be placed on the ballot during general elections —
did not apply to citizen initiatives.5 Ultimately, the court categorized taxes imposed by local
governments as diferent from taxes imposed by citizen initiatives.
The ruling raised an important question: Are special taxes imposed by citizen initiatives exempt
from the two-thirds vote requirement that applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local
governments? A memo from the San Francisco attorney’s ofce interpreting the ruling seemed
to indicate that the answer was yes.6 But the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association disagreed.
In 2018, the Association sued San Francisco for allowing two separate citizen-driven measures
to pass with a simple-majority vote rather than a supermajority vote. A judge ruled against the
Association, afrming that the special tax measures were rightfully passed by majority vote
since they were proposed by citizens.7 A state appeals court shot down the Association’s further
attempts to overturn citizen-initiated local taxes passed in 20208 and 2021.9

2024 ballot cycle that would have mandated any special tax initiative to require a two-thirds
majority vote regardless of whether a local government or citizens proposed it.11 But in June
2024, the California Supreme Court ruled unanimously that passage of the initiative would lead
to a “revision,” rather than an amendment, of the state constitution, “based on its far-reaching
changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained at the
state and local levels.” While amendments may be made by citizen initiatives, revisions require
“a constitutional convention and popular ratifcation.”12 Thus, enacting the proposal by initiative
would be unconstitutional.

ballot that would have amended the state constitution to require a two-thirds majority to pass

and Senate (35-1), its author, Assemblymember Bufy Wicks (D-14), announced on June 29 that

California Constitution to require that
citizen-driven special tax initiatives
require a two-thirds majority vote
for passage. It would add Section
4.5 to Article XIII A of the California
Constitution, detailing that any local
government — including voters
within a local government exercising
the initiative power — must obtain
a two-thirds vote to enact, extend,
or increase a special tax starting on
January 1, 2027.
The amendment also prohibits local
government and members of the
electorate from levying ad valorem
property taxes — taxes based on the
value of real estate or tangible per-
sonal property — except for certain
preapproved, dedicated property
taxes, whose terms are delineated in
the Constitution.17

The California Legislative Analyst’s
Ofce (LAO) estimates that Propo-
sition 43 would reduce local govern-
ment tax revenues. The total fscal
impact is largely unknown, however,
as it depends on future decisions by
voters and local governments.18

Restricts New Special Taxes by Requiring Audits and Performance Reviews
and Denying Exemption from State Spending Cap
PROP
41 Purpose
Proposition 41 is a citizen initiated measure that would require the California State Auditor
to review programs to be funded by proposed special taxes and publish its fnancial and
performance audit before California residents vote on these tax proposals. The State Auditor
would also be required to periodically review programs funded by special taxes created or
raised after January 1, 2026 in order to improve program efciency. Finally, Prop. 41 would
prevent revenues raised by new state taxes from being exempted from the Gann Limit on state
spending approved by voters in 1979.1
CALIFORNIA
Research Assistant: Dhriti Jagadish ’27
Background
In 1979, Californians passed Proposition 4,
also known as the Gann Limit, which capped
spending at 1978-79 levels, adjusted each year
for infation and population growth. If state and
local governments collect more tax revenue
than they are allowed to spend for two consec-
utive years, they must split the excess between
taxpayer rebates and additional spending on
schools.2 Prop. 41’s drafters charge that special
interests have “repeatedly passed new taxes that
exempted themselves” from the Gann Limit.
Proposal
Proposition 41 has three key provisions:
First, it would require that when a “special tax” — one that would raise
funds for a specifc purpose or program rather than for general government
operations — is proposed as a ballot initiative and achieves 25% of the
necessary signatures, the California State Auditor would conduct a
pre-election audit of any programs to be funded by the tax. The results of
the audit would appear in the Ofcial Voter Guide for the election. The audit
would address the following:
• Whether the program is currently acquiring its resources at the lowest
cost for the necessary quality;
• Whether the program is maximizing output for every dollar spent;
• Whether the program is achieving its intended goals and outcomes;
• Whether the program is following the relevant laws, regulations, and
internal policies;
• Whether there is “actual and potential fraud, waste, and abuse” in a
program and how adequate its internal prevention systems are;
• Whether the program has identifed its “biggest threats” and has a
plan to mitigate them;
• Whether the program is using adequate and reliable data;
• Whether the program has adequate oversight and accountability;
• Whether the program’s costs compare favorably to similar non-
governmental programs; and
• How the program could cut its costs by at least 10%.
ROSEINSTITUTE.CMC.EDU
These fndings must be sent to the governor, the legislature, and the
secretary of state and be made available to the public. If the special tax
initiative qualifes for the ballot, an executive summary must be printed
in every Voter Information Guide (VIG) prior to the election.
Second, for all special taxes enacted by the legislature or by a ballot
initiative on or after January 1, 2026, the California State Auditor must
conduct ongoing fnancial and performance audits every four years for
each of the programs that receive revenue from these taxes. With the
assistance of the California Legislative Analyst’s Ofce (LAO) — as well
as public input on the State Auditor’s measurements of efectiveness —
the State Auditor must provide:
• The same assessments required of the pre-election fnancial and
performance audit; and
• Further recommendations on how a program can improve its
efectiveness, cut costs, or otherwise reduce taxpayer burden.
Third, the Proposition would require that all revenues raised by state
taxes that take efect on or after January 1, 2026, be subject to the state
spending limit, also known as the Gann Limit. It would prohibit the
state from imposing, collecting, or enforcing any state tax that claims an
exemption from the Gann Limit. This provision would directly contradict
Proposition 40, which exempts appropriations funded by the “2026
Billionaire Tax Reserve Fund” from the Gann Limit.3
Prop. 41 expressly states that if it receives more votes than a conficting
measure on the same ballot, even if that other measure receives a
majority, the conficting measure would not become law.
Fiscal Impact
The Californa Legislative Analyst’s Ofce
(LAO) expects Proposition 41 to have a
number of fscal efects.4
The LAO predicts that Prop. 41 would increase
State Auditor costs. These costs would
depend on the number of new or increased
special taxes the State Auditor must review
as well as the complexity of the programs
being reviewed on a recurring basis. The LAO
estimates that this would likely be in the range
of the low millions of dollars annually, but
would increase over time.
The LAO also expects that the State Auditor’s
summarized reviews, which must appear
in every Voter Information Guide (VIG) if
a special tax is proposed through a ballot
initiative, could add several pages to the VIG,
increasing printing and mailing costs by a few
hundred thousand dollars per ballot initiative.
Pre-election and ongoing audits of special
taxes and their associated programs would
be paid for by the revenues collected by the
special taxes. Pre-election audit costs for
special taxes that do not qualify for the ballot
or are rejected by voters would be paid for by
the state’s General Fund.
Altogether, the net fscal impact remains un-
known. The LAO suggests that Prop. 41 could
result in “possible savings” or “improved
services” based on the recommendations of
the State Auditor. These savings, however,
cannot be predicted in advance.

chief sponsor of “Yes on 41 - Californians for a More Transparent

Arguments for Proposition 4111
Supporters of Proposition 41 argue that:
• California’s state government will spend more than $350
billion this year, a 79% increase from 2019, and outcomes
in education, health care, and infrastructure have barely
improved.
• The legislature and “special interests” continue to propose
new taxes for new programs without monitoring their
spending and thoroughly reviewing the efcacy of existing
programs.

credible information” on proposed taxes and the programs
they would support.
• Though the Gann Limit on state spending was democratically
approved by voters, it has been consistently undercut by
exemptions.

Arguments Against Proposition 4115
Opponents of Proposition 41 argue that:
• Proposition 41 was put on the ballot in the name of tax
oversight and transparency, but its primary purpose is to
undo Prop. 40’s “billionaire tax.”

poured millions of dollars into Propositions 41 and 42 to
void Prop. 40.
• By potentially voiding Prop. 40, Prop. 41 would cost the
state much-needed revenue.
OPPOSITION TO PROPOSITION 41
A YES vote on Proposition 41 would require the California State
Auditor to conduct pre-election and ongoing performance
and fnancial audits of programs funded by special taxes. It
would also prevent exemption of new special taxes from the
state spending limit, thus directly competing with — and likely
overriding — Proposition 40.
A NO vote on Proposition 41 would not introduce any new
performance and fnancial audits of programs funded by
special taxes and would not change current state spending
limit requirements.

CALIFORNIA Prohibits Enactment of New Taxes on Asset Ownership and Retroactive Taxes
Purpose
Proposition 42 is a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment that would make it more difcult
to adopt a wealth tax in California by prohibiting enactment of new taxes on ownership of
fnancial assets or other personal property, or taxes that would apply retroactively based on a
taxpayer’s past activities.1
Research Assistant: Kaylin Nydam ’29
Background
Currently, individuals who reside or work in
the State of California must pay income and
capital gains taxes on income from investments.
However, the state does not tax ownership of
fnancial assets such as stocks, bonds, and
retirement accounts, or most other forms of
personal property.2
Proposal
Proposition 42 would prevent the state from imposing new taxes on
ownership of “retirement holdings, individually-owned assets, and other
forms of personal savings,” which are defned to include pensions,
retirement accounts, mutual funds, and all tangible and intangible
personal property, including business interests, digital assets, intellectu-
al property, and personal belongings.3
Furthermore, the measure would prevent the state from taxing individu-
als retroactively based on their past activities or residency status—such
as billionaires who have left the state to avoid taxes on their wealth.4
Proposition 42, like Proposition 41, aims to make it more difcult to
impose a wealth tax on billionaires, as proposed by Proposition 40.
Specifcally, Proposition 40 would levy a one-time tax of fve percent
on the personal property assets of taxpayers and trusts with net worth
exceeding one billion dollars; most of the resulting revenue would be
used to fund health care programs.5 Proposition 42 contains language
stipulating that if it and a conficting measure both pass, the conficting
measure would be nullifed if Proposition 42 receives more votes.6
Fiscal Impact
By limiting the types of assets that can be taxed, this measure potentially
decreases future state tax revenue. According to the Legislative Analyst’s
Ofce (LAO), the extent to which future revenues would be reduced is
unclear.7 Moreover, blocking the billionaire tax could help the state keep
some of its wealthiest residents, averting the loss of income tax revenue
from those residents.

Proposition 42 is a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment that would make it more difcult

Research Assistant: Kaylin Nydam ’29
Background
Currently, individuals who reside or work in

Proposition 42 would prevent the state from imposing new taxes on

personal property, including business interests, digital assets, intellectu-

impose a wealth tax on billionaires, as proposed by Proposition 40.

on the personal property assets of taxpayers and trusts with net worth
exceeding one billion dollars; most of the resulting revenue would be
used to fund health care programs.5 Proposition 42 contains language
stipulating that if it and a conficting measure both pass, the conficting
measure would be nullifed if Proposition 42 receives more votes.6

By limiting the types of assets that can be taxed, this measure potentially
decreases future state tax revenue. According to the Legislative Analyst’s

would address the following:
• Whether the program is currently acquiring its resources at the lowest
cost for the necessary quality;
• Whether the program is maximizing output for every dollar spent;
• Whether the program is achieving its intended goals and outcomes;
• Whether the program is following the relevant laws, regulations, and
internal policies;
• Whether there is “actual and potential fraud, waste, and abuse” in a
program and how adequate its internal prevention systems are;
• Whether the program has identifed its “biggest threats” and has a
plan to mitigate them;
• Whether the program is using adequate and reliable data;
• Whether the program has adequate oversight and accountability;
• Whether the program’s costs compare favorably to similar non-
governmental programs; and
• How the program could cut its costs by at least 10%.

local government must receive a two-thirds vote from the electorate before being enacted,2
with a special tax being defned as any tax imposed for a specifc purpose rather than general

voter approval, and reafrmed that special taxes require two-thirds voter approval.4

California Supreme Court ruled in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland that a signifcant
requirement for general taxes — that they be placed on the ballot during general elections —
did not apply to citizen initiatives.5 Ultimately, the court categorized taxes imposed by local
governments as diferent from taxes imposed by citizen initiatives.

from the two-thirds vote requirement that applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local

to indicate that the answer was yes.6 But the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association disagreed.

to pass with a simple-majority vote rather than a supermajority vote. A judge ruled against the
Association, afrming that the special tax measures were rightfully passed by majority vote
since they were proposed by citizens.7 A state appeals court shot down the Association’s further
attempts to overturn citizen-initiated local taxes passed in 20208 and 2021.9
In 2023, the Association and the California Business Roundtable qualifed an initiative10 for the
2024 ballot cycle that would have mandated any special tax initiative to require a two-thirds
majority vote regardless of whether a local government or citizens proposed it.11 But in June
2024, the California Supreme Court ruled unanimously that passage of the initiative would lead
to a “revision,” rather than an amendment, of the state constitution, “based on its far-reaching
changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained at the
state and local levels.” While amendments may be made by citizen initiatives, revisions require

Restricts New Special Taxes by Requiring Audits and Performance Reviews
and Denying Exemption from State Spending Cap
PROP
41 Purpose
Proposition 41 is a citizen initiated measure that would require the California State Auditor
to review programs to be funded by proposed special taxes and publish its fnancial and
performance audit before California residents vote on these tax proposals. The State Auditor
would also be required to periodically review programs funded by special taxes created or
raised after January 1, 2026 in order to improve program efciency. Finally, Prop. 41 would
prevent revenues raised by new state taxes from being exempted from the Gann Limit on state
spending approved by voters in 1979.1
CALIFORNIA
Research Assistant: Dhriti Jagadish ’27
Background
In 1979, Californians passed Proposition 4,
also known as the Gann Limit, which capped
spending at 1978-79 levels, adjusted each year
for infation and population growth. If state and
local governments collect more tax revenue
than they are allowed to spend for two consec-
utive years, they must split the excess between
taxpayer rebates and additional spending on
schools.2 Prop. 41’s drafters charge that special
interests have “repeatedly passed new taxes that
exempted themselves” from the Gann Limit.
Proposal
Proposition 41 has three key provisions:
First, it would require that when a “special tax” — one that would raise
funds for a specifc purpose or program rather than for general government
operations — is proposed as a ballot initiative and achieves 25% of the
necessary signatures, the California State Auditor would conduct a
pre-election audit of any programs to be funded by the tax. The results of
the audit would appear in the Ofcial Voter Guide for the election. The audit
would address the following:
• Whether the program is currently acquiring its resources at the lowest
cost for the necessary quality;
• Whether the program is maximizing output for every dollar spent;
• Whether the program is achieving its intended goals and outcomes;
• Whether the program is following the relevant laws, regulations, and
internal policies;
• Whether there is “actual and potential fraud, waste, and abuse” in a
program and how adequate its internal prevention systems are;
• Whether the program has identifed its “biggest threats” and has a
plan to mitigate them;
• Whether the program is using adequate and reliable data;
• Whether the program has adequate oversight and accountability;
• Whether the program’s costs compare favorably to similar non-
governmental programs; and
• How the program could cut its costs by at least 10%.
ROSEINSTITUTE.CMC.EDU
These fndings must be sent to the governor, the legislature, and the
secretary of state and be made available to the public. If the special tax
initiative qualifes for the ballot, an executive summary must be printed
in every Voter Information Guide (VIG) prior to the election.
Second, for all special taxes enacted by the legislature or by a ballot
initiative on or after January 1, 2026, the California State Auditor must
conduct ongoing fnancial and performance audits every four years for
each of the programs that receive revenue from these taxes. With the
assistance of the California Legislative Analyst’s Ofce (LAO) — as well
as public input on the State Auditor’s measurements of efectiveness —
the State Auditor must provide:
• The same assessments required of the pre-election fnancial and
performance audit; and
• Further recommendations on how a program can improve its
efectiveness, cut costs, or otherwise reduce taxpayer burden.
Third, the Proposition would require that all revenues raised by state
taxes that take efect on or after January 1, 2026, be subject to the state
spending limit, also known as the Gann Limit. It would prohibit the
state from imposing, collecting, or enforcing any state tax that claims an
exemption from the Gann Limit. This provision would directly contradict
Proposition 40, which exempts appropriations funded by the “2026
Billionaire Tax Reserve Fund” from the Gann Limit.3
Prop. 41 expressly states that if it receives more votes than a conficting
measure on the same ballot, even if that other measure receives a
majority, the conficting measure would not become law.
Fiscal Impact
The Californa Legislative Analyst’s Ofce
(LAO) expects Proposition 41 to have a
number of fscal efects.4
The LAO predicts that Prop. 41 would increase
State Auditor costs. These costs would
depend on the number of new or increased
special taxes the State Auditor must review
as well as the complexity of the programs
being reviewed on a recurring basis. The LAO
estimates that this would likely be in the range
of the low millions of dollars annually, but
would increase over time.
The LAO also expects that the State Auditor’s
summarized reviews, which must appear
in every Voter Information Guide (VIG) if
a special tax is proposed through a ballot
initiative, could add several pages to the VIG,
increasing printing and mailing costs by a few
hundred thousand dollars per ballot initiative.
Pre-election and ongoing audits of special
taxes and their associated programs would
be paid for by the revenues collected by the
special taxes. Pre-election audit costs for
special taxes that do not qualify for the ballot
or are rejected by voters would be paid for by
the state’s General Fund.
Altogether, the net fscal impact remains un-
known. The LAO suggests that Prop. 41 could
result in “possible savings” or “improved
services” based on the recommendations of
the State Auditor. These savings, however,
cannot be predicted in advance.
Proposal, continued

• California Republican Party

Committee)9
The proponents’ ofcial website is https://www.yesonprop41.org/.
As of September 19, 2026, proponents had raised $92,294,500 to
promote Prop 41. Google co-founder Sergey Brin has contributed
$102 million this year to Building a Better California, which is the
chief sponsor of “Yes on 41 - Californians for a More Transparent
and Efective Government.”10
Arguments for Proposition 4111
Supporters of Proposition 41 argue that:
• California’s state government will spend more than $350
billion this year, a 79% increase from 2019, and outcomes
in education, health care, and infrastructure have barely
improved.
• The legislature and “special interests” continue to propose
new taxes for new programs without monitoring their
spending and thoroughly reviewing the efcacy of existing
programs.
• Independent performance audits give voters “objective,
credible information” on proposed taxes and the programs
they would support.
• Though the Gann Limit on state spending was democratically
approved by voters, it has been consistently undercut by
exemptions.
SUPPORT FOR PROPOSITION 41
Opponents of Proposition 41 Include:
• California Democratic Party12
• Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare
Workers West (SEIU-UHW)13
As of September 19, 2026, opponents had raised $340,225
against Prop. 41.14
Arguments Against Proposition 4115
Opponents of Proposition 41 argue that:
• Proposition 41 was put on the ballot in the name of tax
oversight and transparency, but its primary purpose is to
undo Prop. 40’s “billionaire tax.”
• Billionaires, some of them Donald Trump’s donors, have
poured millions of dollars into Propositions 41 and 42 to
void Prop. 40.
• By potentially voiding Prop. 40, Prop. 41 would cost the
state much-needed revenue.
OPPOSITION TO PROPOSITION 41
A YES vote on Proposition 41 would require the California State
Auditor to conduct pre-election and ongoing performance
and fnancial audits of programs funded by special taxes. It
would also prevent exemption of new special taxes from the
state spending limit, thus directly competing with — and likely
overriding — Proposition 40.
A NO vote on Proposition 41 would not introduce any new
performance and fnancial audits of programs funded by
special taxes and would not change current state spending
limit requirements.

CALIFORNIA Prohibits Enactment of New Taxes on Asset Ownership and Retroactive Taxes
Purpose
Proposition 42 is a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment that would make it more difcult
to adopt a wealth tax in California by prohibiting enactment of new taxes on ownership of
fnancial assets or other personal property, or taxes that would apply retroactively based on a
taxpayer’s past activities.1
Research Assistant: Kaylin Nydam ’29
Background
Currently, individuals who reside or work in
the State of California must pay income and
capital gains taxes on income from investments.
However, the state does not tax ownership of
fnancial assets such as stocks, bonds, and
retirement accounts, or most other forms of
personal property.2
Proposal
Proposition 42 would prevent the state from imposing new taxes on
ownership of “retirement holdings, individually-owned assets, and other
forms of personal savings,” which are defned to include pensions,
retirement accounts, mutual funds, and all tangible and intangible
personal property, including business interests, digital assets, intellectu-
al property, and personal belongings.3
Furthermore, the measure would prevent the state from taxing individu-
als retroactively based on their past activities or residency status—such
as billionaires who have left the state to avoid taxes on their wealth.4
Proposition 42, like Proposition 41, aims to make it more difcult to
impose a wealth tax on billionaires, as proposed by Proposition 40.
Specifcally, Proposition 40 would levy a one-time tax of fve percent
on the personal property assets of taxpayers and trusts with net worth
exceeding one billion dollars; most of the resulting revenue would be
used to fund health care programs.5 Proposition 42 contains language
stipulating that if it and a conficting measure both pass, the conficting
measure would be nullifed if Proposition 42 receives more votes.6
Fiscal Impact
By limiting the types of assets that can be taxed, this measure potentially
decreases future state tax revenue. According to the Legislative Analyst’s
Ofce (LAO), the extent to which future revenues would be reduced is
unclear.7 Moreover, blocking the billionaire tax could help the state keep
some of its wealthiest residents, averting the loss of income tax revenue
from those residents.

Issue Brief
What Would Proposition 41 Mean for California?
Understanding the Proposed Audit Requirements for Special Taxes and the Prohibition on Excluding Revenues from the State Spending Limit
September 2026 | By Kayla Kitson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kayla-kitson/)
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Prop. 41 would 1) impose new audit requirements for programs funded with state special taxes and 2) prohibit the collection of new state taxes that are excluded from the state’s spending limit. The primary intent of the measure is to invalidate Prop. 40 — the billionaire tax also appearing on the November ballot — but Prop. 41 could also make it harder for the state to meet the needs of Californians in the future.
What Would Prop. 41 Do?
Prop. 41 would amend the state Constitution to impose new rules related to state taxes. The measure would require “financial and performance audits” of programs receiving revenues from special taxes and would also prevent state taxes from being excluded from California’s spending cap, also known as the “Gann Limit.”
Creates New Audit Requirements for Special Taxes
Prop. 41 would create new pre-election and ongoing audit requirements for programs receiving — or proposed to receive — revenues from state-level special taxes. In contrast to a general tax, which can be used for any purpose, a special tax raises revenue for specific purposes.
Pre-election audits: The State Auditor would be required to perform an audit of any program that would be funded by a special tax proposed through a statewide voter initiative. The audit would be required while the initiative is being circulated for signatures — before it officially qualifies for the ballot — and a summary of the audit findings would be included in the voter information guide. The full audit would also be made available to the public.
Ongoing audits: The State Auditor would be required to audit programs receiving revenues from special taxes enacted by the Legislature or approved by voters through a statewide initiative on or after January 1, 2026. These audits would be required every four years.
The audits would assess programs based on specific criteria outlined in Prop. 41, and would require the State Auditor to recommend how programs could reduce costs by at least 10% annually.
The State Auditor would be reimbursed for the costs of these audits with revenues from the relevant special tax. If, however, a special tax initiative fails to qualify for the ballot or is rejected by voters, the audit costs would be absorbed by the state’s General Fund.

Prop. 41 would prevent the state from collecting or enforcing any state tax that is 1) enacted on or after January 1, 2026 and 2) excluded from the state spending cap, also known as the Gann Limit (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/). Under the state Constitution, if state revenues exceed the limit over two consecutive years, the excess must be split equally between refunds to taxpayers and spending on TK-14 education. In effect, the spending limit restricts the ability of state leaders to raise and spend revenue to meet the most pressing needs of Californians.
Conflicts with Other Measures on the Ballot
The California Constitution states that if provisions of multiple measures on the same ballot conflict, the provisions of the measure receiving the higher number of votes will prevail. Prop. 41 broadly specifies that if another measure on the same ballot either 1) imposes different audit rules on special taxes or 2) contains a tax that is exempted from the state spending limit, the entirety of the other measure would be invalidated if Prop. 41 receives more votes.

(https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/) This is because Prop. 40 would create a one-time tax on the wealth of billionaires and exclude the revenues from the state spending limit, which Prop. 41 prohibits.
If both measures were to be approved and Prop. 41 received more votes, Prop. 40 could be invalidated. Alternatively, if both measures pass but Prop. 40 receives more votes, the billionaire tax could be collected, but it is possible that audits would be required of Medi-Cal and other programs receiving Prop. 40 dollars. If both measures pass, there may be litigation regarding the application of conflicting provisions, and the final decision would be made by the courts.

The primary intent of Prop. 41 is to invalidate the Prop. 40 billionaire tax, but it would also create new barriers to raising state revenue and effectively meeting the needs of Californians.
Prop. 41 would also increase state costs related to conducting audits for programs that are often already subject to close scrutiny — reducing funding available to support critical state services. The pre-election audit requirement could dissuade voters from approving special tax initiatives that would raise needed revenue to support and improve state services that help Californians stay healthy, housed, and economically secure. For example, because the State Auditor would be required to recommend options to cut program costs by 10%, voters may assume this means the program is inefficient even if that is not the case.

While policymakers would be under no obligation to implement these recommendations, if they did it could result in cuts to core services rather than simply “inefficient spending.” For example, if a program receiving special tax revenues is already operating efficiently but the Auditor must identify ways that costs could be reduced by 10%, lawmakers may be under pressure to adopt those recommendations — particularly in difficult budget times. Additionally, the “High-Risk” audit program requires the Auditor to periodically review programs or agencies determined to be at high risk for “waste, fraud, abuse, or mismanagement” or those raising concerns related to efficiency or effectiveness.
Prop. 41’s additional audits would increase state costs, reducing the resources available to directly support services for Californians. Moreover, in the case of program audits related to a proposed special tax, the audit costs would be absorbed by the state’s General Fund if the ballot initiative were not enacted, leaving less funding for critical state services like education, health care, and human services.

The audits would assess programs based on specific criteria outlined in Prop. 41, and would require the State Auditor to recommend how programs could reduce costs by at least 10% annually.
The State Auditor would be reimbursed for the costs of these audits with revenues from the relevant special tax. If, however, a special tax initiative fails to qualify for the ballot or is rejected by voters, the audit costs would be absorbed by the state’s General Fund.
Prohibits Taxes That Are Excluded from the State Spending Limit
Prop. 41 would prevent the state from collecting or enforcing any state tax that is 1) enacted on or after January 1, 2026 and 2) excluded from the state spending cap, also known as the Gann Limit (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/). Currently, the measure would apply only to Prop. 40 if both measures pass and Prop. 41 receives more votes, but it could potentially be applied to other tax policy proposals in the future.
California’s spending limit was established by Prop. 4 (1979) and is based on state spending in 1978-79, annually adjusted for population changes and inflation. Under the state Constitution, if state revenues exceed the limit over two consecutive years, the excess must be split equally between refunds to taxpayers and spending on TK-14 education. In effect, the spending limit restricts the ability of state leaders to raise and spend revenue to meet the most pressing needs of Californians.
Conflicts with Other Measures on the Ballot
The California Constitution states that if provisions of multiple measures on the same ballot conflict, the provisions of the measure receiving the higher number of votes will prevail. Prop. 41 broadly specifies that if another measure on the same ballot either 1) imposes different audit rules on special taxes or 2) contains a tax that is exempted from the state spending limit, the entirety of the other measure would be invalidated if Prop. 41 receives more votes.
Prop. 41 is in direct conflict with Prop. 40. (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/) This is because Prop. 40 would create a one-time tax on the wealth of billionaires and exclude the revenues from the state spending limit, which Prop. 41 prohibits.
If both measures were to be approved and Prop. 41 received more votes, Prop. 40 could be invalidated. Alternatively, if both measures pass but Prop. 40 receives more votes, the billionaire tax could be collected, but it is possible that audits would be required of Medi-Cal and other programs receiving Prop. 40 dollars. If both measures pass, there may be litigation regarding the application of conflicting provisions, and the final decision would be made by the courts.

The primary intent of Prop. 41 is to invalidate the Prop. 40 billionaire tax, but it would also create new barriers to raising state revenue and effectively meeting the needs of Californians.
Prop. 41 would also increase state costs related to conducting audits for programs that are often already subject to close scrutiny — reducing funding available to support critical state services. This would come at a time when Californians are already dealing with affordability concerns as well as the consequences of the steep federal cuts to health care and food assistance enacted in H.R. 1 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/timeline-of-funding-cuts-to-medi-cal-and-calfresh-in-california/), signed by President Trump in 2025.
Impacts of Audit Requirements
The pre-election audit requirement could dissuade voters from approving special tax initiatives that would raise needed revenue to support and improve state services that help Californians stay healthy, housed, and economically secure. A summary of the audit would appear in the voter guide, and voters could interpret it as evidence that the programs to be funded are inefficient or ineffective. For example, because the State Auditor would be required to recommend options to cut program costs by 10%, voters may assume this means the program is inefficient even if that is not the case.
Additionally, the requirement for cost-cutting recommendations could result in service cuts with real human impacts. While policymakers would be under no obligation to implement these recommendations, if they did it could result in cuts to core services rather than simply “inefficient spending.” For example, if a program receiving special tax revenues is already operating efficiently but the Auditor must identify ways that costs could be reduced by 10%, lawmakers may be under pressure to adopt those recommendations — particularly in difficult budget times. Those cuts could lead to fewer Californians being served, reductions in benefit levels, or decreased service quality.
While it is clearly important for tax dollars to be spent efficiently and effectively, many state programs are already subject to occasional or ongoing audits. The State Auditor currently performs audits as a result of (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/about-us/#where-our-work-comes-from) existing state laws, legislative requests, and whistleblower tips. Additionally, the “High-Risk” audit program requires the Auditor to periodically review programs or agencies determined to be at high risk for “waste, fraud, abuse, or mismanagement” or those raising concerns related to efficiency or effectiveness.
Prop. 41’s additional audits would increase state costs, reducing the resources available to directly support services for Californians. Moreover, in the case of program audits related to a proposed special tax, the audit costs would be absorbed by the state’s General Fund if the ballot initiative were not enacted, leaving less funding for critical state services like education, health care, and human services.
Impacts of State Spending Limit Provisions
The primary impact of preventing new revenues from being excluded from the spending limit would be the invalidation of the billionaire tax proposed by Prop. 40 — if both measures pass and Prop. 41 receives more votes.

In fact, previous initiatives have explicitly excluded new tax revenues from the limit, such as tobacco taxes enacted under Prop. 10 (1998) and Prop. 56 (2016). However, legal challenges are possible and there is no certainty on how courts would rule.
State policymakers already lack the authority to exclude new tax revenues from the spending cap without voter approval because the cap is enshrined in the state Constitution.

Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 41?

This same group is also opposing Prop. 40 and supporting Prop. 42. Prop. 41 is also endorsed by the California Republican Party, the California Chamber of Commerce, and the California Taxpayers Association.
There is no official campaign against Prop. 41. However, prominent opponents include the Service Employees International Union – United Health Workers West (SEIU–UHW) — the main proponent of the Prop. 40 billionaire tax measure — as well as other labor groups including the California Federation of Teachers and the California Federation of Labor Unions. ​ Yes on Proposition 41: Audits and Accountability for California Tax Dollars.
​
Billions of our tax dollars have flowed into state programs like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. Californians deserve better education, healthcare, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
​
Proposition 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct financial and performance audits of the programs funded by any new tax measure, with results posted publicly. It also requires that all new taxes comply with the state's voter-approved spending limit - so that excess tax revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
If approved by voters, Prop 41 would require ongoing public audits to evaluate spending, identify waste, fraud or abuse, assess whether they are meeting their intended goals, and recommend improvements.
Learn More About Prop 41 (https://www.yesonprop41.org/about-prop41)
Endorsements
YES on Prop 41 is supported by a growing coalition of small businesses, taxpayers, good government advocates, elected officials, accountants and auditing experts.
Prop 41 is also supported by more than a million Californians who helped qualify the measure for the ballot.
Our Coalition (https://www.yesonprop41.org/)
"California families pay billions in state taxes every year and they deserve to see where that money goes and what it delivers. Proposition 41 brings real accountability and clear metrics to state spending. We're proud to support it."
Tracy Hernandez, Co-Founder and CEO of the New California Coalition
"This commonsense, long overdue reform will finally instill some transparency and accountability in state spending - ensuring Californians get better government services for the taxes we pay. It provides an independent, public report card for government spending, so government programs work better for everyone."
​
Pat Fong Kushida, President/CEO of the CalAsian Chamber
"Californians are paying more for everything, including some of the highest taxes in the country. Now more than ever, Californians deserve some relief from our state's high taxes. Prop 41 delivers."
​
Steve Westly, former Controller of California
California can't afford to keep funding programs with no accountability.

​ Yes on Proposition 41: Audits and Accountability for California Tax Dollars.
​
Billions of our tax dollars have flowed into state programs like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. Californians deserve better education, healthcare, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
​
Proposition 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct financial and performance audits of the programs funded by any new tax measure, with results posted publicly. It also requires that all new taxes comply with the state's voter-approved spending limit - so that excess tax revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
If approved by voters, Prop 41 would require ongoing public audits to evaluate spending, identify waste, fraud or abuse, assess whether they are meeting their intended goals, and recommend improvements.
Learn More About Prop 41 (https://www.yesonprop41.org/about-prop41)
Endorsements
YES on Prop 41 is supported by a growing coalition of small businesses, taxpayers, good government advocates, elected officials, accountants and auditing experts.
Prop 41 is also supported by more than a million Californians who helped qualify the measure for the ballot.
Our Coalition (https://www.yesonprop41.org/)
"California families pay billions in state taxes every year and they deserve to see where that money goes and what it delivers. Proposition 41 brings real accountability and clear metrics to state spending. We're proud to support it."
Tracy Hernandez, Co-Founder and CEO of the New California Coalition
"This commonsense, long overdue reform will finally instill some transparency and accountability in state spending - ensuring Californians get better government services for the taxes we pay. It provides an independent, public report card for government spending, so government programs work better for everyone."
​
Pat Fong Kushida, President/CEO of the CalAsian Chamber
"Californians are paying more for everything, including some of the highest taxes in the country. Now more than ever, Californians deserve some relief from our state's high taxes. Prop 41 delivers."
​
Steve Westly, former Controller of California
California can't afford to keep funding programs with no accountability.
Current and former public auditors and a growing list of California residents and transparency advocates support Prop 41. Add your name to the list and join us in promoting greater accountability and better results.

​ Yes on Proposition 41: Audits and Accountability for California Tax Dollars.
​
Billions of our tax dollars have flowed into state programs like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. Californians deserve better education, healthcare, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
​
Proposition 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct financial and performance audits of the programs funded by any new tax measure, with results posted publicly. It also requires that all new taxes comply with the state's voter-approved spending limit - so that excess tax revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
If approved by voters, Prop 41 would require ongoing public audits to evaluate spending, identify waste, fraud or abuse, assess whether they are meeting their intended goals, and recommend improvements.
Learn More About Prop 41 (https://www.yesonprop41.org/about-prop41)
Endorsements
YES on Prop 41 is supported by a growing coalition of small businesses, taxpayers, good government advocates, elected officials, accountants and auditing experts.
Prop 41 is also supported by more than a million Californians who helped qualify the measure for the ballot.
Our Coalition (https://www.yesonprop41.org/)
"California families pay billions in state taxes every year and they deserve to see where that money goes and what it delivers. Proposition 41 brings real accountability and clear metrics to state spending. We're proud to support it."
Tracy Hernandez, Co-Founder and CEO of the New California Coalition
"This commonsense, long overdue reform will finally instill some transparency and accountability in state spending - ensuring Californians get better government services for the taxes we pay. Pat Fong Kushida, President/CEO of the CalAsian Chamber

Steve Westly, former Controller of California
