Endorsement: Prop 41 is a cynical poison pill. And it isn’t the only one on California’s ballot
Prop 41 is one of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
It wouldn’t be a California election without a few petty, revenge-motivated ballot measures.
Proposition 41 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop41-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is one of two poison pill attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax. The measure explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 41 or its cousin initiative Prop 42 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-proposition-42-taxes-22449389.php) pass with a larger number of votes.
Backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php), Prop 41 would require new special taxes that raise money for specific purposes to adhere to state spending rules, while mandating regular audits of the programs they fund.
What’s so bad about ensuring California spends tax revenue wisely?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Well, nothing — if that’s what the measure actually does. But it’s a cheap ruse to nullify Prop 40.
The measure targets an obscure — but extremely consequential — spending rule embedded in California’s Constitution.
Known as the Gann Limit (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4416), that rule prevents the state from spending more money per taxpayer than it did in 1979 — the year voters approved the measure — once adjusted for inflation. Any money the state collects over the limit must be either refunded to taxpayers or spent on certain purposes, such as infrastructure or education.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 41 would prohibit any state tax taking effect on or after Jan. 1, 2026 from sidestepping those requirements. That would neuter Prop 40, which explicitly exempts its one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires from the Gann Limit to backfill federal healthcare cuts.
Loren Kaye, former president of a California Chamber of Commerce-affiliated think tank and a Prop 41 supporter, told us in an endorsement interview that the measure establishes a “level playing field so that everybody is similarly affected once you reach the limit.”
We agree that budget carveouts generally aren’t a good idea. But the Gann Limit isn’t sacrosanct; there are perfectly legitimate reasons for excluding certain revenues from its rules.
Consider California’s Hospital Quality Assurance Fee Program (https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/providers-partners/hospital-quality-assurance-fee-program-hqaf/), which charges hospitals a fee to unlock matching federal healthcare funds and improve services for low-income patients. These funds are currently exempt from the Gann Limit (https://funds.dof.ca.gov/app/download/3158) — a provision voters approved when they green-lighted Prop 52 in 2016 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=52&year=2016).
But the federal government, which has to approve the tax, could easily demand changes to its structure. If that were to happen and Prop 41 passes, the hospital fee program could arguably be considered a “new” special tax — and thus be subject to the Gann Limit, diverting money away from hospitals, argued David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and Prop 41 opponent.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
California’s financial regulations are impossibly complex after decades of ballot-box budgeting. Adding another restriction is only bound to make things worse.
Meanwhile, Prop 41’s audit requirements are, as Darien Shanske, a UC Davis School of Law professor and Prop 41 opponent, put it, meant to be “the chocolate coating that’s supposed to attract people.”
But they’re largely redundant and would decrease efficiency.
Prop 41 requires the state auditor to evaluate programs that will receive funding from new citizen-proposed special taxes and include its findings in the official voter information guide. But the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office already assesses each ballot initiative’s fiscal and practical impact (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop41-110326.pdf) — including at the 25% signature-gathering threshold Prop 41 identifies — and those analyses are included in the voter guide.
The measure’s ongoing audit requirement could also be counterproductive; tax measures typically contain accountability provisions, and adding an untold number of audits to the already overworked auditor’s office could distract from other critical investigations. Furthermore, Prop 41 directs the state auditor’s office to find 10% annual savings in program costs, which is arbitrary and dilutes the office’s independence.

Successive waves of federal cuts to California’s safety net are hitting our shores — and hospitals.
H.R. 1 (aka the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”), the spending plan written by House Republicans and signed into law last year by President Donald Trump, included the largest reductions in U.S. history to food assistance and health care programs. Its intentionally punitive and retaliatory cuts to California’s Medicaid program, Medi-Cal, are projected to cost the state billions of dollars per year and lead to more than a million Californians losing access to health care.
In the Bay Area, these cuts are becoming painful.
As our news organization documented this month, the number of uninsured people in emergency rooms at Santa Clara Valley Healthcare and Alameda Health System has spiked year over year.

Those county-run systems expect to collectively lose more than a billion dollars annually. Notably, while our systems and residents are scrambling to survive, rural America is receiving a $50 billion lifeline from House Republicans and President Trump to protect their health care systems.
Proposition 40 was written to prop up this state’s safety net in the face of these devastating cuts.
However, this measure is the wrong solution to a real problem.
We advise California voters to reject short-sighted, self-sabotaging Proposition 40.
And we recommend they reject equally myopic Propositions 41 and 42 — countermeasures that would not only nullify the billionaires tax but senselessly shackle the state’s fiscal future.
Killing Golden Goose
Proposition 40 risks long-term pain for short-term gain. It’s the ballot equivalent of eating your seed corn.
Here’s how it would work:
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% levy on the net worth of billionaires who were residents of California on January 1. The tax would be due next year, but the state’s 250 or so billionaires could spread the payments out over five years.
Ninety percent of the revenues raised — estimated anywhere between $40 billion to $100 billion, depending on the expert — would fund health care services. The rest would go toward education and food assistance and administration.
What distinguishes this tax isn’t just that it’s targeting a very base of extremely high-net worth individuals but also that it applies retroactively and taxes wealth, not income.
Wealth taxes are unpopular with many economists, including liberal ones, for several reasons:
They can force the sale of productive assets (e.g. stock shares, patents, copyrights, farmland, etc). They’re difficult to administer because determining the value of some intangible assets, unlike income, is more art than a science. And most injuriously, they can encourage capital flight, especially when executed by a state acting alone.
To be sure, the capital hasn’t fled California yet, but the capitalists have been.
Founders of some of Silicon Valley’s largest companies, including Sergey Brin, Larry Page, Peter Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg and Travis Kalanick, have changed their residencies or announced plans to cut ties with the state in one way or another.
What makes Proposition 40 so dangerously self-destructive is California’s extraordinary dependence upon taxing high-income earners. Over the last two decades, the top 1% of earners have paid approximately 45% of the state’s income taxes.
For that reason, the state’s most respected, nonpartisan authority on policy, the Legislative Analyst’s Office, forecasts short-term benefits but long-term costs:
California will “probably collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax,” according to the LAO. But those gains would likely be temporary.
That’s because the LAO worries that “billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away.”
In fact, the LAO projects that billionaires leaving the state would reduce the state’s General Fund revenues by “less than a billion per year.”
But the union that pushed this proposition — Services Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West — wants to gamble.
Its leaders created this to help themselves first and foremost, even at the expense of their typical allies. Opposition to this proposition includes the California Teachers Association, the Association of California School Administrators and the California Professional Firefighters, among several other public and private sector unions. These unions know they’ll suffer when the state’s General Fund takes a hit.
Even the liberal governor of this state is fiercely opposed.
“We can’t let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state’s tax code on its own terms,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom.
We couldn’t agree more.
Self-shackling
To counter Proposition 40, Building a Better California — a political action committee formed earlier this year and backed by Silicon Valley billionaires including Sergey Brin, Vinod Khosla and Eric Scmidt — created two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42.
If either Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax won’t take effect.
The problem is that these two propositions would do far more than nullify the billionaires tax. They would tie the hands of the state far into the future in ways we cannot abide.
Proposition 41
This initiative’s requirement for more audits could be valuable. It would mandate that the State Auditor scrutinize special taxes before they appear on the ballot as well as ongoing programs funded by special taxes. The LAO sees possible savings if the auditor’s recommendations are followed.
However, the problem with Proposition 41 is its second provision. It would prevent any new special taxes from being excluded from the “Gann Limit” — a strict state spending cap enacted in 1979. That means that voters could approve a new tax to address a pressing public need, only to discover that the state cannot spend the money it collects without being constrained by a constitutional limit written half a century ago.
California has changed radically sinc

e the 1970s. And its fiscal rules must leave the state with the flexibility to address issues voters of the era never had to deal with — six-figure college costs, seven-figure mortgages and 13-figure wildfire costs.
The state must not surrender its future freedom of action to defeat a single, one-time tax proposal.
Proposition 42
This initiative would prohibit the state from taxing retroactively. And it would permanently ban the state from any new taxes on ownership of financial assets or other personal properties — think stocks, bonds, intellectual property, artwork, etc.
Taxes on wealth are rarely ideal, and our opposition to Proposition 40 reflects that.
However, we are witnessing an explosion of inequality, and the unpredictable course of AI’s development risks supercharging the gap between the haves and have-nots. Joint Venture Silicon Valley’s latest research shows that 78% of Bay Area residents are concerned AI will increase economic inequality.
Proposition 42 was written by this tech boom’s beneficiaries, who are now among the wealthiest humans in history. If this initiative had limited itself to nullifying Proposition 40, we could have supported it. However, amid this era’s technology- and climate-induced uncertainty, California must keep its options open.
Proposition 42 would needlessly and recklessly narrow them.
Reject Propositions 40, 41 and 42.

By The Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: September 21, 2026 at 2:39 PM PDT | UPDATED: September 21, 2026 at 2:56 PM PDT

The most hotly debated initiative on the November ballot is Proposition 40, which would impose a 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires. As this Editorial Board opined (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/13/endorsement-no-on-proposition-40s-reckless-wealth-tax/) in our opposition, the union-created Billionaire Tax Act would send a dangerous message to current and future entrepreneurs, and “have a chilling effect on investment.”
But two closely related measures, Propositions 41 and 42 (https://www.bakersfield.com/opinion/our-view/our-view-vote-no-on-propositions-40-41-42-tax-propositions-hurt-state-californians/article_1c8492b8-5fb9-4897-9f1c-c9ba56460e0d.amp.html) , have received much less attention — partly because they’re so complicated. By adding related measures to the ballot, opponents of Prop. 40 are hoping that voters approve one of these alternatives that will derail Prop. 40. Because these two measures have elements that contradict Prop. 40, the one that gets the highest vote totals (if voters OK them all) would go into effect.
Adding similar-sounding measures also muddies the waters, thus increasing the likelihood that confused voters vote “no” on all of them — thus accomplishing the main goal of stopping the billionaires’ tax. But our goal isn’t to map out political strategies (https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/nash-game/) . It’s a worthy effort to try to stop a disastrous new tax scheme.
Besides their intended purpose of blocking Prop. 40, the measures could protect taxpayers for years to come.
Specifically, Prop. 41 would require one-time audits of programs that any proposed special taxes would fund. Those audits, which must be completed before the initiative appears on the ballot, would be required to identify ways that such programs could cut annual costs by 10%, per an analysis (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026) from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
While Prop. 40 exempts itself from state spending limits, Prop. 41 also requires new special-tax revenues to count toward the Gann Limit (https://www.sheehystrategygroup.com/news/2026/3/9/californias-state-appropriations-limit-gann-limit) — the 1979 constitutional amendment that caps the revenue the state can spend each year. The state has passed a number of workarounds over the years, but applying new revenues to this formula would potentially require the return of certain additional tax revenues to taxpayers (https://www.yesonprop41.org/about-prop41) and the earmarking of revenues to infrastructure.
Prop. 42 is more straightforward. Per theLAO (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=42&year=2026), the initiative prohibits “new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.” California doesn’t currently tax the ownership of financial assets and only taxes personal property in a limited way (e.g., vehicle license fees), but the measure’s passage “could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes.” It also limits imposition of retroactive taxes.
So would the Editorial Board support these measures even if they were standalone initiatives? The answers are unequivocal: Yes and yes.

California voters should know what Proposition 41 is about. Here is the truth | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 2, 2026 3:42 PM
Prop. 41 would mandate audits for voter-approved special taxes, add ongoing reviews every four years, and may undermine the one-time billionaire tax.
Viorika
Getty Images/iStockphoto
Proposition 41 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317005690.html) is a constitutional amendment billed as a way to add transparency and accountability to ballot measures for special taxes.
Voters should beware. Prop. 41 is supported by Building a Better California, which is funded by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other CEOs and entrepreneurs. These people have created Prop. 41 and Proposition 42 to confuse voters. Why? They want to undermine Proposition 40, the so-called “billionaire tax” also on your ballot.
Perhaps the most controversial measure on your ballot,Prop. 40 would levy a one-time 5% wealth tax (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317269166.html) on California residents with more than $1 billion in total assets.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 41 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317005690.html)
How could Prop. 41 invalidate Prop. 40? As The Bee wrote last week, “One of the most important provisions of Prop. 41 would ban taxes on or after Jan. 1, 2026, that are exempt from state spending limits.” That’s important because Prop. 40, as it is written is exempt from state spending limits.
So if Prop. 41 gets more “Yes” votes than a competing measure such as Prop. 40, the provisions of Prop. 41 would prevail over the provisions of Prop. 40, according to the California Constitution. We don’t believe enough voters understand this because while Prop. 40 has garnered a great deal of attention and debate, Prop. 41 has not.
This is why the collective editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee, (https://www.sacbee.com/)Modesto Bee (https://www.modbee.com/), Merced Sun-Star, (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/) Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) urges a “No” vote on Prop. 41. What’s insidious Prop. 41 is that it is presented as a good governance measure when it’s really about defeating Prop. 40. A majority of our board supported Prop. 40, but it wasn’t unanimous. We understand that it’s controversial to tax California’s most wealthy residents.
But as we wrote in our endorsement, “Billionaires have every right to fight a tax that could cost them billions. But voters should recognize the enormous political power that such wealth can buy and ask why so much of that power has been exercised through campaign committees rather than direct public engagement.”
Included in that power is the use of the initiative process to confuse voters with measures competing with Prop. 40. Voters should know that Prop. 41 has a specific target and is funded and supported by wealthy people with a financial stake in defeating Prop. 40.
We hope Californians vote “No” on Prop. 41.

5 tax measures are on the California ballot. Here’s how to make sense of them all
by
Ben Christopher (https://calmatters.org/author/ben-christopher/)
October 5, 2026 October 4, 2026
Republish
Share this:
Share on X (Opens in new window)
X (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/tax-propositions-ballot-measures/)

Mayra Joseph, a teacher at Sylvia Mendez Elementary School in Berkeley, joined members of the California Teachers Association and supporters of public education in a march to the Capitol as part of RedForEd Day of Action in Sacramento on May 22, 2019. Photo by Rich Pedroncelli, AP Photo
In summary
California voters haven’t had to make so many decisions about tax policy at the ballot since 1990. Our analysis shows voters tend to reject new taxes.
Welcome to CalMatters, the only nonprofit newsroom devoted solely to covering issues that affect all Californians. Sign up for WhatMatters (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/whatmatters) to receive the latest news and commentary on the most important issues in the Golden State.
California voters will soon be asked whether they want to keep taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) the incomes of the rich.
And they’ll be asked whether to start taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) the accumulated wealth of the even richer.
Wait, there’s more. They’ll also get to weigh in on whether we should ban wealth taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/) altogether, subject the money raised by future taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) to a state spending cap and make it harder for voters to pass certain local taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/).
That doesn’t include any of the other propositions on the November ballot that are likely to affect the state budget. Nor does it include the roughly 300 (https://www.caltax.org/elections/local-tax-elections/2026-Local-Elections.pdf?_gl=1*pjll0w*_ga*NTYyOTYwNzgyLjE3NzYyODUwNTE.*_ga_RR9B893WL0*czE3OTA3MjI1MTEkbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGo0MyRsMCRoMA..*_ga_98RV0P0X7N*czE3OTA3MjI1MDckbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGozOSRsMCRoMA..) tax and bond measures that will be popping up in local elections across the state.
And you thought tax season only came in April.
With 14 measures in total, the 2026 California ballot (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) is a busy one. Voters haven’t been presented with this many choices in a decade. It’s an especially active year for tax-related measures — those that hike taxes, cut them, introduce new ones, jettison old ones or change the rules by which taxes are approved and enacted.
Five of those are on the ballot this time around, the most since 1990.
Altogether they have the potential to reshape the state’s finances, beef up or starve some of our largest public spending programs, change the rules around taxation and — if opponents of the proposed wealth tax (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) are to be believed — trigger a Randian exodus of the state’s wellest-to-do.
The ‘black hole’ on the ballot
Though five tax measures are on the ballot, voters are really just seeing three big questions.
The first: Should California be the first state in the nation to introduce a wealth tax?
That question is “the black hole into which all political energy is going right now,” said Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a group that advocates for low taxes.

Three measures — Propositions 40, 41 and 42 — provide opposing answers.
Prop. 40 would slap every Californian with a net worth of at least $1 billion (all approximately 200 of them) with a one-time 5% tax on their wealth, excluding real estate and retirement accounts.
This isn’t an income tax, which skims off a share of a person’s earnings, but a tax on the assessed, unrealized value of investments. Think of this like the property tax that homeowners pay on their houses, except it applies to stocks, bonds, business shares, Bugattis and the occasional machine gun collection (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/#:~:text=machine%20gun%20collection).
A sign displayed at the Billionaire Tax Now booth at the 2026 California Democratic Party State Convention in San Francisco on Feb. 21, 2026. Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that the measure has the potential to raise tens of billions of dollars. Almost all of it would be set aside for the state’s public health insurance programs, which are bracing for dramatic federal cuts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/medi-cal-the-cut-healthcare-threatened/).
That’s assuming the measure passes and survives the blizzard of inevitable legal challenges (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/07/31/opinion-why-flawed-wealth-tax-could-backfire-on-california/). Though a number of countries (https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/eu/wealth-taxes-europe/) have introduced wealth taxes at either the national or regional level, California’s would be the first in the United States.
No surprise, many of the state’s billionaires are pushing back hard. They’re doing that in the usual way, with literally hundreds of millions of dollars in campaign spending. But they’re also doing it with two additional measures on the ballot itself. Prop. 41 would, among other things (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/), ban the state from collecting taxes that circumvent a 1970s state spending limit (https://calmatters.org/politics/2021/05/newsom-tax-rebate/), which Prop. 40 is written to do.
Prop. 42 would ban new taxes on financial assets, private businesses and most other forms of wealth outright — an explicit reversal of Prop. 40.
If both the wealth tax and either of the countermeasures are approved by the voters, the one with the higher vote tally becomes law. That’s why the wealth tax could go down in defeat even if a majority of voters support it (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/).
But voters shouldn’t think of Props. 41 and 42 as mere “no” votes on Prop. 40, said Kayla Kitson, a tax policy analyst at the California Budget & Policy Center, a left-leaning think tank. Prop. 41 would also require the state’s auditor to conduct a “pre-election” analysis of any program set to be funded by a future tax measure and then make recommendations on how to cut costs by 10%.
Beyond banning future wealth taxes, Prop. 42 would also prevent future taxes from applying retroactively before a tax is approved. That could remove the state’s ability to keep people or businesses from avoiding a tax they know is coming, said Kitson.
Two more tax questions
The other two tax measures have nothing to do with the wealth tax. One would make permanent a boosted income tax rate for higher earners. The other would make it harder for local governments to raise certain taxes in the future.
The high-earner tax is the third, and possibly final, installment in a decade-long electoral trilogy.
First proposed by former Gov. Jerry Brown as a temporary (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2308&context=ca_ballot_props) solution to fund education in the fiscal hangover of the Great Recession, the measure sticks a higher tax bracket on the state’s top 2% of earners (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)). Re-authorized by voters in 2016, the tax has (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)) generated between $5 billion and $16 billion annually (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/). Most of that money has gone to schools.
The tax expires in 2030, which is why the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest K-12 public school educators’ union, was eager to put its permanent renewal on the ballot this year. If it fails, the union will have two more chances.
Hence, Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/), which would make the boosted tax rates for individually earned income above $360,000 per year a perpetual part of the state’s tax code.
Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/)’s backstory also goes back nearly a decade.
The measure would hike the share of votes needed to pass certain local taxes. Specifically, these are taxes that raise money for a specific program (https://debtguide-api.treasurer.ca.gov/guide-pages/chapter-1-legally-incurring-debt-state-law-restrictions-on-public-agency-debt-and-revenues/1-4-local-government-revenue-sources-security-for-and-repayment-of-debt/1-4-6-special-taxes) or purpose and that are placed on the ballot by citizen signature-gathering efforts, as opposed to local elected officials. If Prop. 43 passes, this very particular type of tax would need the support of at least two-thirds of local voters.
Business groups and anti-tax advocates have been wanting to put some version of Prop. 43 on the ballot since 2017 (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) when the state Supreme Court ruled that so-called citizen-initiated special taxes only need a simple majority of the vote to pass. The anti-tax advocates got close two years ago, but were stymied by another court ruling (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/). This year, the measure finally made it, but only after negotiations with the Democrats (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/) in the Legislature pared it down, applying the rule to future taxes only.
California tax measures tend to fail
This all makes for a tremendously confusing voting experience for most Californians.
That’s probably bad news for the supporters of these measures, since uncertain voters tend to err on the side of “no,” said Mark Baldassare, survey director at the Public Policy Institute of California.
“When voters aren’t sure how to proceed, staying with the status quo and letting someone else decide at a later date is a safe bet,” he said.
That may partly explain why tax measures, which are inherently complicated and tend to come with unpredictable consequences, fare especially poorly on the ballot. Since 2000, a solid majority (57%) of non-tax ballot measures have passed compared to a mere third of tax propositions.
The sheer number of open questions (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) surrounding the proposed wealth tax (Is it constitutional? Can the state effectively implement it? Will all the billionaires flee to Florida?) puts it on shakier footing with an electorate that tends to reject uncertainty, said Baldassare. A narrow majority of 52% percent of likely voters said they supported the measure in a recent PPIC poll.
The tax on high earners in Prop. 3, may face better odds because it makes permanent an existing tax rather than introducing a new one. In the same poll, 58% of likely voters indicated that they would support the measure.
“When people see the words ‘renew’ or ‘extend’ it gives them a sense that this is the status quo, we’re not being asked to make a change here,” he said.
But Prop. 3’s backers shouldn’t take too much comfort in that. Support for propositions tend to decline (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2019/10/ballot-california-polling-trend-slump-fact-check-myth-data/) as Election Day approaches. The sheer number of tax measures on offer could also inflict voters with “tax fatigue” leading them to vote “no” across the board, said Baldassare.
Then there’s the general political vibe.
Earlier this year, PPIC asked a sample of Californians whether they preferred lower taxes and fewer services or higher taxes and more services.
Fifty-five percent said they’d prefer the lower tax bill (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/).
For the record: An earlier version of this article misstated the last time voters were presented with five or more tax-related measures on the same California ballot. The most recent year was 1990, not 1994.

California voters will soon decide whether to tax billionaires — but even if a majority says yes, the measure could still lose to either of two billionaire-funded measures designed to cancel it out. The billionaire-backed group Building a Better California designed two countermeasures to undermine the wealth tax and create multiple ways to defeat it. Recent polling shows slim majorities of likely voters support not just the wealth tax, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/), but also Propositions 41 and 42, the measures aimed at killing it, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/). “I don’t think that people at this point realize they’re direct countermeasures because there hasn’t been much said about 41 and 42,” said Mark Baldassare, polling director for PPIC. Only one outcome can prevail. If Prop. 40 captures more votes than both 41 and 42, the wealth tax takes effect, voiding the countermeasures. If either 41 or 42 outpolls Prop. 40, the billionaire tax does not take effect. What each measure does Prop. 40 would levy a one-time 5% tax on California residents whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. The tax would apply based on residency as of Jan. 1, 2026 — a date that had passed when the measure qualified for the ballot — meaning billionaires who left the state afterward would still owe it. Most of the money generated would fund healthcare, while a smaller portion would go to education. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the primary proponent and financial backer of the measure, says the tax would raise about $100 billion and is needed to backfill federal healthcare cuts passed last year. Conservatives argue California’s Medi-Cal program has grown too expensive, and new federal policies will help the state cut back. Prop. 41’s real target is Prop. 40: It would require new tax proposals passed after the start of this year to follow the state’s annual spending limit — a cap passed by voters in 1979 (https://apnews.com/article/california-health-coronavirus-pandemic-business-personal-taxes-228c115a231bcc8ec000c7445e83d8e7) during a period of strong anti-tax sentiment that recent voter-approved special taxes have exempted themselves from. The billionaire tax would automatically violate this provision because it isn’t written to comply with the state spending limit. Prop 41 would also require the nonpartisan state auditor to review new tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. If voters approve a tax, some of the revenue generated would pay for the audit; if a proposal fails, the state would be on the hook for the additional cost. Prop. 42 would bar new taxes on personal property such as businesses, investments, retirement accounts, trusts and art collections — the exact things that Prop. 40 targets. It would also prohibit retroactive taxes, which would block a key part of Prop. 40: taxing wealth accumulated before the measure takes effect. Either provision alone is enough to nullify Prop. 40, if the wealth tax wins fewer votes than 41 or 42. “Prop. 42 is a more direct anti-wealth tax proposal,” said Megan Jones, a tax attorney with Holland and Knight. The Legislature has tried unsuccessfully in the past to pass multiple wealth taxes (https://www.ftb.ca.gov/tax-pros/law/legislation/2023-2024/AB259-011923.pdf), Jones said. If Prop. 42 passes, she said, it could limit lawmakers’ ability to try again in the future. Who’s funding the fights Backers of the billionaire tax — primarily SEIU-UHW — have raised about $31 million to pass the measure, mostly from union coffers. The California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) also supports the measure. PROP
3
PROVIDES PERMANENT FUNDING FOR SCHOOLS AND HEALTH CARE BY EXTENDING EXISTING TAX ON HIGH INCOMES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Most State Money Comes From the Income Tax. The income tax is the state’s largest tax. It pays for most spending from the state’s main operating account, the General Fund. The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. The tax applies to most types of income, such as salaries, wages, interest, and profits from the sale of stocks, property, and other investments. The income tax rate starts out low and gradually goes up for taxpayers with higher incomes. For example, a married couple pays a 1 percent tax on the first $21,000 of income, a 2 percent tax on income between $21,000 and $50,000, and a 4 percent tax on income between $50,000 and $80,000.
Prior Voter-Approved Tax Increases. Voters approved Proposition 30 in 2012 to temporarily increase income tax rates on high-income taxpayers. In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55 to extend these higher rates until 2030. The top 2 percent of California taxpayers pay these higher rates. These taxpayers pay about half of all state income taxes.
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. About half of this spending is for schools, community colleges, and the state’s public universities. (The State Constitution sets a minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state’s low-income health insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
PROPOSAL
Proposition 3 makes the higher income tax rates established by Proposition 30 permanent instead of letting them expire in 2031. Figure 1 shows what income tax rates would be if this measure passes and what they would be if it is rejected.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Proposition 3 Would Bring in Between $5 Billion and $15 Billion Each Year. The amount of money brought in by Proposition 3 will go up and down a lot from year to year. This is because much of the revenue comes from taxing income that is closely tied to the stock market, which is always changing. In a weak year, the proposition might bring in around $5 billion in revenue to the state. In a strong year, the proposition might bring in $15 billion in revenue to the state. In most years, revenue would be in between these amounts.
Funding for Education and Other Programs. Proposition 3 results in funding for education and other programs. Roughly 40 percent of the funding would go to schools and community colleges. The rest would go to other state programs. Part of this amount would be set aside in budget reserves the state could use to fund these programs when revenues decline.

Memorandum
To: Interested Parties
From: Brian Galle (UC Berkeley), David Gamage (University of Missouri), and Darien
Shanske (UC Davis)1
Re: Analysis of the Impacts of Propositions 41 and 42 on California’s Public Finance
Date: August 20, 2026
Introduction
In this memorandum, we will discuss the potential impacts of Propositions 41 and
42 on current and future initiatives and legislation, as well as on current California
Medicaid tax programs, starting with possible impacts on Proposition 3, the measure on
November’s ballot to extend personal income tax rate increases.
The purpose of the memo is to identify legal risks raised by the propositions that
prudent citizens should be aware of given the high stakes. We are not arguing how a court
should decide these issues and we do not claim that we are offering the best or most
persuasive legal arguments. We do, however, believe that there is a real risk courts could
reach these outcomes.
Our bottom line is that both propositions are poorly drafted in a manner that could
pose serious threats to California’s fiscal future, with the potential to undermine key
spending programs and potentially cause or worsen future budget crises. That is not
surprising. These are deceptive measures that were drafted quickly to trick voters that
support the billionaire wealth tax (Prop 40) into voting for competing measures that could
undermine that tax. The billionaire funders of these initiatives are acting with reckless
disregard for the collateral damage to California’s fiscal system and indeed they may even
benefit from weakening California’s existing taxes affecting the most wealthy.
Executive Summary
• The audit requirements of Proposition 41 could hamstring Proposition 3 (the
teacher-sponsored measure to fund education with taxes on million-dollar earners)
or invalidate it outright.
1 Institutional affiliations are listed for identification purposes only.
2
• The audit requirements of Proposition 41 could similarly hamstring many other
revenue raising measures, such as (for example) a tax on large employers who have
many employees on Medi-Cal.
• The prohibition on easing the state appropriation limit in Proposition 41 could
undermine many existing and proposed taxes to fund California’s contributions to
Medi-Cal, including current MCO taxes and the Hospital Quality Assurance Fee
(HQAF).
• The limitations on taxing personal property in Proposition 42 could impact the
ability of the state to tax capital gains income, whether as part of Proposition 3 or
otherwise.
• The limitation on taxing personal property in Proposition 42 could frustrate any
future attempt to reform California’s Vehicle License Fee, a backbone tool for
financing a wide array of local services.
Proposition 41
Proposition 41 makes two significant changes to California law. First, it adds many
new audit requirements, specifically pre-election audits of programs that would receive
funds from a proposed special tax initiative; and recurring audits, every four years, of
programs receiving moneys from special taxes enacted on or after January 1, 2026,
whether enacted by the Legislature or by initiative.2 Second, the proposition prohibits
collecting any state tax enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026 that is exempted
or excluded from the appropriations limit of Article XIIIB, the so-called Gann limit, whether
the exemption comes from an outside-the-General-Fund special fund whose spending is
not counted or from raising the limit itself. Proposition 41, secs. 3, 4(b). The obvious point
of this second change, hidden deep in the Proposition 41 text, is to nullify Proposition 40.
But both changes would likely weaken California public finance by threatening California’s
ability to raise revenues and fund spending programs.
On the Merits
Prop 41 targets the primary (and, in many cases, the only plausible remaining) way
that state tax policy can be done and that state services can be adequately funded. Any
increase in taxes enacted by the Legislature requires a two-thirds supermajority of each
house.3 Statewide initiatives, by contrast, can raise taxes by majority vote. Not surprisingly,
most major tax policy changes over recent decades have therefore occurred via initiative.
Since voters are unlikely to support tax increases for unspecified purposes, the limits on
2 Prop. 41, Secs. 1, 2.
3 Art. XIIIA, Sec. 3(a).
3
measures adopting taxes for specified purposes tilts the deck against most of those
measures. Even if there were eventually an attempt to change Prop 41 through another
ballot measure, the pre-election audit requirement would still apply to any special tax
initiatives on that ballot.
The audits that Prop 41 would impose are slanted to make it more difficult to adopt
and fund new programs. Consider, for example, that a pre-election audit must consider:
“How the program's costs compare to any analogous programs in the non-government
sector”; and also: “Recommendations on how the program could achieve a budgetary
savings of at least 10% annually.” The audits would thus institutionalize a cost-cutting,
private-sector-comparison framework, and the executive summary of the pre-election
audit would be printed in the voter guide immediately after the Legislative Analyst’s
impartial analysis.4
In sum, every proposed special tax initiative would come before the voters bundled
with an official analysis oriented toward finding savings and private alternatives. These
expensive, burdensome and largely redundant5 requirements would hinder special tax
initiatives, making them more difficult to pass and less effective if passed.
The second provision regarding the Gann limit would double down on what has
proven to be a disastrous set of fiscal policies. The existing Gann limit works by capping
government expenditures over a given two-year period. Excess amounts must be split
between taxpayer rebates and education.6 The cap increases only to the extent of growth in
California population and cost of living.7 Given the increasing demands on the state
government, future uncertainties, and the changing nature of federal assistance, the limit
does not act so much as a ceiling as a vise squeezing out funds for core services.8 For
example, what happens if the state government needs to spend more on (say) wildfires? Or,
4 Sec. 1(e)(2).
5 California law is already full of audit requirements and indeed has a powerful and independent
state auditor (Govt Code 8543 et seq, see especially GC 8546.1) that issues regular,
https://www.auditor.ca.gov/reports/, and, often critical, reports about state operations. See, e.g.,
https://www.auditor.ca.gov/reports/reponses-2025-108-all/. And sometimes the state requires
particular audits. See, e.g., Bus. And Prof. Code 6145(b). As further discussed, the income tax
extensions authorized by Proposition 3 are already subject to audit. Art. XIII, Sec. 36(g).
6 Art. XIIIB, Sec. 2.
7 Art. XIIIB, Secs. 8(e), (f).
8 Making a similar point, here is Jason Sisney (an Assembly budget insider): “Therefore, if revenues
push the state to its Gann limit, non-Proposition 98 programmatic spending (such as annual tax-
supported spending on health and human services (HHS), housing, universities, prisons, state
employees and natural resources programs) probably would have to be cut more in this situation.”
https://jasonsisney.substack.com/p/state-moving-closer-to-its-appropriation
4
what if the state government must spend more to backfill vicious cuts from the federal
government?
The state has hit the Gann limit recently (2022) and is about $30 billion under the
Gann limit currently. Suppose Prop 3 passes without incident and the AI boom does lead to
substantial increases in revenue. At that point, the state will be close to the limit. Any
possible new initiatives for education, child care, housing or wildfire abatement could then
well go over the limit.
Threats to Proposition 3
The audit requirements of Proposition 41 arguably apply to Proposition 3 because
Proposition 3 would seem to impose a “special tax” enacted “by a statewide initiative
measure on or after January 1, 2026.” Sec. 2(a)(1). Proposition 3 makes permanent the
existing 1% tax surcharge on income above $1 million that is set to expire in 2030; all of its
revenues are earmarked primarily for education. It thus likely involves a “special tax,”
which is “a tax that can only be used to fund specific, as opposed to unlimited, purposes”
(according to Prop 41), because the Education Protection Account revenues added by Prop
3 may be used only for specified education and health care purposes. Sec. 4(d) of
Proposition 41; Article XIII, Sec. 36(e) of Proposition 3.
As for whether Proposition 3 was enacted after January 1, 2026, a court could
plausibly find that a tax first approved in 2012 is “enacted” in 2026 when the voters delete
its sunset. The new provision is different than the old in that it will never expire; the post-
2030 tax will exist only because of the 2026 vote; and the adoption of the extension is itself
literally an enactment.9
Thus, Proposition 41 might plausibly be interpreted by courts as applying to
Proposition 3. If so, Proposition 41 would require onerous and burdensome audits of the
programs it funds.
Further, if both measures pass and Proposition 41 receives more affirmative votes,
every provision of Proposition 3, including the rate extension itself, could be ruled void.
The terms of Proposition 41 state that it nullifies other conflicting 2026 initiatives if it
receives more votes. Prop 41 defines conflicting measures as “another initiative measure
9 Notably, neither Prop 41’s prohibition nor its grandfather clause discusses extensions, even
though California drafters know how to address extensions expressly. For instance, Proposition 218
reaches taxes that governments “impose, extend, or increase,” and the Proposition 218
implementation statute treats removal of a sunset as an extension. Art. XIII C, Sec. 2(b); Gov. Code
Sec. 53750(e).
5
that …imposes different audit rules on special taxes.” Sec. 5(a). Proposition 3 carries
forward Proposition 30’s audit rules, and those rules are different from Proposition 41’s.10
Threats to the MCO Tax
The sloppy drafting of Proposition 41 implicates policies far beyond Proposition 3.
We will briefly consider spending on health care.
Start with the Managed Care Organization (MCO) tax, which California expects to
generate as much as $8 billion annually in federal matching funds. There are now arguably
two separate MCO provisions that will take effect after 2026 authorization, both of them
threatened by Prop 41.
The first is SB 125, enacted in June 2026, which imposes a tax of $8.85 per enrollee
per month for 2027 through 2029 and deposits the proceeds in the new Medi-Cal Stability
Fund, dedicated to specified Medi-Cal purposes.11 SB 125 is a special tax enacted after
January 1, 2026, so under Prop 41 each Medi-Cal program receiving its moneys would face
recurring State Auditor financial and performance audits, with the private-sector
comparisons and ten percent savings recommendations, and with the Auditor reimbursed
from the tax revenues themselves.12 As explained above, this would be very burdensome
and problematic. And because the Stability Fund broadly co-funds managed care payments
and rates, there is a further risk that a court would rule that the auditable “programs”
include major portions of Medi-Cal managed care, rather than just the marginal SB 125
dollars. Thus Prop 41 could require the state to pay for audits recommending how to
privatize Medi-Cal and slash it by 10%.
Proposition 41 also deprives the state of flexibility to keep SB 125 effective in the
future. As enacted, the SB 125 tax uses up capacity under the Gann limit, narrowing room
for other revenue needs. SB 125 also sunsets in 2030, at a time when there might not be
room under the Gann limit available for renewal. In both cases, the state could be left
choosing between crowding out other priorities under the limit or losing the tax—and the
10 Indeed, on one point the two measures give seemingly incompatible commands about the same
dollars. Proposition 41 provides that the State Auditor “shall be reimbursed from the revenue
generated by the special tax” for the reasonable costs of its audits. Sec. 2(d). Section 36 (Proposition
3), however, provides that moneys deposited in the Education Protection Account for education
“shall not be used to pay any costs incurred by the Legislature, the Governor, or any agency of state
government,” and it separately bars using Account funds for administrative costs. Art. XIII, Sec.
36(e)(5), (6).
11 Ch. 24, Stats. 2026 (SB 125), adding a new Article 7.2 to the Welfare and Institutions Code; the
new tax is expressly made not subject to Proposition 35's chapter. See Dept. of Finance, Manual of
State Funds, Fund 3492 (Medi-Cal Stability Fund classified as included).
12 Sec. 2.
6
federal matching grants it secures— altogether. This would of course have major negative
implications for state funding of Medi-Cal.
In addition, in 2024, Proposition 35 implemented a permanent MCO tax starting in
2027.13 Proposition 35 also used a provision of the Gann limit, Art. XIIIB, Sec. 4, to lift the
ceiling for four years in order to accommodate the new spending.14 Recall that Prop 41
prohibits collecting any tax that modifies the Gann limit if the tax takes effect on or after
January 1, 2026. 15 There is thus a significant risk Prop 41 would prevent Proposition 35
from taking effect.
Threats to the Hospital Quality Assurance Fee (HQAF)
Prop 41 could also bar modifications to the Hospital Quality Assurance Fee (HQAF),
including modifications that might be required by the federal government in order for the
HQAF to remain in effect. The HQAF draws down billions of dollars in federal matching
funds for hospital payments, and the federal government approved the 2025 program in
June 2026. HQAF funds are exempt from the Gann limit.16 A court might conclude that an
HQAF modified after January 1, 2026 “takes effect” after that date for purposes of Prop 41.
That would prevent California from modifying or improving the HQAF, even if required by
federal rule changes, such as those now pending. A Trump or other hostile HHS aware of
this dilemma might go out of its way to require HQAF changes that it knows California
cannot implement.17
We expect that California would argue the HQAF is not subject to Prop 41 limits
because it is a “fee,” not a “tax,” but a court might well rule otherwise. This is because
Proposition 41 does not define “state tax” and because California generally interprets
“taxes” quite broadly. See Art. XIIIA, Sec. 3(b). A multibillion dollar charge that funds not
only services for the payors but also transfers to others, as the HQAF does, will be quite
likely to face a plausible challenge that it constitutes a tax and not a fee.
Note that the stakes of these threats are further magnified because the statute
makes it so that the hospital fee becomes inoperative if a lawsuit is filed and a preliminary
13 Welf. & Inst. Code § 14199.123(b).
14 Proposition 35, Sec. 2.
15 Prop. 41, Secs. 3, 4(b)(2).
16 Cal. Const., art. XVI, § 3.5(d); Dept. of Finance, Manual of State Funds (Hospital Quality Assurance
Revenue Fund classified as excluded from the state appropriations limit). The Finance fund record
predates Proposition 52 and is based on the notion that the revenues are not proceeds of taxes;
Proposition 52 is the source of the constitutional exclusion.
17 It could also be argued that the HQAF takes effect after Jan. 1, 2026 even if it is not modified after
that date. This is because its mechanics operate through discrete, numbered program periods, and
each of these has its own fee model and its own federal approval. Thus, a period beginning after
January 1, 2026 could well be characterized as the tax taking effect after that date.
7
injunction or other order results in a loss of federal financial participation or any net
General Fund cost.18 A qualifying preliminary injunction or other order could thus obstruct
the program well before any final judgment, even if the challenge might ultimately fail on
the merits.
Threats to the Skilled Nursing Facility Fees
Yet another health funding source at risk from Proposition 41 is the skilled nursing
facility quality assurance fee (SNF-QAF). Like the HQAF, this is a provision intended to
generate federal matching funds, and it is expected to bring in several billion dollars over
the next 5 years. The SNF-QAF was extended by the Legislature in July 2026 through the
end of 2027,19 and its revenues are also classified as exempt from the Gann limit. Thus, a
court could well decide based on these arguments that collection of the fee should be
barred, thereby cutting off the federal matching funds and supplemental payments to
nursing facilities that the program exists to generate.
Single-Subject Threats
It is also possible that Prop 41 could make it impossible for any future initiative to
be exempt from the Gann limit, yoking California to the fiscal system of the distant 1970s in
perpetuity. The California Constitution requires that an initiative “embracing more than
one subject” may not be submitted to the voters or have any effect.20 Because Proposition
41's restrictions would be added to the Constitution (if they pass), a future revenue
measure could escape the restrictions only by pairing its new tax with a constitutional
override of Proposition 41. This thus gives opponents of any future revenue measure a
powerful new tool for challenging such measures through litigation. That is, future
initiatives would have to have what are arguably two subjects: their own goals, and also
disabling the Prop 41 rules.
It might be objected in regard to this that provisions suspending Prop 41 rules that
would frustrate a future initiative are part of a single subject, much as today many
initiatives suspend the Gann limit . But would such a structure be effective? The initiative
would now both impose a tax and change the separate constitutional rule that Prop 41
added as to the Gann limit. Arguably, a court could find that these are two separate subjects
that would require two separate measures. Although California’s single-subject test is
lenient, and a combined measure could thus potentially survive challenge, even just the
18 Welf. & Inst. Code § 14169.72.
19 SB 165, signed July 6, 2026; see Dept. of Finance, Manual of State Funds, Fund 3213 (Long-Term
Care Quality Assurance Fund classified as excluded).
20 Art. II, Sec. 8(d).
8
prospects of litigation and the increased potential for challenges could add uncertainty,
substantial and burdensome costs, and delays to any future revenue measures.
Relatedly, this same single-subject concern suggests (to us) that Proposition 41 (and
also 42) might be constitutionally infirm themselves as violating the single-subject rule. We
might suggest that a court should strike them down if they should pass.
Proposition 42
Proposition 42 does at least three things: 1) it offers unneeded21 protection of
retirement assets; 2) it prohibits a tax “on the ownership or control of . . . individually-
owned assets” and 3) it prohibits retroactive taxes. As with Proposition 41, though, Prop
42’s deceptive framing and sloppy language has the potential to cause great collateral
harm.
Threats to Proposition 3
Because of Proposition 42’s broad language, taxpayers will likely argue that it
shields them from the effects of Prop 3. Again, Prop 3 extends the existing but temporary
1% additional income tax on incomes above $1 million, which is set to expire in 2030. Like
Proposition 41, Proposition 42 exempts taxes “in effect, imposed, and first collected” before
2026, and it is uncertain whether a court would find that Proposition 3 qualifies for that
exemption. A court might deem the permanent post-2030 additional income tax on
incomes above $1 million as a new tax because

Prop
41
CA
Prop
41
|
Constitutional Amendment
Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues From State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes.
Requires audits of citizen initiatives for special taxes. Imposes spending limits on all new special taxes.
SPUR's Recommendation
More transparency and accountability in government spending are worthy objectives. However, the Legislative Analyst’s Office and the state auditor already have the authority to evaluate policies and programs to ensure they are equitable and efficient. Prop. 41 was primarily placed on the ballot to defeat Prop. 40, a measure to tax billionaires. In addition, it would constrain local and state governments’ ability to raise revenue now and in the future for much-needed housing, transportation, infrastructure, and social services, which are already facing cuts at the federal and state levels.
Vote NO
What Prop. 41 Would Do
Proposition 41 would require the state auditor, working with the Legislative Analyst’s Office, to conduct an independent review of any state-level citizen initiative that aims to create a new special tax once it reaches 25% of the required signature threshold to be placed on the ballot. (Special taxes differ from general taxes in that they dedicate revenue to a specific purpose.) All new state-level special taxes would be audited every four years.
Additionally, any new special taxes passed after January 1, 2026 — whether proposed through legislation or through voter initiatives — would be subject to the Gann Limit, a voter-imposed revenue spending limit explained in the Backstory section below.
The audit of proposed citizen initiatives would examine the individual programs that would receive funding through the special tax and assess whether the programs are sufficiently cost-efficient in their hiring and operating practices. It would recommend how the programs could save 10% of their costs. The audit information would be included in the voter information guide, which would increase printing and mailing costs by a few hundred thousand dollars per initiative, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
If a special tax passes, the state auditor would be required to conduct audits every four years to assess spending, evaluate efficiency, and recommend improvements. The auditor would consider public input when measuring the program’s effectiveness. The revenues generated would cover implementation costs. However, the state would pay the initial audit cost if voters rejected the special tax.
Prop. 41 is a countermeasure to the so-called billionaire tax, Prop. 40 (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/ca-prop-40-billionaire-tax). If both measures pass, the one receiving more votes would prevail.
The Backstory
Special taxes are taxes whose revenues are dedicated to a specific purpose rather than contributing to the state’s general fund budget. The State Legislature can levy special taxes with two-thirds voter approval, or an initiative placed on the ballot by voter signatures can do so with a simple majority (50% plus one vote). Currently, special taxes have no audit requirements or spending caps.
Since the late 1970s, California has faced numerous tax limitations through Prop. 13 and other constitutional amendments. The Gann Limit imposes requirements on how the state can spend General Fund revenues. If the state’s revenues exceed the Gann Limit — a dollar amount based on the state’s spending level in 1978–1979, adjusted for population and per capita income — half of revenues over the limit must be allocated to K–14 education and the other half returned to taxpayers. 1 Historically, the Gann Limit has rarely affected distribution of the state’s revenues, but if the state experiences strong income gains (including business/corporate/stock gains) over the limit, it could result in decreasing investment in state priorities such as housing, health care, economic development, and infrastructure.
The fiscal impacts of Prop. 41 are unknown. Adding pages to the voter information guide would cost money, but the audits could also create savings. If this measure prevents the state from raising new revenues from future taxes, it could have a significant negative fiscal impact in the longer term.
Prop. 41 is a countermeasure to Prop. 40, a one-time special tax on individuals with more than $1 billion in assets. Prop. 40 is intended to offset federal funding cuts to critical social safety net programs, including Medi-Cal, CalFresh, and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. The revenues generated from Prop. 40 would be exempt from the Gann Limit.
Prop. 41 was placed on the ballot through a signature-gathering effort led by Building a Better California, which is funded by Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other billionaires. It requires a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass. If it passes with more votes than Prop. 40, it would nullify Prop. 40. (Building a Better California has also placed Prop. 42 (https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/ca-prop-42-personal-property-taxes), a separate countermeasure to Prop. 40, on the ballot.)
Equity Impacts
Restricting spending from special taxes could negatively affect efforts to fund health care, food assistance, and other programs that disproportionately benefit lower-income Californians and communities of color.
Pro
Audits of proposed citizen initiatives could help ensure that the programs they would fund are cost-effective.
Cons
Prop. 41 was placed on the ballot to prevent a competing measure from succeeding. It could affect the state’s ability to raise revenue from other tax measures in the future.
Applying spending limits to new revenue measures could constrain local and state governments’ ability to fund urgent priorities amid unprecedented federal and state budget cuts.
Vote NO
on
Prop
41
-

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 41, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026), would require an audit on new or increased special taxes before they appear on the ballot and ongoing audits of programs that receive funding from special taxes. Special taxes may also be subjected to spending limits.
Voting “yes” would mean that the state auditor reviews programs funded by special taxes before they’re on the ballot and on an ongoing basis while opening the possibility that spending limits are attached to the special taxes.
Related Articles
We asked the No on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the No on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should reject the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/)
Because of the requirements it imposes on new special taxes, voting “yes” could also mean that Proposition 40 (the “billionaire tax”), even if it gets enough votes, is stopped from becoming law if the courts determine that it conflicts with Prop. 41.
Voting “no” would mean that the state auditor’s role in reviewing government programs stays the same, as would spending limit requirements.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Prohibit Excluding New State Taxes from Spending Limit and Require Special Tax Audits Initiative, favor the increased transparency, oversight and analysis regarding special taxes. More information for the voters.
Generally, opponents don’t like the extra restrictions on how voter-approved tax money is raised and spent and how the programs meant to be funded could be weakened or stalled. They also suggest that Props. 41 and 42 were heavily supported by billionaires in order to defeat Prop. 40.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem is Prop. 41 solving?
State spending is up 79% since 2019. Every year, billions of taxpayer dollars flow into state programs, like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. Californians deserve better education, health care, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned tax money we pay to the state.
While this is a city wide example, it’s exactly the kind of reason why we need audits and transparent accountability before it’s too late to put programs back on track: Audit: San Jose failed to adequately track $300 million in homelessness spending (https://www.mercurynews.com/2024/04/13/audit-san-jose-failed-to-adequately-track-300-million-in-homelessness-spending/).
Why is this the best solution to the problem?
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by new special tax measures, with the results posted publicly in the state Voter Information Guide.
This ensures voters have detailed information about the programs they’re being asked to raise taxes to fund.
If taxes are approved, Prop. 41 also requires ongoing public audits of the programs funded by those taxes to evaluate spending, identify waste, fraud or abuse, assess whether they are meeting their intended goals and recommend improvements.
It also requires that all new taxes comply with the state’s voter-approved spending limit — so that excess tax revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
Why is it necessary to audit a tax proposal before it even officially qualifies for the ballot?
Providing pre-ballot information about proposed initiatives is very typical. The Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) and the attorney general are required by state law to provide pre-ballot information on every measure that is filed.
Prop. 41 is actually much narrower — the auditor only commences with an audit once a measure collects 25% of the signatures needed to qualify for the ballot; and it only applies to initiatives that increase taxes.
Prop. 41 requires the independent state auditor to conduct pre-election financial and performance audits of the programs to be funded by proposed new state special taxes. The state auditor’s findings must be shared widely with the public, including in the state’s official Voter Information Guide.
This pre-election audit will give voters clear, unbiased information on the programs a proposed tax would support. These audits are more extensive than any existing information provided to voters. This fills in a critical gap in the information provided to voters. The current initiative analyses from the LAO are required by law to provide only a description of the measure. Alternatively, under Prop. 41 the auditor will also provide voters a performance evaluation of programs funded by new taxes.
If a proposed tax fails to make the ballot, the state’s general fund still has to pay for the audit. Why should taxpayers foot the bill for failed political ideas?
The value to voters in seeing this detailed information about programs before they’re asked to vote far outweighs the marginal cost of conducting the audit and printing it in the Voter Guide.
Again, this is very typical under the status quo. The LAO and the attorney general already have to provide a description and a title and summary for each and every initiative measure — including those that fail — and the General Fund pays for those costs. It is also important to recognize that the extra costs imposed on the General Fund by Prop. 41 are exceedingly small. The LAO found that Prop. 41 would impose only minimal costs upon the General Fund. Further, providing more impartial, expert information to voters when decided to approve higher taxes is money well spent.
This also fails to take into account Prop. 41’s upside. As the LAO noted in the Voter Guide, Prop. 41 would result in taxpayer savings or improved services by implementing the auditor’s recommendations.
Prop. 41 contains conflict provisions stating that if it receives more “yes” votes than a competing tax measure like Prop. 40 (the billionaire wealth tax), then Prop. 40 is nullified entirely. How do proponents respond to claims that Prop. 41 is merely a “poison pill” designed to defeat the wealth tax rather than a stand-alone oversight tool?
California has faced issues with ineffective and inefficient state spending for years: homelessness, state technology programs, EDD are just a few recent examples. Prop. 40 is just the latest proposal that would fuel ineffective spending.
Prop. 40 seeks to raise tens of billions of dollars in new tax revenue, but contains zero transparency, accountability or safeguards to ensure the money is spent as intended. For instance, Prop. 40 contains no safeguards to ensure that billions of dollars don’t flow to health insurance company profits and CEOs under the guise of “saving health care.”
