content.text:
se, even if the Leg. had approved some such prop. (the CA Democratic Party
Darien's Guide to the California Ballot Propositions: November 2026 Elections 10 of 15
supports it), with Governor Newsom opposing it (along with most other tax increases), it wouldn’t have
become law. In other words, sometimes only an initiative is able to grapple with a hot issue.
Prop. 40 taxes walth to pay for health care. So far, few politicians (nor most others) have
offered real ways to reduce health care costs (since they’re mostly ignoring Single Payer Healthcare –
which the public tends to support!). (Do you want to know more about why? Cal Matters has a good
(fairly short!) article about a 181-page report on that!) And health care costs keep on increasing.
Worse yet, due to Trump’s huge federal health care cuts, CA faces millions in costs in 2027 –
and, possibly, beyond. So a healthcare workers’ union, Service Employees International Union-United
Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW), put together this proposal to keep the workers their jobs and
our state its healthcare funding: Tax the very rich (who got Trump tax cuts)! And – since the rich
manage to avoid most income taxes – this tax is based on the value of their assets, their wealth.
In response, the threatened billionaires have a massive campaign (at nearly $200 million)
against 40 – including putting the competing Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. If either of those passes
with more votes than Prop. 40, then their provisions would block 40 – even if 40 gets a majority vote.
And also some non-billionaires oppose 40. Will it drive wealthy people and businesses out of
California, reducing our tax base and annual state budget revenues? Good question, but I suggest CA
can manage well enough. CA offers many advantages to individuals and businesses (even beyond
beautiful natural wonders and reasonable weather): many well educated people, a location that attracts
employees, good freeways, international ports, commercial centers, etc. Would the wealthy leave Calif.
over this one-time tax? That’s likely the biggest question on 40. And no one knows the answer,
We do know what 40 woulf enact, and that is only one thing: a “wealth tax”, at 5%, on
Californians whose net worth exceeded $1 billion as of 1/1/26. That net worth would be measured
based on assest like stocks, bonds, cars, privately owned businesses, intellectual property, and art and
other collections. Entirely excluded from the calculation and tax would be real estate (already covered
under property taxes) and nearly all pensions and retirement accounts. (Nearly all? Well, if you’ve
got a Roth with over $10 million, that could count.) Only some 200 Californians would be subject to
the tax (out of about 34 million Californians) – not likely you, not likely ever.
The resulting revenues – some tens of billions of dollars – would go 90% to “health care
services for the public” and 10% to other public-friendly services.
A lot of this info is in your very helpful Official Voter Information Guide. Not in there are the
reservations that some progressives have and their objections to aspects of 40. They note that other
state programs need funds, too – 90% for healthcare only? However, this measure does give the
Legislature some flexibility in the kinds of healthcare spending, and the Prop. 40 money frees us other
revenues for other kinds of programs, beyond what is under the remaining 10%. Others point to con-
cerning collateral effects: sowing division in the labor movement between different sectors, instead of
seeking a more collaborative approach. And, further – once Prop. 40 funds are used up – will there be
any money for currently existing programs, like ob-gyn services from Planned Parenthood?
Will the Legislature seek to amend the tax after passage, as 40 allows and some are concerned
about? Of course, legislative flexibility is something helpful that initiatives usually lack, so that’s
Darien's Guide to the California Ballot Propositions: November 2026 Elections 11 of 15
helpful. In any case, the Leg. membes worry about re-election; I expect they’ll be very careful not to
alienate their voters with either a weaker tax or one that extends to more people or other assets.
Then again, if 40 proves to be surprisingly popular, and even successful, this one-time tax might
open up the public imagination! The idea of wealth taxes could enter the realm of serious political
discourse, and that could be what really scares the very wealthy.
I do wish for us to be able to maintain people’s access to health care in California, which is not
only an ethical position but also a sound public health practice (and, often, a money saver – vs. ER
visits and care after something is severe). And I don’t see other promising options on the near horizon.
In my philosophy of governance, I support 40 because it funds a robust society by taxing the
wealth that society helps generate, with all our (costly) infrastructure,. And I believe Calif. has the
capacity to generate new wealth.
At the same time, how feasible is Prop. 40? On the one hand is the challenge of accurately
assessing individuals’ wealth, and on the other hand are the many legal challenges the wealthy are
likely to assay.
What if 40 does not pass (or passes but with fewer votes than Props. 41 or 42, so that it’s
invalidated by the “poison pill” in those two props)? Or, even if it does go into effect, it may get tied
up in the courts for years. If so my wish may become another challenging project. But let’s try!
Yes – P&F, Dem, Cour, CFT, CNA, UHW (of course!)
No – CTA, PPar, Jarv, Ref, CofC, Rep
• Prop. 41 – To Make the 1979 Gann Limit Live on and on – No
Overall, 41 is targetted at 40 – at the least, to foment confusion but also to stop 40 if 41 gets
more votes. Beyond that, 41 would bind future voters by restricting the possibilities to enact flexible
responses to future state financial needs.
Remember the Gann Limit? I talked about that fairly extensively above, under Prop. 2. Please
review that, because I think I presented a strong case that the Gann Limit has become harmful. In my
view (apparently supported by former Calif. Controller Betty Yee’s 2022 report). That limit makes the
CA budget almost unworkable; it would be a mistake to stiffen its effects!
Nonetheless, Prop. 41 basically seeks to give the 1979 Gann Limit a transfusion of fresh blood;
41 would require all future propositions to be bound by that limit.
The Gann constraints are from an era that sought to severely limit government expenditures,
even when the government had the revenues to support them. However, I believe more voters now
appreciate government programs. In more recent years, propositions seeking special income sources
(I.e., taxes) have been careful to include in their language an exemption from the Gann Limit. (For
example, Prop. 40 does so – as it would have to, since its revenue would go way beyond what that limit
allows.) The fact that so many other props. have also done so – and yet have often been approved by
the voters – is an indication that the severe restrictions of the Gann Limit are no longer realistic.
As you can see from the supporter and opponent list, some folks do want to return to that era of
fewer government programs. Their attitude about such programs is reflected in the actual language of
Darien's Guide to the California Ballot Propositions: November 2026 Elections 12 of 15
the prop., which at one point (in (d) of section 1 – bold added) states, “Before asking taxpayers to pay
even more of their hard-earned money to support programs that are ineffective...”. It’s likely that
those same folks would oppose Prop. 40, and Prop. 41 serves those interests with a “poison pill”. (I
explained more about poison pills near the end of the Prop. 3 discussion.) If 41 passes with more votes
than 40, then all of 40 is invalid.
Prop. 41 also includes a requirement for a state audit on any tax proposals and/or initiatives.
The audit will look for possible spending cuts. If such propositions are defeated – or don’t even qualify
for the ballot – the state would be stuck with paying millions a year for the required audits.
It’s all a bad idea!
No – P&F, FCL, Dem, UHW, Lgue, ACLU
Yes – Jarv, Ref
• Prop. 42 – No Wealth Taxes and No Retroactive Ones (so no Prop. 40) – No
I’m assuming you’re familiar with Prop. 40 (or see above!). Remember how it imposes a tax on
certain kinds of wealth (not retirement accounts!)? Prop. 42 would forbid all that: no wealth taxes.
Remember how 40 also imposes its tax on that wealth as of 1/1/26 – a retroactive date (so wealthy
folks can’t easily get around the tax)? Prop. 42 would forbid that, too: no retroactive taxes.
Prop. 40 isn’t the sole target. If this prop. passes, no wealth taxes of any kind may be
considered for California. Why, before any attempts, would voters rule out an entire class of taxation?
The financial support for 42 – nearly $100 million raised so far (per Cal Matters) – comes
mostly from the same billionaires opposing Prop. 40, although some other groups (generally
conservative), especially profession-related ones (peace officers, firefighters, building and
construction), are also supporting 42.
While we’ve learned that nothing is impossible in politics, the claim of an alleged threat to
pensions and retirement accounts is a red herring.
This prop. is on the ballot particularly to oppose Prop. 40: Like 41, Prop. 42 has a “poison pill”.
(See explanation near the end of the Prop. 3 discussion.)
No – UHW, P&F, FCL, Dem, Lgue, ACLU
Yes – Jarv, Ref
• Prop. 43 – A Tough Two-Thirds Vote Requirement on Local Tax Measures – No
For almost any measure, a 2/3 requirement to pass means it hardly ever passes! We’ve already
seen that effect in a number of proposals by local governments (which already suffer from that 2/3
barrier). In a heart-breaking case this spring, the defeated measure got (as I recall) over 65% support.
Prop. 43 would extend the 2/3 bar to local citizen-driven special tax ballot initiatives.
In other words, this measure would seek to suppress citizen-driven efforts by discarding the
maority-rule basis of most democratic decision. I believe that, in a democracy, one must have
compelling reason (such as important minority rights) to consider requiring more than a simple
majority to make most decisions. So what is Prop. 43’s compelling argument?
Darien's Guide to the California Ballot Propositions: November 2026 Elections 13 of 15
In the prop’s pro argument, they speak of (my emphasis) “California families are struggling”.
But 43 certainly is not prioritizing struggling families (who often want to support the services local
governmentsts might provide – fire departments, road repair, local schools, etc.) Let’s take a closer
look at who Prop. 43 would benefit.
The pro argument goes on to say it “protects homeowners”, because “Some cities now charge
real estate transfer taxes as high as 6%”. Well, it’s true that San Francisco, with the highest transfer tax
rate (or one of the highest – the helpful chart at https://taxo.com/transfer-tax-california-2026/ shows
only selected city rates) levies up to 6% in transfer taxes, but thats on homes selling at $25 million and
above! Also, that S.F. rate drops to 2.25% for home under $10 million and over $5 million. (At $5
million and below, it’s a very low .75% – and continues on down.)
The next highest (selected) city rate on the chart is in L.A., at 5.5% for homes over $10 million.
Like the handful of other cities that do tax at more than minimal rates, L.A. rates rapidly graduate
down. In other words, the pro argument doesn’t lie, but it’s certainly irrelevant to struggling families!
I hope these examples make clear that this prop. is written primarily to protect the interests of
wealthy people! But in our democracy, we’re not supposed to be ruled by the (one-third) minority!
As the rebuttal to the pro argument says (slightly paraphrased), Prop. 43 doesn’t cut your taxes,
it cuts the power of your vote.
No – P&F, FCL, Dem, Lgue, Ref, ACLU, CFT
Yes – Jarv, Rep
• Prop. 44 – Do Most of Us Know Enough About Health Clinics to Vote Wisely? – No
What do most of us know about budgets for health clinics? Not much! And, to me, that’s a
reason to object to, or at least be highly suspicious of, props. like this one. It reminds me of the
(defeated) prop. about dialysis clinics – and for good reason! That prop. – like this one – was also put
on the ballot through the efforts of the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare
Workers West (SEIU-UHW).
SEIU-UHW chooses to use initiatives to push for its goals, and that tactic can be good, when it
serves a wider public interest, or bad. SEIU-UHW has used ballot initiatives as a strategy to pressure
its opponents to negotiate on union issues or to otherwise address healthcare worker issues. They’re
the ones who put Prop. 40 on the ballot – challenging the legislative silence on wealth taxes.
Since 2012 they’ve sponsored 48 ballot initiatives, and – although most have failed – the union
has also won some gains for its workers. So I think it’s important to look more at that history when
considering the value of any particular one of their initiatives.
Going back to the 2022 dialysis proposition, I objected then that most of us don’t know much
about the proper operations of a dialysis clinic, so those details aren’t appropriate to be made law
through ballot measure. Why should medical decisions be made by unknowledgeable voters?
I have the same basic objection to Prop. 44.
In both cases, the changes proposed by the prop. sound sort of reasonable on their face; that’s
how SEIU-UHW is able to get people to sign their initiative petitions! In the case of Prop. 44, it calls
for Federally Qualified Health Care Centers (FQHCC), providing care as “safety-net clinics”, to spend
Darien's Guide to the California Ballot Propositions: November 2026 Elections 14 of 15
90% of their annual revenue on health care services. That sounds like a good thing to push for.
However, currently, FQHCC report spending an average of about 80% on health care services, although
the percentage varies. The FQHCC say many of them could go out of business under Prop. 44, leading
to underserved communities with even fewer options.
We elect legislators to work full time (well, sort of!) to hear and consider expert input on the
details of the subjects of laws. I don’t think it’s a good way to run our state, to have voters trying to
decide on laws for areas in which we are unavoidably ignorant. Are clinic executives paid too much?
How should we know the “market rates” for such executive pay, let alone whatever special
circumstances might influence that pay or any other non-health care services costs?
Ideally, the Leg. does its job and makes needed laws. Initiatives are supposed to come in when
the Leg. falls short in an area. But there are many highly technical areas where it makes no sense to
ask the public to hammer out details!
The dialysis prop. was defeated, and I think this one should be. We can’t stop SEIU-UHW from
trying to put initiatives on the ballot, but we don’t have to vote for every one. Better yet, we can have
fewer bad props. by not signing initiative petitions on subjects we don’t know well!
No – FCL, Jarv, PPar, Dem, Lgue
Yes – P&F, UHW, Ref
• Prop. 45 – Reduces Environmental Review Protections – No
This ballot proposal wants to revise the environmental review process,. In California and most
other states, we see numerous examples of adverse environmental consequences from inadequately
reviewed projects, from housing to water projects. At the same time, valuable projects, even essential
ones, can be delayed by and altered in the course of mandated California Environmental Quality Act
(CEQA) environmental reviews, driving up costs.
In the age of data centers and other potentially harmful projects, do we really want to weaken
environmental review and protections?
It isn’t easy or quick to seek to find an agreeable middle ground between concerned people and
project developers. Allowing enough time to identify problems and work out options is important,
even though it may delay work. Also, project planners can better understand local concerns by
consulting and collaborating with affected residents and communities. But when we look at the
specific and basic aspects of Prop. 45, it lacks these foundational aspects – as well as others.
What about time for public participation, careful studies, and analysis? Under 45, very large
projects will be pushed along with the same timeline as smaller ones.
As for community consultation, the prop. requires (per the Official Voter Information Guide –
emphasis added). “the agency and applicant to consult about the project only with California native
tribes that have been formally recognized by the federal government. (Current law requires
consultation with a wider range of tribes.)” That referenced wider range of tribes could include any of
the approximately 160 tribes in California – out of over whom only about 109 are formally
recognized. That leaves out about 32%, nearly one-third, who would not be consulted about what
happens on their ancestral lands!
Darien's Guide to the California Ballot Propositions: November 2026 Elections 15 of 15
Additionally, to identify an approach with reduced harms, it can be very helpful to consider
various options to reach a project’s goal. Yet 45 “Allows the applicant to develop only one project
alternative for the agency to consider. (Current law requires the agency—not the applicant—to
develop and consider multiple project alternatives that could reduce environmental impacts.)”
(Again, per the Official Voter Information Guide, with bold added.)
Remember in Prop. 44, when I decried measures in areas that most of us don’t know so much
about? I have serious doubts that specifying the details of environmental review is an area that is
appropriate for a ballot measure. Somehow, people sign these initiative petitions, but that doesn’t mean
we have to go along with passing a long, detailed initiative that’s not appropriate for a voter decsion!
Also, as the Friends Committee on Legislation of California brings up, it may be possible that
this prop. would “dramatically weaken environmental reviews of proposed data centers.”
No – P&F, FCL, Lgue, CFT
Yes – Jarv, Ref, CoC, Rep
Voter Resources
California Choices – https://www.californiachoices.org/ – State-wide and local measures;
lists of endorsements
Cal Matters – https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2024/ – Scroll down for state-
wide props. and races; helpful info including issues, money, and main & media endorsers/opponents
Progressive Voters Guide – https://progressivevotersguide.com/california – Good partisan
info by Courage California: down-ballot, multi-issue guide detailing recommendations
Friends Committee on Legislation of California – https://fclca.org/ – Scroll down to find the
link to their state ballot propositions page; brief analyses
Ballotpedia – https://ballotpedia.org/ – Very helpful; lots of background plus local races info.
League of Women Voters of CA-- The League has both a site with non-partisan “Pros and
Cons” info on the ballot propositions and one with their ballot measure recommendations:
Pros & Cons –
https://lwvc.org/pros-cons-ballot-measures-november-3-2026-general-election/
Ballot Measure Recommendations – https://lwvc.org/ballot-recommendations/
How to Subscribe or Unsubscribe to Darien's Guide to the California Ballot Propositions
To subscribe, email the word subscribe — in the body or subject line of the message — to
Dariens_Ballot_Guide-request@lists.sonic.net . Or, to unsubscribe, email from the account / address
that you’re unsubscribing, the word unsubscribe.
• With five, alive! Yes on 1-5.
• Vote yes on the single digit propositions (1-5) and no on all the two-digit ones except 40.
• Yes on 40; no on 41 and 42.

content.thinking:
I'm checking how the guide lines up on Prop 41: the opposing side includes Peace & Freedom, the Democratic Party, UHW, and the ACLU, while Howard Jarvis and Reform California back it. 02
CALIFORNIA Strengthens State Rainy Day Fund
Purpose
Proposition 2 is a constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by the legislature, that would
strengthen California’s rainy day fund by increasing the cap on how much money the state can set
aside each year. The measure also would make it easier for the state to use tax revenues to pay
down debt.1
Research Assistant: Arushi Goyal ’28
Background
The Budget Stabilization Account (BSA), also known as the rainy day fund,
is California’s largest state budget reserve. The state uses this fund to save
money when revenues are strong and to reduce cuts to public services when
revenues are weak. This fund is especially important in California because
the state’s revenues depend heavily on taxes on the incomes of high-income
residents, which can vary greatly from year to year, thus creating “boom and
bust” budget cycles.2
The state automatically sets aside 1.5% of General Fund revenues each year.
It also sets aside “excess” capital gains revenues in years when they exceed
8% of General Fund tax revenues. Generally, the state deposits 50% of these
set-aside revenues into the rainy day fund and uses the other 50% to pay
down certain types of state debt. Currently, the state can use these excess
revenues to pay down only pension and retiree health debt, and cannot make
extra payments on other forms of debt such as unemployment insurance
debt and certain education and Medi-Cal obligations. This requirement is
set to end in 2030, after which some or all of that money may be put into the
rainy day fund.3
Under current law, the rainy day fund is capped at 10% of estimated General
Fund tax revenues. When this limit is reached, any dollars that would other-
wise go into the rainy day fund must be spent on infrastructure.4 California
also has a constitutional spending cap, commonly known as the Gann Limit,
which was passed by the voters as Proposition 4 in 1979 and which capped
spending at 1978-79 levels, adjusted each year for infation and population
growth.5 Most spending counts toward this limit, including money deposited
into reserves. Withdrawals from state reserves during budget emergencies
do not count against the Gann Limit, but when state revenues are high, the
spending cap can limit California’s ability to build its reserves.
The rainy day fund can be tapped only during a budget emergency. The gover-
nor must formally declare an emergency before deposits can be reduced or
suspended or money can be withdrawn. The declaration can come late in the
fscal year, sometimes after the legislature’s deadline to pass a budget. This
can leave lawmakers passing a budget that assumes an emergency before
one is ofcially declared.6
In the state legislature the vote to place this measure on the ballot was 59-8
in the Assembly and 29-2 in the Senate.7
Proposal
If approved, Proposition 2 would:8
• Double the BSA cap from 10% to 20% of
estimated General Fund tax revenues.
• Set aside more General Fund revenues during
“boom” years.
• Expand the types of state debt that may be paid
down with set-aside revenues.
• Extend the debt-paydown requirement by 10
years, to 2039-40.
• Change how rainy day fund and other deposits
count toward the Gann Limit.
• Create a simpler process for declaring a budget
emergency.
Fiscal Impact
The LAO estimates that Proposition 2 would
increase the state’s budget reserves. Having more
money in the BSA would make it easier for the
state to balance its budget during downturns. The
measure could also cause the state to pay down
debt more aggressively.9

PROP
03
CALIFORNIA Makes permanent existing voter-approved income tax rates for high-income
Californians
Purpose
Proposition 3, a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature, would make permanent
the existing voter-approved income tax rates on high-income Californians, which are currently set
to expire in 2031, and to allocate the resulting revenues to K-12 schools and community colleges.1
Research Assistant: Shayan Abbasi ’29
Background
The personal income tax is California’s largest revenue source.
It provides more than half of the state’s General Fund, the state’s
main operating account, which funds public services including
education, health care, and corrections. The tax applies to most
types of income, such as wages, salaries, interest, and capital gains,
which the state treats as ordinary income. California’s income tax
rates are progressive, starting low and gradually rising for taxpayers
with higher incomes.2
Over the past two decades, voters have approved or extended tax
increases on high-income earners several times.
• In 2004, voters approved Proposition 63, a 1% surcharge on
income taxes of residents with taxable income of more than
$1 million.
• In 2012, amid the fscal challenges brought on by the Great
Recession, California voters approved Proposition 30, which
temporarily increased income tax rates on high-income
taxpayers to fund state services and stave of cuts to public
education. This measure raised the top marginal rate from
9.3% to 12.3%. Combined with the 1% surcharge, the state’s
income tax on the highest earners became 13.3% — the highest
in the nation.
• In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55, which extended these
higher income tax rates through 2030, with 63% voting yes.3
The top 2% of California taxpayers pay these higher rates (10.3% or
higher), and these taxpayers now pay about half of all state income
taxes. Since Proposition 30’s initial passage in 2012, the measure
has raised more than $104 billion for schools and other state
services and has become a foundational part of the state’s budget
and its Rainy Day Fund.4
Figure 1 shows the income tax rates for Californians under current
law, which will continue if Prop. 3 passes, and how the rates for
high-earners will decrease after 2030 if Prop. 3 is rejected. 5
ROSEINSTITUTE.CMC.EDU
ROSEINSTITUTE.CMC.EDU
Proposal
Proposition 3, ofcially titled “The California Children’s Education
and Health Care Protection Act of 2026,” would amend Section 36 of
Article XIII of the California Constitution to make the higher income
tax rates established by Proposition 30 of 2012 permanent instead of
letting them expire in 2030.6 The measure does not change the exist-
ing rates or brackets, which adjust for infation each year, and it does
not increase taxes on individuals earning less than about $371,000 or
couples earning less than about $743,000 in today’s dollars.7
Revenues would continue to be deposited into the Education
Protection Account, with 89% of the education funds allocated to
K-12 school districts, county ofces of education, and charter schools,
and 11% allocated to community college districts.8 Local school
boards would retain the authority to decide how the revenues are
spent, provided that spending determinations are made in open
session of a public meeting, and none of the funds may be used for
administrator salaries or other administrative costs. Each district
must annually publish online an accounting of how much money it
received and how it was spent, and the funds are subject to an annual
independent audit, with elected ofcials facing prosecution and
criminal penalties if they misuse them.9 The measure also increases
the General Fund revenues available for health care, budget reserves,
and other programs, and it directs that in certain years a portion of
surplus revenues, up to a maximum of $2 billion in a single fscal
year, be allocated to health care services for children and their families
through Medi-Cal.10
Fiscal Impact
If the current income tax rates are allowed
to expire as scheduled, the California
Legislative Analyst’s Ofce (LAO) estimates
that the state would lose between $5 billion
and $15 billion in annual revenue beginning
in 2031.11 For context, this year the state
plans to spend about $250 billion from
the General Fund, with about half of that
spending going to schools, community
colleges, and the state’s public universities,
and about another one-third going to health
and human services programs, mainly
Medi-Cal, the state’s low-income health
insurance program.12

CALIFORNIA Prohibits Enactment of New Taxes on Asset Ownership and Retroactive Taxes
Purpose
Proposition 42 is a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment that would make it more difcult
to adopt a wealth tax in California by prohibiting enactment of new taxes on ownership of
fnancial assets or other personal property, or taxes that would apply retroactively based on a
taxpayer’s past activities.1
Research Assistant: Kaylin Nydam ’29
Background
Currently, individuals who reside or work in
the State of California must pay income and
capital gains taxes on income from investments.
However, the state does not tax ownership of
fnancial assets such as stocks, bonds, and
retirement accounts, or most other forms of
personal property.2
Proposal
Proposition 42 would prevent the state from imposing new taxes on
ownership of “retirement holdings, individually-owned assets, and other
forms of personal savings,” which are defned to include pensions,
retirement accounts, mutual funds, and all tangible and intangible
personal property, including business interests, digital assets, intellectu-
al property, and personal belongings.3
Furthermore, the measure would prevent the state from taxing individu-
als retroactively based on their past activities or residency status—such
as billionaires who have left the state to avoid taxes on their wealth.4
Proposition 42, like Proposition 41, aims to make it more difcult to
impose a wealth tax on billionaires, as proposed by Proposition 40.
Specifcally, Proposition 40 would levy a one-time tax of fve percent
on the personal property assets of taxpayers and trusts with net worth
exceeding one billion dollars; most of the resulting revenue would be
used to fund health care programs.5 Proposition 42 contains language
stipulating that if it and a conficting measure both pass, the conficting
measure would be nullifed if Proposition 42 receives more votes.6
Fiscal Impact
By limiting the types of assets that can be taxed, this measure potentially
decreases future state tax revenue. According to the Legislative Analyst’s
Ofce (LAO), the extent to which future revenues would be reduced is
unclear.7 Moreover, blocking the billionaire tax could help the state keep
some of its wealthiest residents, averting the loss of income tax revenue
from those residents.

Requires a Two-Thirds Vote to Approve Local Special Tax Initiatives
PROP
43 Purpose
Proposition 43 is a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature that would raise the
vote share required to enact special tax initiatives proposed by citizens from a simple majority
to a two-thirds majority.1
CALIFORNIA
Research Assistant: Kahani Malhotra ’27
Background
In 1978, California voters passed Proposition 13, requiring that any special tax proposed by a
local government must receive a two-thirds vote from the electorate before being enacted,2
with a special tax being defned as any tax imposed for a specifc purpose rather than general
governmental need.3 In 1996, Proposition 218 further increased the power of voters to approve
taxes by requiring that any general tax imposed by a local government must receive majority
voter approval, and reafrmed that special taxes require two-thirds voter approval.4
Two decades later, a court decision narrowed the scope of Proposition 218. In 2017, the
California Supreme Court ruled in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland that a signifcant
requirement for general taxes — that they be placed on the ballot during general elections —
did not apply to citizen initiatives.5 Ultimately, the court categorized taxes imposed by local
governments as diferent from taxes imposed by citizen initiatives.
The ruling raised an important question: Are special taxes imposed by citizen initiatives exempt
from the two-thirds vote requirement that applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local
governments? A memo from the San Francisco attorney’s ofce interpreting the ruling seemed
to indicate that the answer was yes.6 But the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association disagreed.
In 2018, the Association sued San Francisco for allowing two separate citizen-driven measures
to pass with a simple-majority vote rather than a supermajority vote. A judge ruled against the
Association, afrming that the special tax measures were rightfully passed by majority vote
since they were proposed by citizens.7 A state appeals court shot down the Association’s further
attempts to overturn citizen-initiated local taxes passed in 20208 and 2021.9
In 2023, the Association and the California Business Roundtable qualifed an initiative10 for the
2024 ballot cycle that would have mandated any special tax initiative to require a two-thirds
majority vote regardless of whether a local government or citizens proposed it.11 But in June
2024, the California Supreme Court ruled unanimously that passage of the initiative would lead
to a “revision,” rather than an amendment, of the state constitution, “based on its far-reaching
changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained at the
state and local levels.” While amendments may be made by citizen initiatives, revisions require
“a constitutional convention and popular ratifcation.”12 Thus, enacting the proposal by initiative
would be unconstitutional.
In 2026, the same two organizations qualifed an initiative for the 2026 general election
ballot that would have amended the state constitution to require a two-thirds majority to pass
citizen-led local special tax initiatives, alongside other tax limiting provisions.13 Following a
legislative compromise, which included the passage of ACA 22,14 the organizations withdrew the
initiative in favor of Proposition 43 being placed on this year’s ballot as a legislatively referred
constitutional amendment.15 Though ACA 22 passed nearly unanimously in the Assembly (68-2)
and Senate (35-1), its author, Assemblymember Bufy Wicks (D-14), announced on June 29 that
she was “adamantly opposed to it.16
Proposal
Proposition 43 would amend the
California Constitution to require that
citizen-driven special tax initiatives
require a two-thirds majority vote
for passage. It would add Section
4.5 to Article XIII A of the California
Constitution, detailing that any local
government — including voters
within a local government exercising
the initiative power — must obtain
a two-thirds vote to enact, extend,
or increase a special tax starting on
January 1, 2027.
The amendment also prohibits local
government and members of the
electorate from levying ad valorem
property taxes — taxes based on the
value of real estate or tangible per-
sonal property — except for certain
preapproved, dedicated property
taxes, whose terms are delineated in
the Constitution.17
Fiscal Impact
The California Legislative Analyst’s
Ofce (LAO) estimates that Propo-
sition 43 would reduce local govern-
ment tax revenues. The total fscal
impact is largely unknown, however,
as it depends on future decisions by
voters and local governments.18

• Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association20
• California Taxpayers Association
• California Small Business Association
• Family Business Association of California
• California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
• Reform California21
• California Republican Party
The proponents’ ofcial website is “Yes on 43: Taxpayer
Protection,” https://yesonprop43.com/.
As of September 19, 2026, proponents had raised a total of
$14,856,760.22
Supporters argue that Proposition 43 would:23
• Restore the protections of Prop. 13 (1978) by closing
loopholes created by courts so that local special taxes
must be approved by two-thirds of voters.
• Make it more difcult for special interests to collude with
local governments to impose costly taxes on homeowners,
renters, and small businesses.
• Ensure that taxpayers are in charge by fully protecting their
right to vote on taxes.
• Prevent other rollbacks of Proposition 13.

• Threaten funding for parks, afordable housing, frefght-
ing, and other crucial local services that rely on local
revenue.30
• Make it more difcult for cities to secure future revenue
measures.31
• Make California “the hardest place in the country” to raise
local revenue.32
• Undermine majority rule by empowering a minority to
block tax measures favored by a supermajority of voters.
OPPOSITION TO PROPOSITION 43
A YES vote for Proposition 43 would increase the threshold
to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives to a two-thirds
majority vote.
A NO vote for Proposition 43 would maintain a simple majority
requirement to pass citizen-led special tax initiatives.

Restricts New Special Taxes by Requiring Audits and Performance Reviews
and Denying Exemption from State Spending Cap
PROP
41 Purpose
Proposition 41 is a citizen initiated measure that would require the California State Auditor
to review programs to be funded by proposed special taxes and publish its fnancial and
performance audit before California residents vote on these tax proposals. The State Auditor
would also be required to periodically review programs funded by special taxes created or
raised after January 1, 2026 in order to improve program efciency. Finally, Prop. 41 would
prevent revenues raised by new state taxes from being exempted from the Gann Limit on state
spending approved by voters in 1979.1
CALIFORNIA
Research Assistant: Dhriti Jagadish ’27
Background
In 1979, Californians passed Proposition 4,
also known as the Gann Limit, which capped
spending at 1978-79 levels, adjusted each year
for infation and population growth. If state and
local governments collect more tax revenue
than they are allowed to spend for two consec-
utive years, they must split the excess between
taxpayer rebates and additional spending on
schools.2 Prop. 41’s drafters charge that special
interests have “repeatedly passed new taxes that
exempted themselves” from the Gann Limit.
Proposal
Proposition 41 has three key provisions:
First, it would require that when a “special tax” — one that would raise
funds for a specifc purpose or program rather than for general government
operations — is proposed as a ballot initiative and achieves 25% of the
necessary signatures, the California State Auditor would conduct a
pre-election audit of any programs to be funded by the tax. The results of
the audit would appear in the Ofcial Voter Guide for the election. The audit
would address the following:
• Whether the program is currently acquiring its resources at the lowest
cost for the necessary quality;
• Whether the program is maximizing output for every dollar spent;
• Whether the program is achieving its intended goals and outcomes;
• Whether the program is following the relevant laws, regulations, and
internal policies;
• Whether there is “actual and potential fraud, waste, and abuse” in a
program and how adequate its internal prevention systems are;
• Whether the program has identifed its “biggest threats” and has a
plan to mitigate them;
• Whether the program is using adequate and reliable data;
• Whether the program has adequate oversight and accountability;
• Whether the program’s costs compare favorably to similar non-
governmental programs; and
• How the program could cut its costs by at least 10%.
ROSEINSTITUTE.CMC.EDU
These fndings must be sent to the governor, the legislature, and the
secretary of state and be made available to the public. If the special tax
initiative qualifes for the ballot, an executive summary must be printed
in every Voter Information Guide (VIG) prior to the election.
Second, for all special taxes enacted by the legislature or by a ballot
initiative on or after January 1, 2026, the California State Auditor must
conduct ongoing fnancial and performance audits every four years for
each of the programs that receive revenue from these taxes. With the
assistance of the California Legislative Analyst’s Ofce (LAO) — as well
as public input on the State Auditor’s measurements of efectiveness —
the State Auditor must provide:
• The same assessments required of the pre-election fnancial and
performance audit; and
• Further recommendations on how a program can improve its
efectiveness, cut costs, or otherwise reduce taxpayer burden.
Third, the Proposition would require that all revenues raised by state
taxes that take efect on or after January 1, 2026, be subject to the state
spending limit, also known as the Gann Limit. It would prohibit the
state from imposing, collecting, or enforcing any state tax that claims an
exemption from the Gann Limit. This provision would directly contradict
Proposition 40, which exempts appropriations funded by the “2026
Billionaire Tax Reserve Fund” from the Gann Limit.3
Prop. 41 expressly states that if it receives more votes than a conficting
measure on the same ballot, even if that other measure receives a
majority, the conficting measure would not become law.
Fiscal Impact
The Californa Legislative Analyst’s Ofce
(LAO) expects Proposition 41 to have a
number of fscal efects.4
The LAO predicts that Prop. 41 would increase
State Auditor costs. These costs would
depend on the number of new or increased
special taxes the State Auditor must review
as well as the complexity of the programs
being reviewed on a recurring basis. The LAO
estimates that this would likely be in the range
of the low millions of dollars annually, but
would increase over time.
The LAO also expects that the State Auditor’s
summarized reviews, which must appear
in every Voter Information Guide (VIG) if
a special tax is proposed through a ballot
initiative, could add several pages to the VIG,
increasing printing and mailing costs by a few
hundred thousand dollars per ballot initiative.
Pre-election and ongoing audits of special
taxes and their associated programs would
be paid for by the revenues collected by the
special taxes. Pre-election audit costs for
special taxes that do not qualify for the ballot
or are rejected by voters would be paid for by
the state’s General Fund.
Altogether, the net fscal impact remains un-
known. The LAO suggests that Prop. 41 could
result in “possible savings” or “improved
services” based on the recommendations of
the State Auditor. These savings, however,
cannot be predicted in advance.

Better California7
• Reform California8
• Building a Better California (top sponsor of the “Yes on 41”
Committee)9
The proponents’ ofcial website is https://www.yesonprop41.org/.
As of September 19, 2026, proponents had raised $92,294,500 to
promote Prop 41. Google co-founder Sergey Brin has contributed
$102 million this year to Building a Better California, which is the
chief sponsor of “Yes on 41 - Californians for a More Transparent
and Efective Government.”10
Arguments for Proposition 4111
Supporters of Proposition 41 argue that:
• California’s state government will spend more than $350
billion this year, a 79% increase from 2019, and outcomes
in education, health care, and infrastructure have barely
improved.
• The legislature and “special interests” continue to propose
new taxes for new programs without monitoring their
spending and thoroughly reviewing the efcacy of existing
programs.
• Independent performance audits give voters “objective,
credible information” on proposed taxes and the programs
they would support.
• Though the Gann Limit on state spending was democratically
approved by voters, it has been consistently undercut by
exemptions.
SUPPORT FOR PROPOSITION 41
Opponents of Proposition 41 Include:
• California Democratic Party12
• Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare
Workers West (SEIU-UHW)13
As of September 19, 2026, opponents had raised $340,225
against Prop. 41.14
Arguments Against Proposition 4115
Opponents of Proposition 41 argue that:
• Proposition 41 was put on the ballot in the name of tax
oversight and transparency, but its primary purpose is to
undo Prop. 40’s “billionaire tax.”
• Billionaires, some of them Donald Trump’s donors, have
poured millions of dollars into Propositions 41 and 42 to
void Prop. 40.
• By potentially voiding Prop. 40, Prop. 41 would cost the
state much-needed revenue.
OPPOSITION TO PROPOSITION 41
A YES vote on Proposition 41 would require the California State
Auditor to conduct pre-election and ongoing performance
and fnancial audits of programs funded by special taxes. It
would also prevent exemption of new special taxes from the
state spending limit, thus directly competing with — and likely
overriding — Proposition 40.
A NO vote on Proposition 41 would not introduce any new
performance and fnancial audits of programs funded by
special taxes and would not change current state spending
limit requirements.

42
CALIFORNIA Prohibits Enactment of New Taxes on Asset Ownership and Retroactive Taxes
Purpose
Proposition 42 is a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment that would make it more difcult
to adopt a wealth tax in California by prohibiting enactment of new taxes on ownership of
fnancial assets or other personal property, or taxes that would apply retroactively based on a
taxpayer’s past activities.1
Research Assistant: Kaylin Nydam ’29
Background
Currently, individuals who reside or work in
the State of California must pay income and
capital gains taxes on income from investments.
However, the state does not tax ownership of
fnancial assets such as stocks, bonds, and
retirement accounts, or most other forms of
personal property.2
Proposal
Proposition 42 would prevent the state from imposing new taxes on
ownership of “retirement holdings, individually-owned assets, and other
forms of personal savings,” which are defned to include pensions,
retirement accounts, mutual funds, and all tangible and intangible
personal property, including business interests, digital assets, intellectu-
al property, and personal belongings.3
Furthermore, the measure would prevent the state from taxing individu-
als retroactively based on their past activities or residency status—such
as billionaires who have left the state to avoid taxes on their wealth.4
Proposition 42, like Proposition 41, aims to make it more difcult to
impose a wealth tax on billionaires, as proposed by Proposition 40.
Specifcally, Proposition 40 would levy a one-time tax of fve percent
on the personal property assets of taxpayers and trusts with net worth
exceeding one billion dollars; most of the resulting revenue would be
used to fund health care programs.5 Proposition 42 contains language
stipulating that if it and a conficting measure both pass, the conficting
measure would be nullifed if Proposition 42 receives more votes.6
Fiscal Impact
By limiting the types of assets that can be taxed, this measure potentially
decreases future state tax revenue. According to the Legislative Analyst’s
Ofce (LAO), the extent to which future revenues would be reduced is
unclear.7 Moreover, blocking the billionaire tax could help the state keep
some of its wealthiest residents, averting the loss of income tax revenue
from those residents.

• California Republican Party

• California Small Business Association

• Reform California
• California Chamber of Commerce

Arguments for Proposition 4210
Supporters of Proposition 42 argue that:
• The measure would protect Californians’ hard-earned
savings from new taxes.
• The state should not double-tax savings and investments
that were already taxed as income.
• The state should not be able to enact new taxes that apply
retroactively to taxpayers’ past earnings.
• A wealth tax would hurt owners of small businesses.
A YES VOTE ON PROPOSITION 42
A YES vote on Proposition 42 would prohibit future state
taxes on asset ownership and retroactive taxes based on a
taxpayer’s past activities.

• Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare
Workers West (SEIU-UHW)13

• The measure is a billionaire-funded initiative placed on the
ballot because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share.
• Billionaires would rather millions of working Californians
lose their health insurance than pay a one-time, modest tax
on their extreme wealth.

A NO vote on Proposition 42 would not prohibit the state from
levying taxes on asset ownership and retroactive taxes.

Requires a Two-Thirds Vote to Approve Local Special Tax Initiatives
PROP
43 Purpose
Proposition 43 is a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature that would raise the
vote share required to enact special tax initiatives proposed by citizens from a simple majority
to a two-thirds majority.1
CALIFORNIA
Research Assistant: Kahani Malhotra ’27
Background
In 1978, California voters passed Proposition 13, requiring that any special tax proposed by a
local government must receive a two-thirds vote from the electorate before being enacted,2
with a special tax being defned as any tax imposed for a specifc purpose rather than general
governmental need.3 In 1996, Proposition 218 further increased the power of voters to approve
taxes by requiring that any general tax imposed by a local government must receive majority
voter approval, and reafrmed that special taxes require two-thirds voter approval.4
Two decades later, a court decision narrowed the scope of Proposition 218. In 2017, the
California Supreme Court ruled in California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland that a signifcant
requirement for general taxes — that they be placed on the ballot during general elections —
did not apply to citizen initiatives.5 Ultimately, the court categorized taxes imposed by local
governments as diferent from taxes imposed by citizen initiatives.
The ruling raised an important question: Are special taxes imposed by citizen initiatives exempt
from the two-thirds vote requirement that applies to special taxes placed on the ballot by local
governments? A memo from the San Francisco attorney’s ofce interpreting the ruling seemed
to indicate that the answer was yes.6 But the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association disagreed.
In 2018, the Association sued San Francisco for allowing two separate citizen-driven measures
to pass with a simple-majority vote rather than a supermajority vote. A judge ruled against the
Association, afrming that the special tax measures were rightfully passed by majority vote
since they were proposed by citizens.7 A state appeals court shot down the Association’s further
attempts to overturn citizen-initiated local taxes passed in 20208 and 2021.9
In 2023, the Association and the California Business Roundtable qualifed an initiative10 for the
2024 ballot cycle that would have mandated any special tax initiative to require a two-thirds
majority vote regardless of whether a local government or citizens proposed it.11 But in June
2024, the California Supreme Court ruled unanimously that passage of the initiative would lead
to a “revision,” rather than an amendment, of the state constitution, “based on its far-reaching
changes to existing processes by which revenue measures are enacted and maintained at the
state and local levels.” While amendments may be made by citizen initiatives, revisions require

Issue Brief
What Would Proposition 41 Mean for California?
Understanding the Proposed Audit Requirements for Special Taxes and the Prohibition on Excluding Revenues from the State Spending Limit
September 2026 | By Kayla Kitson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kayla-kitson/)
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Prop. 41 would 1) impose new audit requirements for programs funded with state special taxes and 2) prohibit the collection of new state taxes that are excluded from the state’s spending limit. The primary intent of the measure is to invalidate Prop. 40 — the billionaire tax also appearing on the November ballot — but Prop. 41 could also make it harder for the state to meet the needs of Californians in the future.
What Would Prop. 41 Do?
Prop. 41 would amend the state Constitution to impose new rules related to state taxes. The measure would require “financial and performance audits” of programs receiving revenues from special taxes and would also prevent state taxes from being excluded from California’s spending cap, also known as the “Gann Limit.”
Creates New Audit Requirements for Special Taxes
Prop. 41 would create new pre-election and ongoing audit requirements for programs receiving — or proposed to receive — revenues from state-level special taxes. In contrast to a general tax, which can be used for any purpose, a special tax raises revenue for specific purposes.
Pre-election audits: The State Auditor would be required to perform an audit of any program that would be funded by a special tax proposed through a statewide voter initiative. The audit would be required while the initiative is being circulated for signatures — before it officially qualifies for the ballot — and a summary of the audit findings would be included in the voter information guide. The full audit would also be made available to the public.
Ongoing audits: The State Auditor would be required to audit programs receiving revenues from special taxes enacted by the Legislature or approved by voters through a statewide initiative on or after January 1, 2026. These audits would be required every four years.
The audits would assess programs based on specific criteria outlined in Prop. 41, and would require the State Auditor to recommend how programs could reduce costs by at least 10% annually.
The State Auditor would be reimbursed for the costs of these audits with revenues from the relevant special tax. If, however, a special tax initiative fails to qualify for the ballot or is rejected by voters, the audit costs would be absorbed by the state’s General Fund.
Prohibits Taxes That Are Excluded from the State Spending Limit
Prop. 41 would prevent the state from collecting or enforcing any state tax that is 1) enacted on or after January 1, 2026 and 2) excluded from the state spending cap, also known as the Gann Limit (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/qa-why-hitting-gann-limit-threatens-ongoing-investments-in-californians/). Currently, the measure would apply only to Prop. 40 if both measures pass and Prop. 41 receives more votes, but it could potentially be applied to other tax policy proposals in the future.
California’s spending limit was established by Prop. 4 (1979) and is based on state spending in 1978-79, annually adjusted for population changes and inflation. Under the state Constitution, if state revenues exceed the limit over two consecutive years, the excess must be split equally between refunds to taxpayers and spending on TK-14 education. In effect, the spending limit restricts the ability of state leaders to raise and spend revenue to meet the most pressing needs of Californians.
Conflicts with Other Measures on the Ballot
The California Constitution states that if provisions of multiple measures on the same ballot conflict, the provisions of the measure receiving the higher number of votes will prevail. Prop. 41 broadly specifies that if another measure on the same ballot either 1) imposes different audit rules on special taxes or 2) contains a tax that is exempted from the state spending limit, the entirety of the other measure would be invalidated if Prop. 41 receives more votes.
Prop. 41 is in direct conflict with Prop. 40. (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/billionaire-tax-explained-what-proposition-40-would-mean-for-california/) This is because Prop. 40 would create a one-time tax on the wealth of billionaires and exclude the revenues from the state spending limit, which Prop. 41 prohibits.
If both measures were to be approved and Prop. 41 received more votes, Prop. 40 could be invalidated. Alternatively, if both measures pass but Prop. 40 receives more votes, the billionaire tax could be collected, but it is possible that audits would be required of Medi-Cal and other programs receiving Prop. 40 dollars. If both measures pass, there may be litigation regarding the application of conflicting provisions, and the final decision would be made by the courts.
How Would Prop. 41 Affect Californians and the State Budget?
The primary intent of Prop. 41 is to invalidate the Prop. 40 billionaire tax, but it would also create new barriers to raising state revenue and effectively meeting the needs of Californians.
Prop. 41 would also increase state costs related to conducting audits for programs that are often already subject to close scrutiny — reducing funding available to support critical state services. This would come at a time when Californians are already dealing with affordability concerns as well as the consequences of the steep federal cuts to health care and food assistance enacted in H.R. 1 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/timeline-of-funding-cuts-to-medi-cal-and-calfresh-in-california/), signed by President Trump in 2025.
Impacts of Audit Requirements
The pre-election audit requirement could dissuade voters from approving special tax initiatives that would raise needed revenue to support and improve state services that help Californians stay healthy, housed, and economically secure. A summary of the audit would appear in the voter guide, and voters could interpret it as evidence that the programs to be funded are inefficient or ineffective. For example, because the State Auditor would be required to recommend options to cut program costs by 10%, voters may assume this means the program is inefficient even if that is not the case.
Additionally, the requirement for cost-cutting recommendations could result in service cuts with real human impacts. While policymakers would be under no obligation to implement these recommendations, if they did it could result in cuts to core services rather than simply “inefficient spending.” For example, if a program receiving special tax revenues is already operating efficiently but the Auditor must identify ways that costs could be reduced by 10%, lawmakers may be under pressure to adopt those recommendations — particularly in difficult budget times. Those cuts could lead to fewer Californians being served, reductions in benefit levels, or decreased service quality.
While it is clearly important for tax dollars to be spent efficiently and effectively, many state programs are already subject to occasional or ongoing audits. The State Auditor currently performs audits as a result of (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/about-us/#where-our-work-comes-from) existing state laws, legislative requests, and whistleblower tips. Additionally, the “High-Risk” audit program requires the Auditor to periodically review programs or agencies determined to be at high risk for “waste, fraud, abuse, or mismanagement” or those raising concerns related to efficiency or effectiveness.
Prop. 41’s additional audits would increase state costs, reducing the resources available to directly support services for Californians. Moreover, in the case of program audits related to a proposed special tax, the audit costs would be absorbed by the state’s General Fund if the ballot initiative were not enacted, leaving less funding for critical state services like education, health care, and human services.
Impacts of State Spending Limit Provisions
The primary impact of preventing new revenues from being excluded from the spending limit would be the invalidation of the billionaire tax proposed by Prop. 40 — if both measures pass and Prop. 41 receives more votes.
In the future, voters may be able to exclude the revenues from a statewide tax initiative from the spending cap if the initiative amends the Constitution to do so. In fact, previous initiatives have explicitly excluded new tax revenues from the limit, such as tobacco taxes enacted under Prop. 10 (1998) and Prop. 56 (2016). However, legal challenges are possible and there is no certainty on how courts would rule.
State policymakers already lack the authority to exclude new tax revenues from the spending cap without voter approval because the cap is enshrined in the state Constitution.
There are some existing state revenue streams that could potentially be affected by Prop. 41, but there are many complications and uncertainties and any conflicts would ultimately be decided by the courts. For example, some health care financing sources that must be occasionally reauthorized — such as the Managed Care Organization (MCO) tax and the Hospital Quality Assurance fee, which both allow the state to draw down additional federal funding for Medi-Cal — could potentially be impacted by Prop. 41. This, in turn, would jeopardize billions of dollars in federal funding for Medi-Cal at a time when Californians are already experiencing the harms of the deep federal cuts to health care resulting from H.R. 1.
Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 41?
The top contributor to the Prop. 41 campaign is a group called “Building a Better California,” which is largely funded (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1486767&view=received) by Google cofounder Sergey Brin and other billionaires. This same group is also opposing Prop. 40 and supporting Prop. 42. Prop. 41 is also endorsed by the California Republican Party, the California Chamber of Commerce, and the California Taxpayers Association.
There is no official campaign against Prop. 41. However, prominent opponents include the Service Employees International Union – United Health Workers West (SEIU–UHW) — the main proponent of the Prop. 40 billionaire tax measure — as well as other labor groups including the California Federation of Teachers and the California Federation of Labor Unions. The California Democratic Party and the League of Women Voters also oppose Prop. 41.

​ Yes on Proposition 41: Audits and Accountability for California Tax Dollars.
​
Billions of our tax dollars have flowed into state programs like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. Californians deserve better education, healthcare, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
​
Proposition 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct financial and performance audits of the programs funded by any new tax measure, with results posted publicly. It also requires that all new taxes comply with the state's voter-approved spending limit - so that excess tax revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
If approved by voters, Prop 41 would require ongoing public audits to evaluate spending, identify waste, fraud or abuse, assess whether they are meeting their intended goals, and recommend improvements.
Learn More About Prop 41 (https://www.yesonprop41.org/about-prop41)
Endorsements

Californians pay some of the highest taxes in the country - on top of our high cost of living. Billions of our tax dollars have flowed into state programs, like homelessness efforts, with too little to show for it. We deserve better education, healthcare, infrastructure and other services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
Proposition 41 (2026) puts independent audits and measurable outcomes at the center of how California funds programs with new tax dollars, so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes.
Q: Does Prop 41 raise taxes?
A: No. Prop 41 does not create or increase any taxes - it protects taxpayers' interests by:
1) Identifying shortcomings in programs and recommending fixes, to help deliver better results for our taxes;
Reducing the waste and fraud that have cost California taxpayers billions of dollars in recent years; and
Requires all taxes to comply with the state's voter-approved spending limit - including its requirement that excess revenues get refunded to taxpayers.
Prop 41 ensures taxpayers get better results, not just a bigger tax bill.
Q: How do the audits work?
Proposition 41 requires the independent California State Auditor to review programs that would be funded by a new or higher special tax proposed to California voters. The first review happens before the tax reaches the ballot. Once a special tax initiative collects 25 percent of the signatures needed to qualify, the State Auditor audits each program that would receive the money, looking at whether the program is achieving its goals, how well it spends its dollars, and where fraud, waste, or abuse may exist. A summary of the findings is printed in the Voter Information Guide so voters can read it before they vote. If a new special tax is approved by voters, the State Auditor reviews the funded programs again every four years and invites public input.
The audits produce findings and recommendations, and both are public. Decisions about funding stay with voters and the Legislature, as they are today, and the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst Office notes that acting on the recommendations "could result in savings or improved
services at existing funding levels." A program funded by a new special tax is reviewed before any change to its funding is made. For a full walkthrough, see the our explainer here (https://www.yesonprop41.org/how-audits-work) .
Q: Who conducts the audits?
A: The audits are conducted by California's independent State Auditor, the state's nonpartisan fiscal watchdog, and shared broadly with the public, including in the Voter Information Guide. The financial and performance audits must:
Track all program spending and assess whether it's achieving its intended outcomes;
Determine whether programs have sufficient oversight and accountability;
Identify areas of waste, fraud and abuse; and,
Recommend how future waste and fraud can be avoided and how programs can be made more effective.
Under Prop 41, the Auditor is required to review programs funded by proposed new tax measures before voters cast their ballots and conduct ongoing audits if those measures are approved.
Q: What happens if an audit finds problems?
A: If the State Auditor identifies concerns about oversight, accountability or program performance, those findings are included in the Voter Information Guide so voters can make a more informed decision.
If a measure is approved, future audits continue evaluating how funds are spent, identify areas for improvement, and recommend ways to make programs more effective over time - so that programs are held accountable to the people who pay for them: taxpayers.
The audit doesn't decide whether a measure passes or fails; it gives voters independent information before they cast their ballot.
Q: What does Prop 41 mean for education, healthcare and other public programs?
A: Every tax dollar we waste is a dollar that could actually help someone. Prop 41 is built to sustain fiscal discipline alongside public investment. It does not cut or eliminate funding for education, healthcare or other public services, and it helps ensure that programs funded by taxpayers are transparent, accountable and delivering results. We deserve better services in return for the hard-earned money we pay to the state.
Prop 41 requires more accountability, transparency and trackable progress of programs funded by our taxes, like homelessness (https://www.yesonprop41.org/homelessness) , so that we stop funding failure and start funding successful outcomes.
Q: Does Prop 41 make it harder for initiatives to qualify for the ballot?
A: No. Prop 41 does not change the initiative process or prevent measures from qualifying for the ballot. Supporters can still gather signatures, qualify initiatives and campaign for their proposals just as they do today.
The difference is that under Prop 41, programs to be funded by new taxes are assessed before voters cast their ballot. The Auditor's findings must be posted in the Voter Information Guide, so voters have access to independent information about how programs are being managed and whether they actually need more funding. Voters deserve the ability to make informed decisions about new taxes without having to rely on information from special interests or politicians.
Q: Who pays for the audits?
A: If a tax measure is approved, the cost of the required audits is paid from the revenues generated by that measure. If voters reject the measure, the audit costs are paid through the state's General Fund.
Many statewide tax measures raise hundreds of millions - or even billions - of dollars over time. Prop 41 ensures a small investment in independent oversight helps taxpayers know whether those dollars are being spent effectively and producing the results promised.
Q: Who supports Prop 41?
Prop 41 is backed by a board coalition of small businesses, taxpayers, good government advocates, accountants, and auditing experts. Endorsers include the California Society of Certified Public Accountants, former State Controller Steve Westly, former California Auditor General Tom Hayes, the NAACP California-Hawaii State Conference, the California Alliance of Seniors, the California Chamber of Commerce, the California Farm Bureau, the California Taxpayers Association, the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, along with dozens of local chambers, taxpayer associations, and regional economic partnerships across the state.
Endorsements also include Democratic organizations and officials. The Chinese American Democratic Club, the San Bernardino Young Democrats, and the Sacramento State College Democrats have endorsed Prop 41, as has Steve Westly, a Democrat who served as State Controller. Local officials who have endorsed include Riverside County Auditor-Controller Ben Benoit and council members and mayors from across California. The full and current list of endorsers is at yesonprop41.org/endorsements (https://www.yesonprop41.org/endorsements) .
Q: How does Prop 41 strengthen taxpayer protections?
A: Prop 41 requires all future state tax measures to comply with California's voter-approved constitutional spending limit. That means future measures must follow the same constitutional rules that already apply to state spending including the requirement that excess revenues be refunded to taxpayers when the spending limit is exceeded.
Prop 41 provides for consistent application of the spending limit, so future state tax measures follow the same constitutional rules that already govern state spending, including the requirement that excess revenues be refunded to taxpayers.

I'm not going to pick a side for you on a partisan tax fight like this one. In yes/no form, though, it comes down to what you think about Prop 40, the billionaire tax:

- **If you want Prop 40 to take effect, vote No on 41.** Prop 41 is built to cancel it. If both pass and 41 gets more yes votes, Prop 40 is thrown out.
- **If you oppose Prop 40, it's a real judgment call.** You don't need 41 to beat 40; voting No on 40 does that. So 41 comes down to its own merits:
  - Vote **Yes** if you want every future state tax held to the 1979 state spending cap (the "Gann limit") and subject to required audits.
  - Vote **No** if you'd rather the state keep that flexibility.

**What Prop 41 does**
- Some ballot initiatives propose a "special tax," meaning the money can only go to a specific purpose. Once one of those campaigns has 25% of its signatures, the State Auditor must audit the programs it would fund. A summary goes in the voter guide, including ideas for cutting costs at least 10% a year.
- Programs paid for by special taxes passed on or after Jan 1, 2026 get audited again every 4 years.
- The state can't collect any tax passed on or after Jan 1, 2026 if its money is kept outside the spending cap. Under the cap, money above the limit for two years in a row gets split between taxpayer refunds and schools. Prop 40 is written to keep its money outside the cap, which is why the two conflict.
- It's a constitutional amendment, so only voters could change it later.
- The Legislative Analyst's Office (the state's nonpartisan budget office) puts audit costs in the low millions per year, rising over time and mostly paid from the new taxes. There could be some savings, and the overall cost is unknown.

**Best case for Yes**
- Voters would get independent information before approving new taxes for specific programs. Supporters point to a 2024 state audit that found about $24B in homelessness spending wasn't consistently tracked.
- New taxes couldn't sidestep a spending cap voters approved, so extra money would go to refunds and schools.
- The cost is small, and the 10% is a recommendation, not a required cut.

**Best case for No**
- Its main job this year is to kill Prop 40. The SF Chronicle wrote that "you don't have to support the billionaire tax" to see it as a poison pill.
- It permanently ties all future state taxes to a 1979 formula, making it harder to respond to things like wildfires or federal funding cuts. The Mercury News opposes Prop 40 and still opposes 41 for this reason.
- The audits mostly repeat work the State Auditor and Legislative Analyst already do, and the 10% target could make tax measures look bad in the voter guide.
- It might spill over onto taxes and fees that help fund Medi-Cal. The California Budget & Policy Center says that's possible but uncertain and would be up to the courts. The scarier claims, like a threat to Prop 3, come from the professors who wrote Prop 40.

**Who's on each side**
- **Yes:** CA Republican Party, CA Chamber of Commerce, CalTax, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the state CPA society, a former State Auditor, former Controller Steve Westly, and the San Diego Union-Tribune and OC Register. Almost all the money comes from a group funded by Google co-founder Sergey Brin.
- **No:** CA Democratic Party, the SEIU health care workers' union that put Prop 40 on the ballot, League of Women Voters (neutral on 40), ACLU SoCal, labor groups, SF Chronicle, Sacramento Bee and Mercury News.
- **Newsom:** no position on 41. He opposes 40 and supports Prop 42, which would also cancel it.

**Polls:** In late October, Berkeley IGS had Prop 41 at 38% yes, 47% no, and PPIC had it at 48% yes, 49% no. Prop 40 was also behind in both, and Prop 42 was polling better than 41.
